posts.title: What’s New in vcpkg (Oct 2026)
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
This blog post summarizes changes to the vcpkg package manager as part of the 2026-10-16 registry release and the 2026-09-26 tool release. These updates include configurable binary-cache compression, improved cache reliability and diagnostics, Boost 1.92, and other improvements and bug fixes.
There are now 2,877 total ports available in the vcpkg curated registry. A port is a versioned recipe for building a package from source, such as a C or C++ library.
41 new ports were added to the curated registry since the July registry release.
806 ports were updated between the July and October registry releases. As always, we validate each change to a port by building all other ports that depend on or are depended by the library that is being updated for our main triplets.
178 community contributors submitted merged PRs included in this release.
The main vcpkg repo has approximately 7,800 forks and 27,600 stars on GitHub.
vcpkg changelog (2026.10.16 release)
Tool improvements
Choose your binary-cache compression level. Use --binary-cache-compression-level=<0-9> or VCPKG_BINARY_CACHE_COMPRESSION_LEVEL to trade ZIP archive size for cache submission time. The command-line option takes precedence. Leaving both unset preserves the default compression level, and the setting does not change package ABIs or prevent restoration of existing archives. NuGet packaging is unaffected (PR: Microsoft/vcpkg-tool#2125, thanks @xiaozhuai!). For example, select a lower compression level when saving ZIP-based binary-cache archives: vcpkg install --binary-cache-compression-level=1
Fixed binary cache prechecks assigning provider results to the wrong packages after filtering the action list, improving cache availability reporting (PR: Microsoft/vcpkg-tool#2112, thanks @miyanyan!).
Standardized binary cache upload failure diagnostics to make cache submission problems easier to identify (PR: Microsoft/vcpkg-tool#2105, thanks @xiaozhuai!).
Preserved underlying registry errors instead of replacing them with a misleading “<port> does not exist” message (PR: Microsoft/vcpkg-tool#2095, thanks @bugale!).
Added the apple platform expression for port metadata, allowing one expression to cover Apple target platforms (PR: Microsoft/vcpkg-tool#2121, thanks @cqundefine!).
Propagated VCPKG_SSL_REVOKE_BEST_EFFORT to spawned processes so the certificate-revocation setting applies consistently (PR: Microsoft/vcpkg-tool#2098, thanks @mem16k!).
Improved Windows bootstrap proxy handling: if malformed HTTPS_PROXY or NO_PROXY settings cause an invalid parameter error, the helper warns and retries using the current user’s explicit Windows proxy settings, or a direct connection if none is configured (PR: Microsoft/vcpkg-tool#2137, thanks @camillebruckmann!).
Fixed NuGet exports to include vcpkg.exe in the generated package (PR: Microsoft/vcpkg-tool#2134).
Made x-add-version updates transactional so an error does not leave partially updated version metadata, while also reducing unnecessary work when processing unchanged ports (PR: Microsoft/vcpkg-tool#2050).
Notable port updates
Boost: 1.91.0 -> 1.92.0, updating the Boost collection of C++ libraries.
curl: 8.21.0#1 -> 8.23.0, updating a widely used networking library.
OpenSSL: 3.6.3 -> 3.6.5#2, refreshing the cryptography and TLS dependency.
libgit2: 1.9.4#1 -> 1.9.7, updating the Git implementation library.
Qt Base: 6.11.1#1 -> 6.11.2, updating the core Qt framework port.
Vulkan SDK components: 1.4.350.0 -> 1.4.357.0, with Vulkan headers updated from 1.4.350.1 -> 1.4.363.0.
Armadillo: 14.4.1#1 -> 15.6.1, bringing a new major version of the linear algebra library.
SDL 3: 3.4.12 -> 3.4.18, updating the cross-platform multimedia library.
22 ports were removed as part of registry maintenance: cppdap, ctp, dx, keccak-tiny, kf5diagram, libfreenect2, qtquickcontrols2, rapidfuzz, sdl1, sdl1-mixer, sdl1-net, septag-sx, shiftmedia-libgnutls, sqlpp11-connector-mysql, sqlpp11-connector-sqlite3, tensorflow, tensorflow-cc, tensorflow-common, threadpool, v8, vcpkg-tool-bazel, and vulkan-hpp.
Other minor improvements and bug fixes.
Documentation updates
The following documentation changes were published recently:
Documented VcpkgManifestInstalledBaseDir for MSBuild solutions that use manifest mode and build multiple triplets, allowing a shared installation base directory with triplet-specific subdirectories (PR: MicrosoftDocs/vcpkg-docs#588, thanks @autoantwort!).
Documented VCPKG_PROVIDED_FORTRAN, including its defaults and how custom triplets can select a different Fortran compiler (PR: MicrosoftDocs/vcpkg-docs#600).
Added documentation for vcpkg print-usage, which displays usage information for installed packages (PR: MicrosoftDocs/vcpkg-docs#599).
Documented the CURL_CA_BUNDLE environment variable for configuring the certificate authority bundle used for downloads (PR: MicrosoftDocs/vcpkg-docs#587).
Expanded the platform-expression reference with the apple and bsd platform families, additional platform identifiers, and the corrected Xbox target condition (PR: MicrosoftDocs/vcpkg-docs#612).
Documented --binary-cache-compression-level=<0-9> and VCPKG_BINARY_CACHE_COMPRESSION_LEVEL, including precedence, defaults, accepted values, and compatibility with existing cache entries (PR: MicrosoftDocs/vcpkg-docs#613, thanks @xiaozhuai!).
Clarified how a repository-level nuget.config containing <clear /> can remove inherited binary-cache sources and cause authentication failures, with guidance for keeping the authenticated source in the effective configuration (PR: MicrosoftDocs/vcpkg-docs#614, thanks @hoshiizumiya!).
Updated GitHub Actions examples to pin actions to full commit SHAs instead of version tags (PR: MicrosoftDocs/vcpkg-docs#617).
Updated the maintainer guide with a policy for AI-reported bugs in new ports: report findings upstream, accept upstream’s assessment, and close the new port submission if upstream does not respond within 30 days. The update also clarifies terminology and other maintainer guidance (PR: MicrosoftDocs/vcpkg-docs#615).

posts.title: Catching Bugs Before They Land: JiTTesting’s Human-on-the-Loop Approach at Full Scale
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Over the last year we’ve been sharing our work leveraging large language models to catch bugs on the fly — a novel approach we call Catching Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests).
Now, we’re sharing the results and positive impact we’ve seen with Catching JiTTests deployed into production.
Our paper, “Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta,” fully details our initial deployment and testing with Catching JiTTests.
Every code change improves our platform, but it also introduces new complexity. With hundreds of millions of lines of code constantly evolving at Meta, traditional testing can’t keep pace. Catching risks proactively, before code lands, enables us to identify risks earlier, respond more effectively, and deliver reliable experiences at scale.
Over the last year, we’ve shared our research into applying large language models (LLMs) to generate software tests. More specifically, we’ve shared our work with Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests), a novel testing approach where we leverage LLMs to catch bugs on the fly, even ones that traditional testing might not catch.
In the five months since we first unveiled this work, we’ve deployed our Catching JiTTests approach to determine its scalability and applicability to the wider industry. Today, Catching JiTTests are no longer a research prototype; they’re part of Meta’s infrastructure, and they’re helping our engineers catch more bugs with less load and a smaller chance of false positives.
The Advantage of Catching JiTTests
Most AI-based approaches to preventing bugs in code use LLMs and/or agentic AI to review code and detect faults based on prior experience. They work through the same review process that a human reviewer would, only faster. Catching JiTTests is a fundamentally different approach (Table 1): It generates executable tests that demonstrate a concrete behavioral difference introduced by the change. While it requires more computational steps, it catches classes of bugs that LLM- or agent-based code reviews might not.
Table 1. Key differences between traditional LLM-based code review and Catching JiTTests.
How We Implemented Catching JiTTests at Meta
JiTTests are automatically generated and designed to fail, surfacing bugs in code changes (diffs) before they land in production. When they’re applied to a codebase as large as Meta’s, one challenge is distinguishing strong catches (i.e., true-positive failures that reveal real bugs) from weak catches (i.e., tests that may be false positives).
It boils down to a specific question: For every proposed diff, how can we automatically generate tests that find the most severe bugs before they cause severe issues, and do so with a high true-positive rate and without impeding the velocity of our engineers?
To address this, we developed two tandem workflows:
An “intent-aware” workflow that infers the intention and risks of a code change and targets test generation toward likely failure points.
A “dodgy diff” workflow that treats every code change as if it were a mutant/bug and generates tests to expose its behavioral differences without reasoning about intent. It implicitly asserts that a diff is buggy (hence the term “dodgy”).
Figure 1. The architecture of the dodgy diff and intent-aware workflows for Catching JiTTests.
To filter false positives, we employed a traditional rule-based approach combined with an ensemble approach we call “LLM-as-Judge,” which aggregates judgements from several state-of-the-art (SOTA) LLMs, all tasked with classifying weak catches as likely true or false positives.
We also maintained human review, with an eye toward reducing review load. Our goal is to maintain the consistency of human labeling but reduce the likelihood of an engineer being brought in to review a weak catch.
How It Works
The entire system workflow happens in five stages:
Stage 1: Targeting and Triggering 
The system runs overnight on spare capacity and targets diffs submitted the previous day that are deemed “risky” using a mechanism similar to Diff Risk Score (DRS) and trained on previous code changes. This helps ensure test generation is focused on diffs that are most likely to contain severe regressions.
Stage 2: Two Diff-Aware Test-Generation Workflows
The dodgy diff workflow treats each diff as if it were a mutant and uses mutation-guided LLM-based test generation to produce tests that distinguish the diff’s behavior from its parent. The goal here is to maximize the pool of weak catches and with it the chances of finding a strong catch among them.
At the same time, the intent-aware workflow uses an LLM to infer the diff’s intention using the code changes, diff title, and summary. The LLM then describes the “risks”— the ways an attempt to implement the intent could produce errors. It then uses those risk descriptions to construct mutants — each representing a bug that could be introduced while implementing the inferred intent.
Tests are generated to kill each mutant (i.e., distinguish mutant behavior from parent).
Those tests are then run on the actual diff. Any that fail are harvested as weak catches.
Stage 3: LLM-as-Judge Ensemble (Automated Assessment)
Once weak catches are generated, the system must determine whether each is a false positive or actually a strong catch (true positive).
The LLM-as-Judge ensemble consists of a collection of LLMs that review:
The weak-catch test-case code.
The test-execution outcome (failure code, message, execution trace).
The code changes between parent and child (the diff).
The inferred diff intent.
Stage 4: Rule-Based Assessor (RubFake)
We complement LLM-as-Judge with a more traditional, rule-based approach called Rule-Based False-Positive Killing Environment (RubFake).
LLM-as-Judge has rich semantics, but its judgements are non-deterministic and challenging to verify. By contrast, RubFake provides verified, deterministic judgments. Working together, RubFake and LLM-as-Judge produce an overall ranking of weak-catch candidates, with those ranked sufficiently highly being worthy of further consideration.
Stage 5: Human-on-the-Loop (Engineer Reach-Out)
Based on the ranking from LLM-as-Judge and RubFake, the system then decides whether to reach out to human engineers.
Rather than a human-in-the-loop approach, where a human engineer reviews every output, we’ve reduced friction through a human-on-the-loop approach, where human engineers set criteria and review outcomes at an aggregate level rather than supervising every output.
Table 2. Operational differences between human-in-the-loop and human-on-the-loop approaches.
The Impact of Catching JiTTests at Meta
With the testing system in place, our goal is to get engineers to engage with its results.
As of this writing, 589 engineers at Meta (64% of our outreach) have engaged with Catching JiTTests. These engineers have reported that Catching JiTTests surfaces genuinely actionable findings, with a 60% rate of true positives.
In the first half of 2026, Catching JiTTests played a key role in catching 74 serious (SEV) privacy bugs at the diff stage, before they landed in production and lowering the overall occurrence of privacy SEVs by 20% during that timeframe.
Figure 2. The impact of Catching JiTTests at Meta in the first half of 2026.
Why It Matters
Agentic software development is helping engineers and developers across the industry write, review, and ship code faster than ever before. But faster deployment means there’s also a need for faster testing. Every bug caught before it reaches production is one that end users never need to deal with. We’ve shown that LLMs can provide an additional safety layer capable of catching what traditional tests may miss, demonstrating that AI-generated testing can scale enough to reduce organizational risk. 
Catching JiTTests is a solution that is scalable, both technologically and socially. Combining these tests with a human-on-the-loop approach helps ensure that engineers rarely need to read test code and only need to confirm whether an observed behavioral change was intended.
The approach is generalizable: Engineers define success criteria early, let AI execute the testing, monitor the outcomes at an aggregate level, and intervene at the policy level rather than per item.
Read the Paper
Our paper, “Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta,” which was presented at FSE 2026 and featured at Product@Scale, details our initial deployment and testing with Catching JiTTests in Meta’s infrastructure.

posts.title: Meta Andromeda: Powering the Next Generation of Ads Retrieval Through Model-System Co-Design
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
This post describes the next generation of Meta Andromeda, Meta’s personalized ads retrieval engine, and how co-designing the model, system, and GPU hardware unlocks a new efficiency frontier for ads retrieval.
In production, the system scores every eligible ad with near ranking-level model performance at retrieval scale and surfaces the top candidates at over one billion ads per second, a new throughput benchmark for ads retrieval-stage models (i.e., a 100x lift compared to the 2024 Meta Andromeda system).
For advertisers, this means better performance automatically from the retrieval system matching ads across a larger candidate pool, within the same latency budget. Since 2025, Meta Andromeda has delivered a 2.4% increase in conversions on Facebook.
Meta Andromeda is Meta’s machine learning system for personalized ads retrieval, the first stage of the ads recommendation pipeline. Retrieval narrows a vast pool of eligible ads down to a small set of strong candidates in milliseconds; a later, more computationally expensive ranking stage then scores those survivors in fine detail. 
Historically, the deep modeling quality of the ranking stage has been too costly to apply at retrieval’s scale. Building on the retrieval foundation established with Andromeda’s 2024 launch on the NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper Superchip, this post shares how co-designing the model, system, and hardware together brings near ranking-level performance to the retrieval scale.
Challenges and Opportunities in Scaling Retrieval
The 2024 Andromeda deployment reimplemented retrieval with an end-to-end optimized retrieval implementation from custom AI hardware with hierarchical indexing and GPU-native operators to a purpose-built ML model, growing model capacity by four orders of magnitude. Since then, generative AI creative tools have helped advertisers rapidly create hundreds of millions of new ads, growing Meta’s ads candidate pool to an unprecedented scale. 
Scoring such a large ad candidate pool with a more accurate model at a much higher system throughput requires fundamental technology breakthroughs in model quality, system architecture, and hardware utilization jointly. 
Higher Model Performance Requires a New Architecture 
Ads retrieval has an outsized ROI on incremental quality: Small improvements in retrieval model performance can drive large gains in advertiser value. The rapid expansion of our ads candidate pool makes optimizing for hardware capacity ROI an increasingly critical factor. The 2024 Meta Andromeda retrieval models have established a highly effective foundation with their GPU-optimized deep neural network architecture. To keep improving retrieval performance at a sustainable compute cost at our current scale, however, we must move beyond that paradigm. This requires a fundamental architectural evolution to push model performance boundaries significantly without a proportional increase in costs.
New System Bottlenecks at Billion Scale 
The 2024 Meta Andromeda system evaluates at tens of millions of ads per second per GPU card. Meeting the new business demand requires a throughput at multi-billion ads evaluated per second per card in the system. At billions of ads per second throughput, the memory bandwidth of passing ad tensors through memory hierarchy becomes the new bottleneck. Intermediate tensors between GPU kernels account for terabytes per second of memory traffic, and shipping ads between local CPU hosts and remote hardware accelerators evaluating models saturates the network link. This requires a new system co-design that unifies these fragmented, distributed workloads into a single GPU pipeline.
Pushing Towards the Hardware Limits 
With retrieval running on GPU, the important optimization question is “How close are we to the hardware ceiling, and how much room remains for future model growth?” Answering this requires pushing each component of the retrieval pipeline to the limits of the current hardware generation, a challenge that motivated a joint collaboration with NVIDIA.
Each of these challenges drove a corresponding advance.
Unlocking Retrieval Performance Through Model-System Co-Design
Next-Gen Retrieval Model Architecture — Retrieval Mixture-of-Experts 
The latest iteration of Meta Andromeda introduces three synergistic architectural innovations that bring large language model (LLM)-inspired mixture-of-experts (MoE) into the retrieval (see Figure 1). With this highly expressive yet inference-efficient architecture, a new retrieval performance-efficiency Pareto frontier has been established: model performance approaches ranking-level in a typical retrieval-then-ranking system, at approximately 300x fewer inference-time FLOPs than the 2024 Meta Andromeda retrieval model.
On the user modeling side, we transitioned from a single user tower to an ensemble of specialized user towers as experts. This captures diverse, time-evolving, and contextualized user interests by integrating a vast array of high-fidelity signals: sequential ad engagement events, user-cohort representations, LLM-derived semantic features, and cross-surface co-engagement signals.
In the candidate ads tower, we employ a joint encoding strategy that incorporates real-time serving context, ensuring that downstream interaction models receive context-aware representations.
In the interaction overarch layer, the interaction model evolved from dense neural networks into an MoE attention-based gating network that dynamically routes candidates across the most relevant user experts, delivering near-ranking-level performance at a fraction of the FLOPs.
A defining property of the new architecture is that its performance is co-designed with the underlying hardware execution model. Model inference throughput has reached over 10 billion ads per second on a single GH200 GPU, and this efficiency allows model capacity to grow further, through richer feature interactions, additional expert sub-networks, and deeper architectures, without a proportional increase in GPU cost. Each incremental model advancement translates into greater advertiser value.
 
Figure 1: Retrieval MoE architecture. Diverse high-fidelity user signals feed an ensemble of heterogeneous user experts. Ad content fused with real-time serving context forms a contextualized ad input that drives an ad-aware MoE router, activating only the top-K most relevant experts to produce the user–ad relevance score. The result is ranking-level matching quality at retrieval scale — ~300x fewer inference-time FLOPs than the 2024 Meta Andromeda and over 10 billion ads/sec on a single Grace Hopper Superchip.
Co-Designing the Model and System Onto a Single GPU Pipeline
The 2026 Meta Andromeda pushes the model-system co-design to the next level with two innovations — a single GPU kernel fusing both model and system workloads per user-ad interaction and a strategy to co-locate per user request logics with per user-ad GPU kernels in a single GPU box. To this end, a highly optimized and fully fused GPU pipeline is built to host the entire end-to-end Meta Andromeda workflow.
Fused Kernel
At a high level, Meta Andromeda’s inference time per user-ad workload is a compact sequence of operations across model execution and system logics — gathering embeddings, executing user-ad interaction models, and scoring. The ~300x FLOPs reduction in the retrieval MoE gating architecture creates the necessary headroom and is less resistant to fully fuse both model execution and non-model system workloads into a single GPU kernel, compared to the 2024 launch where only operations within the model execution were fused. Consequently, the fused kernel now runs at over 10 billion ads per second on a single GH200.
This matters because retrieval workloads are fundamentally memory-bandwidth bound. At billions of ads per second, even a small intermediate tensor per ad multiplies into terabytes per second of high bandwidth memory (HBM) traffic. The memory workload of these intermediate tensors, not arithmetic, becomes the dominant bottleneck in multi-kernel retrieval pipelines.
The fused kernel eliminates this bottleneck entirely. Rather than dispatching multiple small GPU kernels for model and system operations, it executes the entire per user-ad computation in one pass. Intermediate results stay in GPU registers and thread block shared memory and are never materialized to HBM, achieving high utilization of the GPU’s peak memory bandwidth rather than wasting it on redundant intermediate traffic. 
Co-Location Strategy
Measured in isolation, the per user-ad fused kernel runs at multi-billion ads per second on a single GPU. However, per-user request operations such as the index matching (i.e., enforcing advertisers’ targeting rules) and top-K selection run on separate local CPU hosts and communicate with the fused GPU kernel scoring service on remote accelerators through the network connection. At multi-billion ads per second throughput, this traffic alone saturates the network link, making the network bandwidth become the bottleneck rather than GPU compute.
The co-design response was to collapse the system architecture to match the model architecture: co-locate index matching, scoring, and top-K selection on the same GPU. Instead of shipping large candidate lists across hosts, the system sends a compact request payload — user features and a targeting query — to a single GPU server, which runs the entire retrieval pipeline locally and returns only the final top-K results. This reduces network traffic by ~100x and shifts the system back to a GPU-compute-bound regime.
Moving index matching onto the GPU is not straightforward. Ads index matching evaluates complex advertiser-defined targeting logic across tens of feature categories, and must support real-time index updates as ads are created, modified, or expired throughout the day. Supporting this on GPU required redesigning the index structure for GPU-parallel execution while preserving the full fidelity of production targeting semantics.
A Single GPU Pipeline for Meta Andromeda
Combining the aforementioned two innovations, the fully co-located single GPU pipeline processes over one billion ads per second on a single GPU server while scoring every eligible ad in the candidate pool. This is a new throughput benchmark for ads retrieval-stage models, and as the next section describes, significant headroom remains.
Figure 2: System architecture of the single fused GPU pipeline for Meta Andromeda. This pipeline co-locates index matching, fused scoring, and top-K selection on a single GPU server. The fused scoring kernel executes the entire per-user-ad computation — from embedding gathering to MoE interaction and scoring — in a single on-chip pass, keeping intermediate results in registers and shared memory to eliminate HBM bottlenecks. This co-design reduces network traffic by approximately 100x by sending only compact request payloads — surpassing 1 billion ads per second while scoring every eligible ad across Facebook and Instagram.
GPU-Accelerated Retrieval: The Meta-NVIDIA Collaboration
With the production pipeline running at over one billion ads per second, a natural question follows: How close is the system to the ceiling of the current generation hardware, and how much headroom remains for future model growth? In early 2026, Meta and NVIDIA launched a joint collaboration to answer this question — systematically optimizing each component of the retrieval pipeline to push throughput toward hardware limits. NVIDIA contributed optimized GPU kernels, and Meta integrated and benchmarked the full pipeline. Each component achieved 2x to 5x speedup over the baseline.
Interaction Network (Retrieval MoE Gating Network)
The optimized gating kernel improved by 5.3x, from 2.4 billion to over 10 billion ads per second, reaching ~85% of the GPU’s peak HBM bandwidth. At this throughput, the execution time / latency of the gating mechanism is just as fast as what a simple dot-product scoring kernel achieves on the same hardware — while the model is substantially more expressive. This is the co-design validation: the additional model complexity is essentially free on Tensor Core hardware. INT8 quantization achieved a further up to 2x throughput increase over the optimized FP16 kernels, with accuracy on par with 16-bit precision.
Index Matching
Through targeted GPU kernel optimizations, index matching throughput improved over 2x, reaching over 100 billion ads per second — an order of magnitude higher than the scoring network. This headroom means index matching can be re-run across multiple retrieval pathways without becoming a bottleneck.
End-to-End GPU Pipeline
Beyond individual kernels, the collaboration profiled the full retrieval flow and identified that data movement between pipeline components — not computation — accounted for a significant fraction of end-to-end latency. By co-designing data layouts across index matching and scoring to eliminate unnecessary indirection, the team removed this overhead. With all optimizations applied, the full pipeline benchmarks at multiple times the current production throughput on a single GPU server, with further gains expected as additional optimizations integrate into production.
Figure 3: Optimized ads/sec for interaction network, index matching, and E2E pipeline.
Continuing Work on Next-Generation NVIDIA Platforms
Building on the Hopper results above, we are extending our optimization and co-design work to Grace Blackwell. Here, we are focusing on platform design optimizations that enable different CPU-to-GPU compute ratios, which our work so far suggests is an important factor for Andromeda-like workloads. We are evaluating how sensitive end-to-end application performance is to these ratios, using Grace-class CPU performance and Blackwell-class GPU performance for their respective parts of the workload.
More broadly, we are exploring how these findings extend to the next platform generation, where greater flexibility in CPU+GPU execution, resource ratios, and coupling could bring more of these architectural improvements to bear on Andromeda-like workloads.
These results confirm that the co-designed retrieval pipeline is not yet at its ceiling. With quantization unlocking further scoring throughput and index matching operating at an order of magnitude above the scoring network, the architecture is positioned to absorb significantly more model complexity — deeper interaction networks, richer feature spaces, and additional retrieval pathways — without proportional infrastructure growth.
The Path Forward for Ads Retrieval
The advances described here follow a single principle: The largest gains come from designing model, system, and hardware as one integrated stack, rather than optimizing each in isolation. The retrieval MoE gating architecture delivers near-ranking-level expressiveness at no additional serving cost. Fusing the entire retrieval pipeline onto a single GPU eliminates network and memory bottlenecks. And pushing the pipeline towards its hardware ceiling confirms substantial headroom remains.
Looking ahead, the co-design principle that drove these results applies equally to next-generation model architectures and hardware platforms, with the demonstrated headroom enabling continued scaling without proportional infrastructure growth.
For people who use Meta’s products, this translates directly into better ads that are more relevant to them, delivered within the same latency budget. For advertisers, it means better customer matches and more conversions. For Meta, it means increased business from advertisers and lower costs, as each GPU now evaluates more ads per second. As the volume of eligible ads continues to grow, driven by Advantage+ automation and generative AI creative tools, Meta Andromeda’s co-designed architecture scales to meet it.
Acknowledgements
We would like to thank Gosh Arzumanyan, Habiya Beg, Andrew Bocking, Zain Brohi, Rohit Chandel, Claire Chen, Jason Chen, Wenlin Chen, Zhenyu Chen, Yuze Dai, Zhou Fang, Junjie Feng, Stephen Fitz, Chunli Fu, Yicong Fu, Xiaorui Gan, Sohan Gantala, Yingsheng Gao, Golnaz Ghasemiesfeh, Ishu Goyal, Wentian Guo, George Han, Yihan He, Jun Hu, Xuan Hu, Kun Huang, Qin Huang, Tianchen Ji, Crystal Jin, Tao Ju, Rajat Karnwal, Santanu Kolay, Michael Kwan, Ilia Lewis, Baiyu Li, Chao Li, Jim Li, Li Li, Lin Li, Liyuan Li, Mingda Li, Ted Li, Xiaotian Li, Yanyu Liang, Yue Liang, Irene Liu, Gaoxiang Liu, Jason Liu, Siqi Liu, Wei Liu, Xiao Liu, Yuheng Long, Yining Lu, Siyi Luo, Anuj Madan, Swaroop Manjunath, Phalguna Mankar, Jiachen Mao, Yuji Mo, GP Musumeci, Guruswamy Namasivayam, Kexin Nie, Sandeep Pandey, Uladzimir Pashkevich, Clementine Plati, Heng Qiao, Hang Qu, Lei Qu, Anand Rajan, Jatin Sethi, Puneet Sharma, Ruchit Sharma, Yan Shi, Chang Shu, Sean Song, Alec Stashevsky, Matt Steiner, Zheng Sun, Nikhil Vinayak Supekar, Jim Tao, Chintan Thakkar, Tian Tong, Aleksandr Ulanov, Daksh Vasistha, Simha Venkataramaiah, Arunprasad Venkatraman, Abhishek Verma, Ruud Vinke, Vidhoon Viswanathan, Sasha Vorontsov, Eric Walden, Dong Wang, Feng Wang, Haole Wang, Jeff Wang, Senhong Wang, Ye Wang, Di Wu, Haocheng Wu, Shawn Wu, Jimmy Xiang, Nan Xiao, Ruichao Xiao, Chao Xie, Yudi Xie, Fangzhou Xu, Nathan Yan, Tak Yan, Hang Yang, Song Yang, Yuhan Yang, Yavuz Yetim, Bowen Yu, Li Yu, Qifan Yuan, Xiaodong Yuan, Lin Zeng, Siqi (Cindy) Zeng, Caijie Zhang, Joanna Zhang, Min Zhang, Qing Zhang, Zhengkai Zhang, Fangyu Zou, and the entire v-team behind the success of Meta Andromeda.

posts.title: PrivacyLib: Privacy Controls at the Data Access Boundary
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
This latest deep dive into Meta’s Privacy Aware Infrastructure (PAI) takes a look at PrivacyLib. 
A privacy requirement must hold as data moves through Meta’s diverse data and processing systems. Historically, supporting a new requirement meant implementing the same enforcement logic separately in each system. PrivacyLib replaces this with a common library that runs inside the clients of Meta’s data and processing systems.
A system integrates with PrivacyLib once, and new privacy capabilities plug in as modules that reuse that integration. PrivacyLib performs billions of checks every second, and changes are simulated and rolled out per module. 
For internal AI agents, whose data access paths may not be known in advance, tool calls on supported paths carry agent context to PrivacyLib. The propagated context links each access to its session, so modules can observe data use and block operations that are not allowed.
At Meta, many privacy requirements ultimately come down to the same question: Can we prove that a piece of data goes only where it is allowed? At Meta’s scale, rather than relying solely on manual privacy audits, which can go out of sync as systems change, we have developed Privacy Aware Infrastructure (PAI) to answer this question within the infrastructure itself. PAI offers efficient and reliable first-class privacy constructs embedded in Meta’s infrastructure so that products can keep evolving quickly.
In previous posts, we have covered how data understanding, data lineage, and Policy Zones (our information flow control technology) play a role in PAI. Now, we are diving deep into PrivacyLib, a common library that runs inside the clients of hundreds of our data and processing systems at the point of data access.
PrivacyLib plays an important role in the final stage of the broader PAI workflow: continuously enforcing and monitoring data flows.
This blog post focuses on PrivacyLib’s role in the final stage of the PAI workflow.
Before PrivacyLib, we integrated privacy enforcement separately into the clients of each data and processing system for each requirement. With this approach, implementing a new requirement across systems could take months. Each new requirement, whether purpose limitation or data flow discovery, needed the same set of capabilities: covering a wide range of systems; deploying in weeks rather than months; running on every data access without becoming a latency problem; and rolling out enforcement changes without taking the fleet down. Over time, this approach became harder to scale as requirements and systems evolved.
PrivacyLib separates system integration from requirement implementation. We integrate each system once. When a requirement can be met at the point of data access, we implement it as a PrivacyLib module shared across the systems already integrated, so a new requirement no longer needs a separate implementation in each system. 
There are two kinds of modules: 
Enforcing modules can block a data access. For example, Policy Zones enforces purpose limitation.
Observing modules only record a data access. For example, Privacy Probes collects the runtime signals used to discover data flows. 
As internal AI agents became a new way of accessing data, we also added the Agent Observability module to observe agent-related data access events and help safeguard the data that agents can reach. Systems already integrated with PrivacyLib picked it up without new integration work, which is what integrating once buys: each new privacy capability arrives as a module, not as a project.
PrivacyLib replaces repeated implementations across systems.
Engineering Challenges and Approaches of PrivacyLib at Meta’s Scale
PrivacyLib operates across a broad range of data access paths at Meta:
More than a hundred libraries used to access data services, from key/value stores to AI features.
Thousands of production services with versions of the deployed library.
Millions of assets being accessed daily.
Billions of checks every second.
Operating at this scale creates three engineering challenges:
Challenge
Approach


Coverage: Systems can have multiple client libraries and legacy integrations, accept direct network calls, and offer direct database access to backing stores. All of them need to be handled to ensure requirements hold no matter the access path.
We integrate at two levels: typed client libraries, where PrivacyLib has full request context, and lower network boundaries on remaining RPC paths to get full coverage. Each integrated system maps its native APIs to PrivacyLib’s common operations and provides the inputs required by its configured modules. Once those pieces are in place, the same module can be enabled in multiple systems without a separate system-specific integration.


Scale: At billions of checks per second, even a small per-check computational cost becomes consequential across the fleet. Every service in the hot path pays that cost.
We compile requirements at build time into their simplest evaluable form and answer most checks from caches inside the process, so the common path avoids a network call.


Reliability: Privacy logic runs in the hot path of critical systems, owned by teams that release on their own schedules. A change has to be testable in isolation and reversible on its own, because a fleet-wide rollback cannot be the recovery path.
Enforcement is deployed as part of the service that owns it, so a change reaches production through that service’s own pipeline instead of a fleet-wide config push.





To illustrate how everything comes together at Meta’s scale, let’s walk through a privacy requirement that needs to be upheld when processing messaging metadata.
Users exchange messages through apps like Messenger, which supports end-to-end encryption. As Messenger routes and delivers those messages, subject to applicable law, its backend systems process non-content messaging data (i.e., messaging metadata), such as information about when messages are sent or delivered, to improve product performance, detect abuse, and protect users from harmful conduct. 
A variety of these backend services use Logger, a client library that runs in the service process, to write this metadata to data warehouse tables. Before writing a record, the PrivacyLib integration inside Logger invokes Policy Zones, an enforcing module, to check whether the metadata may flow to the destination table. This check is broken down into two parts: what inputs need to be available to make a decision, and how the check is actually evaluated at runtime. After examining these two parts, we look at how PrivacyLib scales across systems and how changes roll out without disrupting the services in the path.
PrivacyLib runs inside Logger’s client in the messaging backend service. It combines the request context with the generated destination metadata, invokes the modules configured for the write, and returns the enforcement decision to Logger.
Annotating Messaging Metadata
Every Logger destination table has a LoggerConfig that describes the records written to it. MetadataTraceLoggerConfig defines one such configuration for message-delivery traces and marks it as containing messaging metadata:
final class MetadataTraceLoggerConfig extends LoggerConfigBase {
  use MessagingTrafficMetadataPolicyTrait;
  public function configure(
    LoggerFieldDefiner $fd,
  ): LoggerFieldDefiner {
    $this->annotateWithTableLevelPolicy();
    // Field and destination definitions
  }
}
A logging destination can have many writers, so the annotation describing its output data belongs to the destination rather than to each service that writes to it. If every service declared the annotation separately, the declarations could disagree, or a new writer could omit it entirely. Declaring it once in LoggerConfig gives every writer the same description of the data.
For this destination, MessagingTrafficMetadataPolicyTrait supplies the MESSAGING_TRAFFIC_METADATA table-level annotation, and annotateWithTableLevelPolicy() attaches it to the destination.
LoggerConfig is Logger’s own schema, and each system describes its data in its own format. To give PrivacyLib a single form to consume, Logger’s code-generation pipeline translates the configuration into a PrivacyLib-compatible artifact. The generated MetadataTraceLoggerConfigPrivacyLibArtifact is derived from MetadataTraceLoggerConfig and carries the destination identity and the messaging annotation:
/**
 * @codegen-source MetadataTraceLoggerConfig
 */
class MetadataTraceLoggerConfigPrivacyLibArtifact
  extends LoggerInputPrivacyLibArtifact {
  
  final public static function getAssetIDImpl(
  ): LoggerInputAssetID {
    return LoggerInputAssetID::get(
      'MetadataTraceLoggerConfig',
    );
  }

  protected static function getPurposePolicyVars(
  ): TPurposePolicyVars {
    return PurposePolicy::makeVars(
      TPurposePolicyName::MESSAGING_TRAFFIC_METADATA,
    );
  }

  // Other generated fields omitted.
}
The generated class above is used by Logger’s client in Hack, Meta’s typed PHP language. For its C++ and Python clients, Logger publishes destination identities and annotations to a central catalog. PrivacyLib uses that information to generate language-specific artifacts. In the C++ example in the next section, PrivacyLib uses the LoggerConfig name to load the C++ artifact for the destination.  
Running the Check
The artifact from the previous section describes one Logger destination. PrivacyLib also needs to know what a Logger write means and which modules should run. Logger’s Hack integration defines that once for all destinations:
$config->libraryConfig()->enablePrivacyLib(
  PrivacyLibOperation::write()
    ->input(
      PrivacyLibInput::instance(
        nameof ILoggerInputPrivacyLibPayloadProvider,
      ),
    )
    ->enforcements(
      PrivacyLibWriteEnforcement::zones(
        ZoneDataType::LOGGER,
      )
        ->withPropagation()
        ->enabled(),
      PrivacyLibWriteEnforcement::telemetryLogging()->enabled(),
      // Other modules
    ),
);
PrivacyLibOperation::write() declares PrivacyLib’s write operation for Logger, and enforcements() lists the modules that run on it. The Policy Zones module can affect the result, while the Telemetry Logging module records the evaluation without affecting it. Adding a module here requires no changes to individual destinations or Logger call sites. ZoneDataType::LOGGER tells Policy Zones that it is checking a Logger destination.
In C++ services, Logger constructs the PrivacyLib request as follows: 
const auto assetList =
      std::vector<std::string>{configName};

PrivacyLibBuilder builder(
      "LOGGER_WRITE_CLIENT",
      assetList,
      LoggerWriteAPIEnumHelper::apiToHashedString(
          PolicyEnforcedLoggerWriteAPI::log),
      Caller::LOGGER,
      getLoggerWriteImplementation());

auto result =
      PrivacyLibRequest(std::move(builder)).dispatch();

PrivacyLib uses configName to load the destination’s artifact. The hashed PolicyEnforcedLoggerWriteAPI::log value maps Logger’s API to PrivacyLib’s write operation. The remaining builder arguments identify Logger as the caller and provide the implementation that performs the write. dispatch() invokes the configured modules and records their outcomes. For the Policy Zones module, PrivacyLib provides the destination annotations from the generated artifact and the current processing context. For this example, Policy Zones evaluates two conditions:
The current context represents an allowed use of messaging metadata.
The destination artifact carries the MESSAGING_TRAFFIC_METADATA annotation.
When enforcement is enabled, the Policy Zones module denies the write if either condition fails. PrivacyLib combines the results from enforcing modules into one response. A denial stops the write before Logger sends the record downstream. Observing modules emit telemetry without affecting the response.
A closer look at module evaluation on a Logger write.
Scaling Privacy Checks Across Systems
PrivacyLib enables privacy checks to scale across heterogeneous systems through a common execution model, lightweight evaluation and telemetry, and coverage for requests that bypass integrated clients. 
A Common Execution Model Across Systems
PrivacyLib’s integrations span systems with very different APIs: key-value stores, graph databases, ML pipelines, filesystems, and logging systems like Logger. Each integration maps its access points to one of five common operations, and PrivacyLib invokes its modules at each:
Read: runs when fetching data.
Write: runs when storing data.
RPC: runs when calling another service.
Request entry: runs once when a service begins handling a request.
Inline execution: wraps a specific computation inside a larger request, such as evaluating a feature. Data accesses made during that computation are evaluated using its inline privacy context.
Modules are written against these five operations rather than against each system’s native API. Reads, writes, and RPCs also have post-operation variants, so observing modules can run after the access decision has been made. Once a system provides the mapping, every compatible module can reuse it, which is why enabling an additional module on an already-integrated system takes only days.
PrivacyLib runs inside the clients of data and processing systems because the clients already have the destination identity and request context that modules need. Keeping the evaluation in the same process avoids carrying those inputs across process boundaries on every access. This design also has two advantages:
Richer context: PrivacyLib can use the caller’s identity, endpoint, and purpose while that information is still available. This information is frequently lost if the check is evaluated on the datastore.
Failure isolation: A faulty change is contained to the service running that version of the code, keeping the shared datastore outside the failure boundary.
Keeping Checks Computationally Inexpensive
In-process evaluation must also be computationally efficient because it runs on every data access. Per-request caches eliminate repeated checks within a request and per-host caches retain frequently used configuration and results. This avoids the remote configuration fetch required by an earlier design (that fetch alone was thousands of times slower than the in-process path). The result is that PrivacyLib performs billions of checks per second across the fleet with low per-check latency, while consuming only a small fraction of Meta’s total compute capacity.
At PrivacyLib’s scale, telemetry must also remain lightweight. PrivacyLib records each module’s status, samples latency, and logs errors, giving us fleet-wide visibility into how enforcement is behaving in production. Recording every invocation in full detail would overwhelm the systems receiving those events, so the goal is to deduplicate repeated events while keeping rare ones visible. 
Two mechanisms work together to achieve this: Bloom filters on each host downsample high-volume patterns at a fixed rate, and fine-grained sampling rates adjust as traffic changes.
Covering Direct RPC Paths
Not every caller accesses data through a PrivacyLib-integrated client library; some issue raw RPCs. The RPC layer can still check those requests, but it sees far less context than the client does. PrivacyLib bridges that gap with a cryptographically-signed token: When a client-side check succeeds, PrivacyLib attaches the token to the request, and ServiceRouter validates it at a lower boundary for supported RPC traffic, confirming that the request already passed the richer client-side check.
When a request arrives at the RPC layer without a token, ServiceRouter falls back to a coarser check based only on the context visible in the network payload. Because that context is limited, the lower layer applies the strictest interpretation, choosing false positives over gaps. Between them, the two layers cover access through Meta-managed clients and supported RPC paths. Paths outside those boundaries are not covered by this mechanism and need their own PrivacyLib integration.
Together, the result is that evaluation stays local and computationally inexpensive wherever possible, with a coarser backstop where local evaluation is unavailable, and modules have one place to run across systems that otherwise share nothing. What remains is the harder operational question: how to change enforcement behavior without breaking live traffic or making incorrect access decisions.
Rolling Out Enforcement Changes Safely
Privacy requirements change over time. Updates to a destination’s annotation or an enforcing module can change whether a write is allowed. PrivacyLib has a safe rollout path for both types of changes.
Changing an Annotation
Adding or removing an annotation changes two lines in a LoggerConfig: the declaration that imports MessagingTrafficMetadataPolicyTrait and the call to annotateWithTableLevelPolicy(). Because the destination may have many writers, that two-line edit can begin blocking writes from many services at once.
Review is therefore built around showing the author and reviewers what the edit will actually do. During code review, Logger’s code-generation pipeline updates the destination’s PrivacyLib artifact. Simulations then replay observed data flows against both the new artifact and the existing one, and any flow whose result changes is reported. The source edit, the generated artifact, and the simulation results are reviewed together, so the decision rests on evidence of the change’s effect rather than only on reading the code change. If the simulation reports an unexpected change, reviewers hold the artifact before release.

Once approved, the artifact reaches services through their usual build and deployment pipeline. That gives two forms of visibility before the change is deployed, from the decision changes reported by the simulation and the generated code showing exactly what will be deployed, plus one form of control, since each service’s own deployment decides when the change reaches production. It also bounds the surface area: An issue found after deployment is limited to the services running that build.
The downside is that changes do not reach the entire fleet at once, making change propagation slower than a global configuration update. In practice, requirement owners use explicit tracking to update the services in scope by the required deadline, while a service that needs the update sooner can use its emergency deployment process.
Simulation reveals decision changes before release, while independent service deployments control timing to limit production impact.
Rolling Out a Module
An annotation change applies to one Logger destination. A module added to Logger’s write path runs for every Logger destination. We therefore deploy the module before enabling it across all traffic.
As an example, here is how Policy Zones was introduced on this path. We first set the Policy Zones module to rollingOut() in Logger’s PrivacyLib write-operation configuration:
PrivacyLibWriteEnforcement::zones(ZoneDataType::LOGGER)
    ->rollingOut()
The rollout key, logger.input.write.zones, identified this combination of Logger input, write operation and the Policy Zones module. rollingOut() placed the module execution behind a runtime control. We then moved that control from 0 to 100% in stages while monitoring denials, errors, and latency. If valid writes began to fail, we could lower the percentage without rebuilding or redeploying the service. The Telemetry Logging module continues to run because it is configured independently. 
Once the Policy Zones module was stable across Logger traffic, we changed the configuration from rollingOut() to enabled(). At this point, the Logger integration ran the module without consulting the rollout percentage.
After deployment, engineers use runtime signals to increase, reduce, or stop a module rollout without rebuilding or redeploying.
Safeguards apply at different stages across the two change paths described above. If a simulation shows unexpected flow changes, we hold the annotation artifact before release. If a module misbehaves after the rollout begins, we lower its rollout percentage using the runtime control.
These safety mechanisms changed what it takes to meet a privacy requirement at Meta. PrivacyLib now runs inside the clients of hundreds of data and processing systems and evaluates billions of checks every second, while consuming a small fraction of Meta’s compute. Requirements built on top of it, such as purpose limitation through Policy Zones and data flow discovery through Privacy Probes, reuse those integrations instead of rebuilding them, so enabling a module on systems that are already covered takes days rather than the months bespoke integrations used to take. When a change does go wrong, the failure stays inside the service running the deployed change. We can now use that foundation for a newer class of workload: AI agents.
PrivacyLib Controls for AI Agents
AI agents are harder to reason about than traditional services because their behavior is dynamic and the data they access is determined at runtime. Therefore, we have to design for agent safety up front by enforcing controls, such as Policy Zones, not only on what we expected the agents to access when we built them but also on what they attempt to access at runtime. Where enabled, these controls can block a disallowed access before any data is returned.
Agents invoke tools to carry out tasks. A single tool call may cross several services in a nested manner before reaching data. To tackle this new challenge, we built AgentLib, a common runtime based on PrivacyLib’s design principles, for observing and governing tool calls made by internal agents. On supported paths, AgentLib associates each tool call with its agent session, and downstream clients and services propagate that context until the call reaches a system integrated with PrivacyLib. At that data access boundary, PrivacyLib combines the context, the requested operation, and the destination’s annotations, then passes them to individual modules to make a final decision.
Within PrivacyLib, the Agent Observability module records the agent session and tool-call identifiers alongside the destination, client API, integration point, and any errors. Engineers can query these events by session to investigate the services and destinations involved in a tool call. When we introduced the Agent Observability module, PrivacyLib’s existing broad coverage enabled us to instrument systems already integrated with the library instead of manually integrating the module into hundreds of systems. Even with AI-assisted development, this would have been a daunting task. 
To enforce certain policies, we used the existing Policy Zones module without modification because it relies on the same inputs for enforcement. On paths where this control is enabled, it considers the destination annotations and agent context before allowing an operation. When Policy Zones blocks an operation, PrivacyLib propagates that result back through the call chain to the agent environment. Policy Zones applies this check even when the agent chooses a tool that its developer did not anticipate. The access decision does not depend on the agent behaving as intended.
AgentLib associates supported tool calls made by internal agents with agent context, which services propagate to PrivacyLib at the data access boundary. PrivacyLib uses that context for observation and enforcement.
Lessons Learned From Building and Operating PrivacyLib
Building and operating PrivacyLib across Meta’s systems taught us a few important lessons.
Design for evolving systems and requirements: Before PrivacyLib, we added privacy controls to the individual call sites needed to satisfy each new requirement. Over time, Meta built new data and processing systems, services gained new ways to process data, and privacy requirements expanded. Each change created more integration work, and new access paths sometimes appeared faster than we could cover them. The lesson was to integrate at a stable data access boundary, define the small set of operations that systems share, and keep annotations with the data. Modules can reuse the same integrations and reduce engineering effort over time.
Reliability earns adoption: Early on, an invalid config crashed processes across the fleet, breaking our own safe rollout principles. Other incidents came from annotation changes that compiled successfully but changed access decisions and caused product failures. These incidents showed that service owners will trust PrivacyLib in a critical data access path only when they can see how changes affect their traffic before release and recover from a problematic change without a fleet-wide rollback. 
Coverage includes deployment: When new requirements need changes to modules or supported policies and annotations, older services need to deploy versions with the updated PrivacyLib capabilities. We have ensured that explicit inventory, tracking, and rollout mechanisms are in place to coordinate these deployments, so that requirement owners can meet deadlines safely by updating only the services in scope.
Looking Forward
These lessons shape where we are taking PrivacyLib next, as AI pushes data access into environments and call paths that are increasingly novel. We continue to enrich PrivacyLib’s capabilities in two areas:
AI training: Data used for training reaches our systems from a variety of environments. Much of it is produced or transformed in various places. We are extending PrivacyLib-style approaches to this domain so the same guarantees scale with it. For more on how Meta approaches AI training data, see AI at Meta: Transparency About Our Training Data.
Internal AI agents: Observing attempted data accesses and blocking disallowed ones is just the starting point rather than a finished picture for agents used internally at Meta for engineering and productivity. The harder problems come next: evaluating internal agent behavior while it is happening, and reasoning about communication between these agents, where a single data access may be several agents removed from the person who asked for it.
Acknowledgements
The authors would like to acknowledge the contributions of many current and former Meta employees who have played a crucial role in developing PrivacyLib over the years. In particular, we would like to extend special thanks to (in alphabetical order) Adwait Sathe, Andrew Vaslas, Darrien Glasser, Diana Marsala, Hanzhi Zhang, Kousik Nandy, Matthew Hillman, Matthieu Martin, Michael Dietz, Nathan Maue, Ramy Wassef, Sen Luo, Spencer Baumgardner, Vince Yang, and Zhong Hu. posts.title: Python Typing Survey 2026: AI Tools and the Shifting Checker Landscape
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
The 2026 Python Typing Survey received 1,794 responses. 
Type hint use changed little across three years, but checker selection changed sharply. 
Among respondents who reported which checkers they use, half selected more than one, and missing library type information was the most common difficulty.
For the third consecutive year, we asked Python developers how they use and experience Python typing: the language features, specifications, and tools used to describe and check types in Python code. We run the survey to learn what is working and what library maintainers, tool builders, documentation authors, and standards contributors should tackle next.
Most respondents were experienced Python developers: 76.4% had used Python for at least five years. The clearest change was the shift in checker choice, while missing library type information remained the most common difficulty.
Key Takeaways From the 2026 Python Typing Survey
This year’s findings show several recurring opportunities: 
Broader and more accurate type information would help users of data-science packages: Dynamic frameworks pose a different challenge because current type systems cannot express some runtime behavior. Possible directions include new typing features and checker support tailored to individual libraries and frameworks.
Tool builders could focus on editor feedback and an initial checker run that requires little configuration: Error messages could link to short explanations and examples. Typing documentation can assume Python experience. Projects using multiple checkers would benefit from clear explanations of intentional differences between them.
Better callable syntax remains a practical area for standards work, especially if improvements keep common typing tasks straightforward.
AI usage remains an open question: The findings on AI leave an open question about which interactions between AI tools and type checkers help developers. Further empirical study could inform future designs.
AI Tools Now Write Types and Respond to Checker Errors
The share of respondents who selected “Makes AI-generated code more accurate/reliable” rose from 18.5% in 2025 to 38.4% in 2026. AI tools wrote type hints for 42.5% of 1,517 respondents, while 32.6% wrote types to improve AI-generated code. Respondents also used AI to fix or explain type errors. Across all four activities listed for AI tool use in typing, 61.0% of respondents reported they used at least one of these options.
Some respondents said their AI coding tool runs the checker and then fixes the errors. Of the 1,517 developers who answered how they run a checker, 24.4%, said an AI coding tool invoked their checker. Among the 370 respondents, 61.6% also used AI to fix checker errors. The rate was 19.3% among everyone else.
Some respondents described AI-generated types that are too broad and agents that suppress checker errors:
“I fix AI coded type hints because AI often gets lazy and uses object for everything.”


“Lazy coding agents that spam #type: ignore comments everywhere.”

When asked how useful types are for better AI-assisted coding, 29.8% of 1,551 respondents chose “I’m not sure.” The uncertainty rate for AI-assisted coding was nearly four times the 7.7% rate for runtime guarantees, the next-highest of the six benefits. We still need empirical evidence about which interactions actually help.
The Pyrefly team is already studying how AI coding tools and type checkers work together. At the 2026 Python Typing Summit, the team presented Type Checking in Agentic Workflows.
Library Gaps Lead Overall; Occasional Users Struggle With Complexity
Missing type information in third-party libraries was the leading difficulty, selected by 65.1% of 1,486 respondents. Another 44.6% said the type system could not describe everything their code does.
Developers can still have a poor experience after a library ships dedicated stubs. Among 156 people who wrote their own answer, 22 described dynamic constructs, decorators, metaprogramming, or framework behavior. Ten described arrays, dataframes, or scientific typing, and at least eight described annotations that were inaccurate, incomplete, or too broad. Respondents repeatedly named Django, SQLAlchemy, Pydantic, NumPy, pandas, and Polars.
“Django does so much black magic it’s a wonder a type checker works at all.” — survey respondent

Library maintainers need annotations that capture how frameworks and data-science libraries behave. The Pyrefly team has been working with Quansight to improve third-party library typing, including contributions to pandas-stubs and NumPy.
Frequency of use changed which problems stood out. Among developers who used type hints rarely or sometimes, 41.6% found the type system too complex or verbose. The rate was 14.5% among developers who used type hints often or always. Missing library typing affected 36.2% of the lower-frequency group and 70.0% of the higher-frequency group.

“I use the straightforward parts and avoid the parts that are difficult to understand.” — survey respondent. 

Years of typing experience showed a different pattern. Complexity was reported by 18.2% of respondents with zero to two years of typing experience, 16.0% with three to six years, and 21.0% with seven or more. Newer typing users were often regular users and experienced Python developers: Of the 396 respondents with zero to two years of typing experience, 306 (77.3%) used type hints often or always and 345 (87.1%) had used Python for at least three years.
Guidance for developers who are new to typing should assume Python experience and show how to add types to an existing repository. Occasional users need a useful first check with little configuration and easy-to-understand errors. As we change the type system, we should aim to support more patterns without making common tasks harder.
Better Callable syntax is one practical place to start. It was the most selected missing feature, chosen by 45.7% of the 1,486 respondents who answered the question. The selection rate was similar for respondents who reported complexity and the rest of the sample.
Newer Checkers Gained Ground Quickly
Frequent type hint use remained between 85.5% and 88.0% across the three surveys: 88.0% in 2024, 85.9% in 2025, and 85.5% in 2026. A different group answered each year, but the overall rate remained consistent.

Checker choice was far less stable. When the 2024 Python Typing survey asked what feature was missing from the Python type system, one response now reads like a preview of the changes captured in this year’s results:
“A faster Mypy. Its lack of speed led to ecosystem fracturing and other type checkers don’t support Mypy plugins and behave differently in general.” – survey respondent

By 2026, developers had several newer open-source checkers to choose from. Speed or performance topped the reasons for choosing a checker, at 56.5%. Using the same list of checkers in both years, 49.9% selected two or more in 2026, up from 46.0% in 2025.
Pyrefly is developed by Meta. Respondents could select more than one checker, so the percentages may overlap.
Developers Mix Checkers Across Their Workflows
Of the 700 respondents who selected Mypy, 297 also selected its editor plugin. Another 314 selected a different named checker integration without selecting the Mypy plugin.
Most Pyrefly respondents also selected another checker: 220 of 264, or 83.3%. In the free-text responses, developers described why their teams divide work between checkers:
“Because my team members use different IDEs, we use multiple type checkers for development, but rely on Mypy for linting (local and CI).” — survey respondent
“Locally we primarily use Pyright because it’s the only option we’ve tried that fully understands all the more niche typing patterns within our codebase. In CI/CD, we do a Pyrefly run and only run Pyright on files where Pyrefly fails, to improve performance of the check.” — survey respondent 

Among the 1,486 developers who answered the question about difficulties, 33.3% reported inconsistencies between checkers. Among the 738 respondents who selected multiple static checkers and answered the difficulty question, 315 (42.7%) reported inconsistencies between checkers.
IDE Support Remains Central as Typing Help Moves Away From Stack Overflow
Readability or documentation was the most selected reason to use type hints, chosen by 93.6% of 1,571 respondents. Editor support also ranked highly: 84.8% of the 1,494 people who gave it a numeric rating chose 4 or 5. About 39% of the 103 developers who supplied their own reason mentioned completion, navigation, hover information, or editor error messages.
“Drastically improves IDE tooltip/autocomplete.” – survey respondent 

Real-time editor feedback was widespread: 82.9% of 1,517 respondents ran a type checker in an editor. VS Code was the most selected editor or IDE, at 59.3%.
Where developers look for help has changed as well. From 2024 to 2026, Stack Overflow use fell from 46.4% to 22.9%, while large language model (LLM) chat rose from 26.0% to 41.7%. Python typing documentation rose from 56.2% to 65.9%. Checker-specific documentation ended at 60.5%, up from 52.2% after a dip in 2025. General Python documentation fell from 66.7% to 62.2%.

As developers move from Stack Overflow to typing- and checker-specific documentation, the quality of those sources matters more. Error messages should link to short, relevant explanations and examples. Links to documentation would also give LLM chat tools better information to work with.
Survey Results and Raw Data
Download the full results and data from the Python Typing Survey 2026.
Acknowledgements
The survey ran from August 5 through September 2, 2026. It was developed with support from the Pyrefly team at Meta, the PyCharm team at JetBrains, the Python team at Microsoft, the ty team at Astral/OpenAI, and community contributors on discuss.python.org. We shared it through Reddit, X, Mastodon, newsletters, the Python typing forum, LinkedIn, Bluesky, Discord, Slack, and type-checker project websites and social accounts. We lightly edited quotations for spelling, grammar, and punctuation. We thank everyone who responded, shared the survey, reviewed the data, or contributed to the Python typing community.
