posts.title: Meta Networking at the 2026 OCP Global Summit: Open Innovation for Scale-Up, Scale-Out, and Scale-Across AI Networks
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
At the 2026 Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit, Meta shared the networking innovations that are directly supporting our latest AI models, including Muse Wonder and Muse Spark, and our gigawatt-scale Prometheus cluster. 
Highlights
IcePack & IceCube: Meta’s first liquid-cooled network rack with 102.4T switch blades (128×800G, Broadcom Tomahawk 6C and NVIDIA Spectrum-6 variants), running FBOSS. 
Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF) for scale-out: Meta’s multi-plane scale-out fabric where each GPU connects to eight network planes. 3-tier → 2-tier Clos, NIC-level packet spraying, and a combined host+switch control plane. Built with NVIDIA and shared with our cloud partners.
Scale-across: BAG, our petabit-scale super-spine joining buildings, campuses, and regions in our gigawatt-scale Prometheus cluster, plus SRv6 regional backbones on FBOSS + SAI.
Ethernet for scale-up: Tahan, the Ethernet scale-up switch for MTIA 300 based on Broadcom Tomahawk5; a preview of 72 accelerators per rack on 102.4T silicon; and ESUN progressing from 1.0 → 1.1.
OSPA: a new OCP initiative co-led by Meta, Microsoft, and Alibaba to standardize the switch platform layer. v1.0 spec submitted to OCP.
MetaRoCE: our RDMA transport for AI networks, now going open source.
We shared insights into key networking-related initiatives through talks from many of the Meta network and hardware teams. Those talks and their slide decks are now available to everyone! 
Keynote and Executive Sessions

Concrete to Code: Engineering AI Infrastructure at Gigawatt Scale (video)
AI has changed the shape of infrastructure. Santosh Janardhan, Head of Infrastructure at Meta, shares how Meta is designing, building, and operating at a scale that requires rethinking the network, the facility, and the systems that hold it all together.
Speaker: Santosh Janardhan, Head of Infrastructure, Meta
Betting on the Network: Meta’s Case for Full-Stack, Open AI Networking (video)
 AI progress now depends on the network as much as on compute. The path forward is a full-stack, open approach built in the open ecosystem rather than behind proprietary walls.
Speaker: Omar Baldonado, Senior Director, Data Center & AI Networking, Meta
Breaking the Walls: Open Scale-Across for the AI Era (video)
Training compute is compounding faster than infrastructure can scale. This talk lays out why open scale-across networking is needed to connect AI capacity across data centers and regions.
Speakers: Vipul Deokar, VP, Core Network Infrastructure, Meta; Rakesh Chopra, SVP, Silicon & Systems Architecture and Engineering Fellow, Cisco; Tom Williams, VP, Marketing, Cisco
Switch Platforms, Optics, and Interconnect
Meta 102.4T Ethernet Switch (video)
IceCube is Meta’s 102.4T switch that goes into our liquid-cooled Icepack rack. Icecube and N-IceCube are based on a 2OU, hybrid liquid/air-cooled, PHY-less design and incorporate either the Broadcom Tomahawk 6C or NVIDIA Spectrum-6 ASICs with 128x800GE of non-blocking capacity.
Speakers: Rongchun Zhou, Network Hardware Engineer, Meta; Reza Niazmand, Network Technical Program Manager, Meta
Integrated Optics at Scale: From 51.2T CPO Validation to Meta’s 102.4T (video)
A look at why integrated optics matter for rack-scale AI — power, density, disaggregation, and reliability — and what Meta learned validating 51.2T co-packaged optics that could carry over to 102.4T.
Speakers: Granthana Rangaswamy, Hardware Engineer, Meta; Siamak Amiralizadeh, Optical Engineer, Meta; Xu Wang, Hardware Engineer, Meta
Operating Linear Pluggable Optics at Hyperscale (video)
At AI scale, the per-module retimer DSP is a repeated tax in power, heat, and cost across millions of links — but removing it moves equalization and triage onto the host. This talk answers whether linear optics can match retimed reliability at fleet scale.
Speakers: Amin Yekani, Optical Engineer, Meta; Qing Wang, Optical Engineer, Meta
Large-Scale Deployment of 800G AECs in Meta Data Centers (video)
The economics of AI networking are set at the short-reach link. This session covers Meta’s large-scale deployment of 800Gb/s active electrical cables and the component quality work behind it.
Speakers: Jingyu (Kevin) Yu, Component Quality Engineer, Meta; Abhijit Chakravarty, Quality Head, Optics & Interconnects, Meta
Beyond Pluggables: Building the NPO Ecosystem for Scaling AI
A look at what it takes to build a near-package optics (NPO) ecosystem capable of supporting AI scaling beyond what pluggable modules can deliver.
Speaker: Nan Ge, Technical Sourcing Manager, Meta 
FBOSS and Open Platforms

Open Switch Platform Architecture (OSPA) — A Unified Network Switch Platform Reference Design (video)
While SAI has made data plane software portable, the switch platform layer remains proprietary and fragmented, adding months of duplicated bring-up work per platform. This talk introduces OSPA, which proposes a unified, multi-vendor reference design for that layer, and the 1.0 specification that has been contributed to OCP.
Speakers: Tao Ren, Tian Fang, and Xu Wang, Meta; Guohan Lu, Individual; Ying Xie, Microsoft; Yiyuan Huang and Zhiping Yao, Alibaba
NVIDIA SDK + FBOSS: Building Production-Ready AI Network Fabrics (video)
How NVIDIA’s Spectrum-X switch, SDK, SAI implementation, and simulator come together with FBOSS, Meta’s network operating system, to build production AI fabrics. The talk covers the CI/CD and test-driven workflow that made rapid joint integration possible.
Speakers: Parvez Shaikh, Meta; Harish Krishnamoorthy, Alan Elder, and Tom Zhu, NVIDIA
Open, AI-Ready FBOSS: From Platform Bring-up to Solution Qualification (video)
A tour of the FBOSS software stack — routing, forwarding, platform services, and board support — and how a config-driven approach can more quickly and easily take a platform from board bring-up to qualified status for the OCP ecosystem.
Speakers: Srikrishna Gopu, Software Engineer, Meta; Benoit Sigoure, Software Engineer, Nexthop AI
Experiences With Scale-Out and Scale-Across
High Performance at Scale and Reliability by Design: Operating Meta’s Largest AI Clusters (video)
What it takes to operate Meta’s largest AI clusters reliably, walking the full training stack from GPUs and scale-up fabrics through FBOSS, drivers, communication libraries, and the scheduler.
Speakers: Jose Leitao, Production Engineering, Meta; Guille Cobo, Network.AI, Meta
Scaling AI Infrastructure Across DC and Beyond: Meta’s Journey with BAG (video)
An overview of Backend Aggregation (BAG) — its purpose, architecture, and performance benefits — with lessons from deployment in Meta’s Prometheus cluster. The talk also covers the engineering challenges of platform fit, distance management, reliability, and capacity planning, especially given the quickly evolving AI ecosystem.
Speakers: Jalpa Patel, Technical Program Manager, Meta; Hany Morsy, Network Engineer, Meta
SRv6 Powered Backbone Networks (video)
This talk delves into why Meta chose SRv6 for a new layer of its backbone, how the data plane and control plane work in production on FBOSS (including using shallow buffers at WAN distances), and the accelerated timeline from concept to deployment in a matter of months. 
 Speakers: Jasmeet Bagga, Software Engineer, Meta; Andrey Golovanov, Network Engineer, Meta
Bridging On-prem and Cloud: GPU Networking at Meta Scale (video)
A look at how Meta uses cloud GPU capacity, and what lessons Meta brings from its on-premises deployments into clouds to make them highly performant and reliable for AI workloads.
Speakers: Adi Gangidi, Technical Lead, Meta; Carmen Au, Software Engineering Manager, Meta
Scale-Across Networking Panel (video)
A cross-industry panel on what scale-across AI clusters demand from routing and optical transport equipment. Panelists compare approaches across hyperscalers, silicon, and systems vendors.
Panelists: Jeff Rahn, Meta; Tad Hofmeister, Google Cloud; Yawei Yin, Microsoft Azure; Xiguang (Henry) Wu, Broadcom; Vijay Vusirikala, Arista Networks (moderator)
Scale-Up and ESUN
Tahan: An Open, Ethernet-Based Scale-Up Switch for MTIA (video)
We introduce Tahan, an Ethernet-based scale-up switch for our rack-scale MTIA 300 AI system. This talk walks through Tahan’s bandwidth and latency characteristics and scale-up feature set, demonstrating Ethernet’s strengths in scale-up and moving toward ESUN for future scale-up designs.
Speakers: Vimal Vasudevan, Technical Program Manager, Meta; Ashutosh Grewal, Software Engineer, Meta
ESUN: Open Ethernet for the AI Scale-Up Era (video)
We partnered with the community last year to launch ESUN: Ethernet for Scale-up Networking. This talk covers progress since the last OCP Global Summit, with the 1.0 specification released earlier in the year and the upcoming 1.1 specification. 
Speakers: Manoj Wadekar, AI Network Technologist, Meta; Pratik Marolia, AI System Architect, Microsoft
Validation Methodologies for the ESUN Ecosystem (video)
A validation methodology for the ESUN ecosystem, situating scale-up within the broader set of AI scaling domains — scale in, up, out, across, edge, and above.
Speakers: Manoj Wadekar, AI Systems Technologist, Meta; Venkat Pullela, CTO, AI Infrastructure, Keysight
Test Methodology for Multi-Accelerator Copper Scale-up Interconnect (video)
In a copper scale-up domain, thousands of connections per rack mean roughly 10 bad links even at 99.9% yield — and blind-mate cartridges leave no per-link serviceability. At Meta, we look at this as a statistical problem rather than a set of isolated debugging problems. This talk shares our test methodology.
Speakers: Yao Rong, Systems Engineer, AI Systems, Meta; Karthik Ganesan, AI/HPC System Performance Engineer, Meta
RDMA Transport
MetaRoCE: Rethinking RDMA for AI (video)
The network is now in the critical path for AI clusters, with all-reduce and all-to-all performance gated by the slowest node across hundreds of thousands of accelerators. This talk covers the MetaRoCE transport specification.
Speakers: Arvind Srinivasan, Meta; Sandeep Nagaraja, Meta; Balakrishnan Raman, AMD
MetaRoCE in Software (video)
Meta is making its MetaRoCE software implementations available in open source, starting with a user-space version on GitHub (libsoftmetaroce) with a DPDK-based version coming soon. 
Speakers: Ashkan Nikravesh, Software Engineer, Meta; Yiorgos Nikolaidis, Software Engineer, Meta
Watch Everything From the 2026 OCP Global Summit 
You can watch all of the recorded talks from the event on the 2026 OCP Global Summit website.
A huge thank-you to every presenter from our Meta network and hardware teams and to our great partners across the industry who made this possible! 
Images courtesy Open Compute Project (OCP).

posts.title: Making Failure Diagnosis Reliable with Pensive AI
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
By Praneeth Yenugutala, Victor Dusa, Anastasia Samoilova, Megan Ren, Justin Wei, Marcelo Mayworm
At Netflix, data and machine learning practitioners run millions of workloads each day across orchestration systems and compute engines such as Titus, Spark, Trino, and Druid. On peak days, roughly 100,000 workloads fail. When workloads fail, the failure itself is only the beginning. Someone still needs to find the useful signal in several logs, decide whether the cause sits in their code or the platform, and determine whether to retry, reconfigure, or escalate. Even a small share of difficult failures can consume engineering time, waste compute, and interrupt critical data pipelines.
Our first answer to that problem was Pensive, an auto-diagnosis and remediation system in Netflix’s data platform. Pensive collected logs from failed workloads, used regular expressions and hand-authored Java rules to extract and classify errors, then passed retry or remediation guidance to products such as Maestro. It made ~ 50% of failures self-service and, in some cases, automatic.
Rules work well for known patterns, but their coverage grows only when someone recognizes a new failure mode, understands the logs, writes a rule, and keeps it current as engines and log formats change. Over one three-month period, Pensive processed roughly seven million job-failure classifications, yet about half fell into the unknown bucket. We needed a way to expand coverage without giving up the deterministic parts of Pensive that already worked.
To solve this ambiguous and complex problem at Netflix scale, we invested in Pensive AI to add AI-assisted error extractions and focused diagnosis and remediation guidance to our data and ML practitioners. The goal was not simply to place a model in front of a large collection of logs. We needed bounded extraction, predictable evaluation inputs, responsive product behavior, and quality checks that could follow the system from local development through production. Those requirements shaped every layer of the design, which we will discuss in this blog. Pensive AI wraps AI around deterministic processes, which gives broader coverage, low latency, controlled AI costs, and easier maintenance across the software development lifecycle. Building on this foundation, we plan to explore more agentic debugging experiences, as Part 6 describes.
Early results are encouraging. AI error extraction now covers 100% of failures, including the failures that legacy Pensive classified as unknown. Failed step attempts where no one used Pensive AI averaged 321% more manual debug-log exploration actions than attempts where someone did (an observational comparison, not a causal claim).
Figure 1. Pensive AI architecture. Always-on error extraction and on-demand debugging complement each other and share log sources, the LLM gateway, tracing, and the cache. Archived logs feed offline evals and release gates.
The two paths complement each other. Error extraction improves an existing capability and is always on. It lets the user of a failed Maestro workload quickly check the parts of the logs that may point to an immediate root cause. It has low latency and low cost, and it can help in a large share of cases. On-demand debugging enables a new capability. It looks at symptoms across the logs and adds the LLM’s own knowledge and reasoning for a deeper analysis, at slightly higher latency and cost. Extraction gives a fast first look at every failure, and on-demand debugging triggered by the user goes deeper when that first look is not enough.
Part 1: Finding the useful errors
Legacy Pensive rules are precise, but each one captures a particular log shape. A simplified rule looks like this:
- name: SparkContainerOOM
logSource: GENIE_STDERR
restartable: false
regex: "Container.*is running beyond physical memory limits.*Killing container"
summary: Spark AM container runs out of memory
With Pensive AI, we wanted to find useful errors that had no corresponding rule and adapt more easily when familiar errors changed shape after a platform upgrade. Data Portal (our UI for data pipelines) surfaces these extracted errors when available and links back to the source logs, giving practitioners a focused starting point for triage. That raises a question: how can we ask a model to identify an error without asking it to repeat a long stack trace token by token?
Producing output tokens is much slower than reading input tokens. A direct transcription approach would make long errors expensive and slow. Instead, Pensive numbers the lines of each log and gives the model a sequence of {lineNumber, text} records. The model identifies the first and last lines of the error span, and Pensive reconstructs the selected text from its own log copy, leading to lower cost and better latency. This way, the model always returns two integers (start and end line number), whether the selected logs span a few lines or hundreds of lines. The displayed content comes directly from the original log, reducing hallucinations. The model can still choose the wrong range, which is why extraction quality remains an integral measurement for our AI evals, as we will discuss later.
For orchestrated workflows, “Pensive AI Error Extraction” runs automatically whenever a step fails. A step attempt is one execution of a step within a Maestro workflow. Maestro already calls Pensive for a regex-derived error and restartability classification, so AI extraction runs in the same request and returns its results alongside the established fields. The overall Pensive response must return within Maestro’s hard 90-second post-processing timeout for a failed step attempt.
Figure 2. Error extraction. Legacy rules always run. The AI call is bound by a shared deadline, and late calls are excluded. Pensive merges both results into one response and caches it.
That deadline shaped the extraction path. Pensive extracts errors from the logs in parallel to reduce latency, and the per-log calls share one deadline set well inside Maestro’s timeout limit. A per-log extraction call that misses the deadline is excluded from the result, allowing the overall request to return on time.
The data contract between Pensive AI and the various consumers needed the same care. The legacy data model contained one flattened error string; AI extraction instead returns a list of errors, one for each log source, with deep links back to the originating logs. Changing the old field in place would have broken existing clients. We introduced the new data model beside the legacy non-AI error extraction data model and continued producing both. Data Portal, our user interface for monitoring and observing data pipelines, preferred AI errors when available and fell back to the legacy value when they were not during the rollout. That allowed a gradual rollout and ensured that historical failures still display an error, since we chose not to backfill the old data due to log retention issues.
The migration is still in progress today. The Data Portal UI surface used for failed Maestro steps reads the new AI extracted error field today, while the query editor (for editing and running SQL), Workbench notebooks (managed compute platform and UI to edit and run jupyter based notebooks) and some slack clients calling Pensive still use the legacy error extraction path. Each client needs a compatible schema change before it can consume the new data. Keeping both fields populated lets teams adopt the new behavior at their own pace without forcing a coordinated cutover as we continue evolving Pensive AI.
Part 2: Full failure diagnosis and the product experience
Beyond error extraction, we built Pensive AI Debugging, a tool that analyzes failed step attempts and provides root-cause analysis and suggested remediations. It is available through programmatic APIs, MCP, and the product UI (Data Portal), all backed by a common entry point across the Netflix Data Platform. This shared model supports consistent behavior and custom product experiences.
This diagnosis still has to arrive quickly and remain consistent across investigations. A debugging response can take tens of seconds or a minute to generate, compared with a few seconds for error extraction. We run full AI-based debugging on demand instead of automatically, which keeps costs under control because most failed steps are never opened. We treat the failed step attempt, not the person who triggered it, as the unit of work, so everyone investigating the same failed attempt sees the same diagnosis.
That choice gives us a stable unit of work for caching. We cache each debugging response by step attempt. A second request becomes a key-value read instead of another AI inference call. The cache also prevents duplicate work, reducing latency and lowering costs further. This also means that a debugging generated in the Data Portal is cached and immediately retrieved for the MCP path instead of incurring another AI inference call. A conditional write creates an in-progress record, one caller starts generation, and other callers wait for the shared result to avoid conflicts when concurrent requests come in for the same step attempt failure. If generation remains in progress past an abandonment timeout, Pensive treats the record as abandoned and reclaims it. Completed responses expire after 90 days to help control costs and optimize storage because debugging requests for much older workloads are uncommon.
Pensive AI supports multiple ways to initiate debugging responses. A caller can (1) read a cached response, (2) generate one if no cache entry exists, or (3) regenerate and overwrite an existing response. Those semantics support the product UI, programmatic access, and the evaluation harness while keeping the response associated with a single immutable workload failure.
Figure 3. On-demand debugging. Three client actions share one entry point. A conditional write claims the step attempt. A cache hit returns the cached result. A won claim generates and streams a response, and the result persists even if the client disconnects.
For users, the most important behavior is that a long-running answer feels alive. Pensive streams the response as it is produced. The service emits server-sent events, and the GraphQL layer republishes them as a WebSocket subscription for the Data Portal client.
Each event carries the complete response generated so far. That duplicates a small amount of text, but it keeps the client simple: it does not need a replay buffer or token reassembly logic, and the next event corrects the display after a dropped or late event. Generation is independent of the connection that requested it. A disconnect does not cancel the work, and the final answer still reaches the cache. A hard reload can show a loading state and poll for the completed result. Within the single-page application backing the Data Portal UI, active streams are maintained independently of view and component lifecycle, so navigation does not interrupt a response in progress.
Part 3: Measuring and improving the behavior we want
LLM-assisted systems need more than a demo or a few working examples. Before shipping in production, we need confidence in both error extraction and debugging guidance, and we need to know that we have not regressed on failures that legacy Pensive already handled. We built separate evaluation frameworks focused on the two distinct jobs.
Building labeled data is often the expensive part of evaluation. For error extraction, legacy Pensive’s hand-written rules provide reference labels for failures they recognize. They also serve as excellent ground truth in most cases. We run those rules over production logs and compare their extracted spans with Pensive AI’s output. This gives us a reliable regression set without relabeling every example by hand, though it is not an absolute ground truth (since our human-built rules could also have been stale). For now, we keep these rules frozen as a label source. This lets us continue to build comparison evals and run them on top of the existing system.
Stable inputs are essential for repeatable evaluation experiments where we A/B test new models/configurations or context injections to improve response quality. The logs Pensive AI uses can expire after as few as seven days or as many as 30 days. Production Pensive AI requests archive fetched logs to S3 object storage asynchronously during workload execution time so the upload is not on the user-facing critical path. Uploads do not overwrite an existing object, preserving the exact snapshot used to create an evaluation case. Evals use those archived logs, so score changes remain attributable to the system under test. The archive also prevents parallel experiments from overloading the source systems and lets us run them without affecting production. Cached S3 log inputs further reduce costs when running evaluations.
Concretely, we measure four complementary signals for error extraction:

Inclusion: An LLM judge compares the legacy Pensive error for a failure with the errors Pensive AI extracted and determines whether the known error is still represented, even when wording differs.
Precision: A second judge sees only the extracted AI errors and evaluates whether each is meaningful and actionable on its own.
Repeated noise: A script looks across the whole dataset for lines that recur too often. A generic status line may look harmless in one answer but become distracting if it appears in a large share of failures. Lines appearing in more than about 30% of workflows are candidates for explicit exclusion. In practice, the exclusion list has only three lines, each of which otherwise appeared in nearly every extracted error.
Latency: We record the latency of every extraction call. Quality scores alone cannot reveal when an apparent improvement requires too much additional work, which often correlates with increased AI costs.

This combination gives us an actionable feedback loop. Prompt changes can reduce general noise, while the dataset-level view exposes the stubborn boilerplate that prompt changes do not eliminate. Existing rules act as a regression floor, and archived logs give us a repeatable way to compare changes. At Pensive AI’s scale, model and system choices must satisfy quality, latency, maintainability and cost constraints together.
To seed the debugging ground-truth dataset for evaluation, we mine internal engineering-support Slack threads and use an LLM to identify threads that link to an orchestrated workflow, describe a resolved problem, and match the class of issue Pensive AI handles. A second model synthesizes a reference debugging response from the relevant discussion. Paired with logs from that workflow failure, it becomes a concrete evaluation row in our evals dataset. This approach works only retrospectively, because Pensive AI in production aims to provide debugging guidance before such a Slack discussion happens.
We also made the debugging generation process visible. Tracing follows the request through Pensive, with child spans for each log fetch and extraction tool call. Our tracing backend based on Braintrust brings the prompt, completion, tool calls, and latency into a single view. During early product development, that visibility helped us inspect low-performing debugging responses in context instead of guessing which input or operation caused them. Tracing helped us improve the responses and fill context gaps even before we had comprehensive evals. In production, the API and UI return the trace identifier with the response, so feedback can lead directly to the trace for in-depth analysis.
Part 4: Keeping quality in the release path
Evaluation is not only for experiments with LLM orchestration, models, prompts, or context changes. Changes to log selection, trimming logic, or a source system can change what the model sees and therefore change extraction quality. We use the same evaluation harness and evaluators throughout local development and Pensive AI deployment so those effects are visible before users encounter them.
For each pull request, the code branch is deployed to an isolated preview environment and a CI job runs an experiment with our evals against that isolated environment. Precision and inclusion thresholds gate the merge. The job also runs after a build is promoted, catching interactions that were not present when individual pull requests were evaluated in isolation. If the promoted build misses its thresholds, it alerts the on-call engineer to investigate or roll back.
The evaluator runs on a schedule against production to surface gradual drift or external changes. Developers can also trigger evaluation experiments remotely while iterating, using the same deployed-environment path as CI. Consistent infrastructure makes the results comparable across local iteration, preview builds, promoted builds, and production.
Part 5: Looking for feedback signal from users
The system is only valuable if it reduces the amount of manual debugging and log chasing done by our users. We wanted a measurement that was available from product telemetry and close to the behavior Pensive AI was designed to change. Manual debug-log exploration became one of the main signals. The Pensive interface already offers links to logs for a failed step attempt. To estimate whether the feature reduced raw-log hunting, we compared failed step attempts where someone interacted with Pensive AI with those where no one did. The second group averaged 321% more manual debug-log exploration actions. This observational comparison does not establish causality or a specific reduction in mean time to resolution, but it suggests that focused diagnosis often allows practitioners to inspect fewer raw logs. Programmatic MCP access also lets teams build operational flows with their terminals or custom agentic experiences around the same diagnosis service.
Another more explicit signal we collect is thumbs up and thumbs down on the debugging response. These feedback signals land directly alongside the internal traces so we can quickly associate feedback to the complete log of inputs/outputs and the path the AI took to arrive at the answer. More importantly, we created an internal business-hours alerting system where each thumbs down response sends us a Slack alert. This was valuable to resolve a lot of rough edges and context gaps initially in the product and is helping us improve the product continuously even today.
Figure 4. Feedback loop. A thumbs up or down joins the exact LLM trace that produced the response, by the same logId stamped during generation. Traces and feedback feed ground truth and eval datasets, and each thumbs down sends a Slack alert during business hours.
Part 6: Future Work building on these foundations
Pensive AI is the foundation for more work that goes beyond diagnosis and recommended remediations. We are exploring “Pensive AI Deepthink,” an opt-in managed agentic experience with higher cost and latency. It builds on the precise, low-latency analysis produced by Pensive AI Debugging and gathers additional context from internal documentation, manuals, past Slack discussions, source code, read-only warehouse queries, and Spark execution details. A routing step directs the investigation to the appropriate skill, such as Spark failures, data-audit failures, or late workflows. This keeps the shared starting point stable and deterministic while allowing the investigation to become more specialized, further improving recall. We are also in talks with the Spark team to leverage Pensive AI responses for failure debugging analysis and A/B comparison for upcoming platform migrations.
We also plan to invest in “Pensive AI Error Classification”. Hard-to-maintain legacy rules also classify failures by restartability and by whether they are platform or user caused. Maestro acts on those labels and changes its retry behavior accordingly like failing fast or tuning the default number of retries (platform errors are tried more than user errors by default). Error classifications must meet a higher bar than error extractions and debugging alone. Moving the majority of the error classifications to AI would let us retire most of the remaining rule-maintenance burden and avoid retrying unknown failures that were unlikely to succeed. For restartability, the costliest error is classifying a recoverable failure as non-restartable, because Maestro will turn a step that could have been recovered into a hard failure, leading to end user alerts and manual remediations. The evaluation framework will need to be tuned around that outcome before AI-enabled classifications can take on those decisions. Equally important, we must avoid retrying non-transient failures that will not succeed, because retries waste compute and delay data pipelines.
Our work on Pensive AI in Data Platform addresses concrete user pain points in debugging, improves maintainability for platform owners, and improves precision and recall for error extraction. Pensive AI extends coverage to failures that legacy Pensive previously classified as unknown. Reliability comes from the system around the AI model calls: bounded error extractions, compatible client data contracts, responsive delivery, reproducible evaluations, caching and tracing, and release controls that keep quality and cost visible as the platform changes.
Part 7: Acknowledgements
This work would not have been possible without our stunning colleagues across Data Platform and our Data Engineering and Analytics partners who provided early feedback. While we cannot name everyone individually, we are deeply grateful for their contributions, which shaped both response quality and the product experience. Special thanks to Adith Swaminathan for advising on evaluations and inference improvements and acting as a thought partner. Thank you to the Orchestration team members, especially Deepak Ramalingam and Malcolm Ramirez for their additional engineering contributions.
For dogfooding and integrating Pensive AI as part of user support, we also thank the engineering support organization (ESO Team). We also thank Abhishek Kapatkar (Data Developer Experiences Team) and Emmie Dong (Data Movement Team) for their feedback to improve the Pensive AI integrations with the rest of the ecosystem. Special thanks to the AI Platform team (Kyle Ahn, Rob Mann) and Braintrust Team for helping with distributed tracing, evals infrastructure and model gateway runtime support.
We also thank Kamran Masood, Ely Spears, Ronald Leung, Anjali Norwood, Prashanth Ramdas, Charles Smith, Harikrishna Menon and other leaders for their constructive feedback and support on the Pensive AI project.

posts.title: Multi‑Ratio Video Resizing for Mobile Feed and Marketing
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Serdar Cellat, Yuchen Xie, Bernadette Marcu, Blaid Burgess, Cody Jarrett, Carlos Pereira, Qing Shi, Samuel Carvajal, Manuel Pamplona, Dorothy Jung, Feiko Ritsema, Benjamin Klein, Alex Woo, Eugene Lok, Anna Pulido, Rebecka Swe, Sanford Holsapple, Ranjith Kumar Shetty
Introduction
Clips in the Netflix mobile app.
At Netflix, a crucial part of our mission is ensuring our content looks stunning on any device. Vertical formats are increasingly important for Netflix, as we have 1.2B followers across our social media accounts, and have recently rolled out Clips, our vertical video feed in the Netflix mobile app. Traditionally, creating vertical assets meant editors and producers manually reframed horizontal videos in editing tools, a process that doesn’t scale as our catalog and use cases grow. To support both our in‑app feed and external marketing campaigns at scale, we built an automated multi‑ratio video cropping system, tightly integrated into our internal production tools, that can generate high‑quality vertical and other aspect‑ratio variants with minimal manual effort.
Our Video Resizing Approach
Converting cinematic 16:9 footage into mobile‑friendly aspect ratios takes more than a simple center crop. Filmmaking often involves dynamic character blocking and complex camera movement. We need an intelligent “virtual camera” that can follow the key action, respond to how each scene is composed, and produce crops that feel as intentional as the original shot.
We address this challenge by framing video resizing as a tracking and temporal optimization problem. Our pipeline processes each asset in three main stages, designed to produce 9:16, 4:5, and 1:1 crops in a single pass, without incurring additional computational overhead.
An overview of the three-stage process converting horizontal footage into mobile aspect ratios.
Shot Detection and Splitting
First, we segment the video into atomic shots using a neural‑network–based shot boundary detector. In many cases, shots contain multiple characters conversing on opposite sides of the frame. To better handle these scenarios, we use an Active Speaker Detection based approach to logically split a single continuous shot into multiple sub‑shots. This allows our virtual camera to cut and re-focus on different speakers as the conversation flows. Our Active Speaker Detection leverages an internal face detector and LipFlap to reliably identify active speakers in both live‑action and animated titles.
Shot splitting via Active Speaker Detection. The magenta box represents the dynamic vertical crop.
Focus Region Discovery
Once shots and sub‑shots are defined, we identify the most important region in each frame. We combine face detections with visual saliency maps to filter and prioritize the faces that should be in focus. In scenes with multiple characters, we further rank faces using signals such as active speaker status and relative size. Our model aggregates these cues with shot‑level content understanding to establish a continuous “focus region” for the virtual camera.
Blue box shows the focus region around the primary character for reframing.
Temporal Reframing
Once we’ve established the focus region, the next challenge is deciding how the crop should move over time. Tracking the focus region on a strict frame-by-frame basis would produce a shaky, distracting viewing experience, so we apply a set of heuristics that consider how the focus region moves over the course of a shot. When its displacement is small, we lock a static crop window that consistently covers the relevant area. When there is significant motion, we compute a dynamic tracking window and smooth its path so that any panning feels intentional and cinematic.
The vertical crop (magenta box) follows the character’s movement with a smooth panning path.
Tooling and Workflow Integration
We integrated the resizing algorithm directly into our internal Clips tool, so editors and producers can access it as part of their existing workflow. The interface enables them to automatically generate multiple aspect‑ratio versions of a clip with smart reframing. A unified in‑app module provides intuitive shot‑reframing controls, allowing users to review the algorithm’s crops, and quickly make targeted adjustments where needed.
For more complex shots or custom campaigns, producers can export the resizing parameters as XML and load them directly into external timeline editors such as Adobe Premiere. This allows agencies and external partners to start from the algorithm’s framing decisions instead of recreating crops manually or relying on tools like Premiere’s Auto Reframe. In our internal test, our resizing algorithm outperforms Auto Reframe on a curated evaluation set, so the XML export effectively brings those higher‑quality crops into external workflows. By bringing automated resizing and manual refinement into a single place, this pipeline significantly reduces production time and manual effort while preserving creative control.
Video resizing interface with reframing controls
Conclusion
Our work on multi-ratio video resizing is one step in a broader effort to make content creation more scalable, without compromising creative intent. By pairing algorithm-driven reframing with editor-friendly tools, we’ve reduced the time teams spend on repetitive resizing tasks and unlocked faster experimentation across mobile feeds and marketing campaigns. As we continue to broaden these capabilities to new formats and workflows, our goal remains the same: to give creatives more time to tell great stories, and to deliver a consistently high-quality viewing experience for our members and fans.

posts.title: Beyond API Compatibility: Building a Tool to Measure the Blast Radius of Library Changes
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
By Roberto Perez Alcolea, Java Platform Team
Quasar connects a proposed API change with observed references in consumer repositories, giving the producer evidence for a release decision
At Netflix, shared Java libraries support applications developed across a large, independently evolving repository ecosystem. A library change begins in one repository, but its impact can reach many others. Producers can see the API diff in front of them. What they often cannot see is who still depends on the symbols that changed.
The need for that visibility grows as coding agents take on more of the software development lifecycle. An agent can accelerate a local edit, but without cross-repository context it cannot judge downstream risk or help plan consumer migrations. The evidence a producer uses to assess a change can also guide the agent working on it.
Consider a common case: removing a deprecated API. Deprecated entry points expand the surface producers must test, document, and support, and they can constrain how a library evolves.
Suppose a replacement has been available for several releases and the old method cannot express options required by new behavior. The library’s tests pass, and a compatibility checker flags the removal. The producer still cannot answer the questions that determine what to do next:

Does any consumer still call this method?
Are consumers concentrated on one version or spread across several generations?
Does another library implement or wrap the API, multiplying its impact?
Is direct coordination sufficient, or does this require a deprecation and migration campaign?

At small scale, producers can ask nearby teams or search a handful of repositories. Across many repositories, it is harder to find every caller of a method and the library version each one uses. Those answers are scattered across consumer codebases and builds.
Without that evidence, a producer may release a breaking change and discover the impact through consumer failures, or preserve an old API indefinitely because the risk is unknown. Libraries need to evolve, and their producers need evidence that helps them do so intentionally.
We built Quasar to index symbol definitions and references across Netflix repositories. For library producers, that shared index helps answer two questions:

What changed in the library’s public API?
Which repositories use the exact symbols that changed?

The first identifies a potentially incompatible change. The second estimates its observed blast radius. Together, they turn a generic compatibility warning into evidence a producer can act on before merging or releasing.
From API Changes to Consumer Impact
Existing techniques each see a different part of the problem. Binary and source compatibility tools identify contract changes, but cannot tell who uses the changed API. Dependency graphs show declared reach, but cannot prove that code calls a particular method. Text search may miss overloads, inheritance, or the artifact version behind a call. Consumer builds provide strong validation, but running them across the fleet is expensive.
Quasar builds on SCIP, an open interchange format for semantic code intelligence. Language-specific indexers encode definitions, references, and relationships using stable symbol identifiers. Quasar retains API definitions for library versions and commits alongside references from consumer repositories. That shared identity lets it connect an API change in one repository to exact usages elsewhere, even when those repositories were indexed independently.

On each enrolled CI build, language-specific indexers submit SCIP indexes to Quasar’s ingestion service. It writes API definitions and consumer references as Parquet in Amazon S3, retaining the symbol identity, dependency version, and source location needed to investigate a change.
During pull-request review, Quasar compares indexed base and head definitions and counts direct consumer references with Amazon Athena. Quasar exposes those findings through its REST and GraphQL APIs and MCP server; follow-up usage queries provide dependency-version breakdowns and source locations. A separate compatibility-impact assessment can also follow implementations and their callers when a producer supplies a changed JVM symbol.
Consider this simplified API change:
public interface Client {
- Result getLegacyValue(Request request);
+ Result getValue(Request request, Options options);
}
For a detailed compatibility-impact assessment of this removal, a producer-side tool supplies the old method descriptor. Quasar constructs its canonical symbol identity. This abridged excerpt from the direct-reference portion of Quasar’s Amazon Athena query shows the essential match:
SELECT c.change_id, 'DIRECT_REFERENCE' AS evidence_kind,
       r.scm_type, r.org, r.repo, r.dep_version, r.file_path
FROM requested_changes c
JOIN quasar.symbol_refs r
  ON r.symbol_canonical = c.target_canonical
requested_changes contains the API changes submitted by the producer. The SQL excerpt finds repositories that call the removed method. Quasar also checks implementations and calls through them, so it can count each affected repository once. It returns sample dependency versions and file locations to help investigate the result.
For the Client change, this tells the producer which repositories still use getLegacyValue, which versions they use, and where some of those calls occur. That helps the producer decide whether to coordinate a migration before removing the method.
Bringing the Analysis Before Release
Version-to-version comparison is valuable when planning an upgrade or writing a migration guide. Producers benefit even more when feedback arrives during code review.
For pull-request analysis, Quasar stores API definition snapshots keyed by commit. Given a base and head commit, it classifies symbols as added, removed, or signature-modified. Removals and modifications then become candidates for consumer-impact analysis.
An incompatible change is not automatically a high-risk change. Quasar reports the observed impact so the producer can decide what to do; it does not enforce a release policy. “No references observed” means only that Quasar found none in the indexed population. Reflection, configuration, dynamic loading, stale branches, or incomplete indexing can hide consumers. The result needs to show whether the requested commits were indexed, how fresh the consumer indexes are, and whether evidence was truncated.
Pull-request review requires indexed snapshots for the exact base and head commits. If either is unavailable, Quasar reports that it cannot compare them; it does not substitute a default-branch snapshot. This keeps a missing comparison from looking like a clean API diff.
Return to our Client change. This illustrative report brings together signals available through Quasar's API comparison, consumer-usage queries, and library-level criticality. It is not a literal response from one API:
{
  "change": "REMOVED",
  "symbol": "Client#getLegacyValue(Request)",
  "affectedRepositories": 137,
  "versionDistribution": [
    { "version": "4.2.1", "repositories": 86 },
    { "version": "4.1.7", "repositories": 38 },
    { "version": "3.9.4", "repositories": 13 }
  ],
  "sampleConsumerLocations": [
    {
      "repository": "checkout-service",
      "filePath": "src/main/java/com/example/checkout/CheckoutClient.java",
      "lines": [84, 129]
    },
    {
      "repository": "client-wrapper",
      "filePath": "src/main/java/com/example/client/ClientAdapter.java",
      "lines": [57]
    }
  ],
  "libraryCriticality": {
    "tier": 1,
    "basis": "highest-tier downstream application"
  },
  "comparison": {
    "baseShaFound": true,
    "headShaFound": true
  }
}An impact report shows 137 affected repositories distributed across library versions 4.2.1, 4.1.7, and 3.9.4.
The repository count is symbol-specific: in this example, 137 indexed repositories refer to the removed method. The version distribution reveals a dominant cohort on 4.2.1 and a smaller long tail still on 3.9.4. A producer can inspect affected repositories and retrieve indexed file paths, with line numbers where the index provides them. The JSON shows only two sample locations to keep the example readable. The filePath and lines shape mirrors Quasar's query contract. The tier is broader context about the library, inherited from its highest-criticality downstream application; it does not imply that all 137 callers are Tier 1.
Together, those signals change the producer’s plan. Instead of merging the removal and waiting for failures, the producer can retain and deprecate the old method, publish a migration path, coordinate a broader migration, and track the long-tail versions before removal. File paths and available line numbers turn that scope into a concrete work list for engineers or coding agents. The same API diff paired with weak or stale evidence would lead to a different action: refresh the indexes before deciding. The value is not merely detecting the removal; it is choosing a proportionate next step.
A pre-release workflow enriches API changes with consumer impact and evidence quality before the producer decides how to proceed
A Polyglot Foundation with SCIP
The shared SCIP format also lets Quasar index several language ecosystems. Each language indexer resolves its own code, while Quasar can use the resulting symbol identities to find references across repositories.
Conceptually, client-lib indexes Client#getLegacyValue(Request) as a definition, while checkout-service indexes a reference to the same symbol. Quasar can then connect the library API to its consumer across repositories.
Language-specific indexers emit SCIP definitions, references, and relationships into Quasar’s shared semantic graph.
Relationships are especially useful when generated code separates the API a producer owns from the symbols consumers invoke. For example, Quasar can trace a Protobuf definition through its generated Java members to the repositories that use them, even when consumer code never names the .proto element.
SCIP records symbols and their references; it does not determine whether an API change violates an ecosystem’s compatibility rules. Today, Quasar compares indexed JVM and Protobuf API definitions and traces Protobuf changes through generated Java to find affected repositories. A separate JVM compatibility-impact path uses breaks identified by a producer-side tool to query affected repositories. Go, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Rust support usage queries, but Quasar does not yet assess their breaking API changes.
Moving Risk Assessment Earlier
Today, Quasar surfaces API-change findings on pull requests, including observed consumer counts and confidence. Producers can use its other queries to inspect dependency versions and source locations, with library criticality as broader context. Together, those signals support a decision before merge.
We want to move that context earlier. An agent writing library code should recognize when it is changing a public symbol and consult Quasar before the change becomes a pull request. Quasar’s APIs and Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration provide an access path, but access alone does not create awareness. The coding workflow must also recognize public API edits so the agent knows when to query impact and when to involve the producer.
Today Quasar assesses risk on a pull request. The future workflow gives agents consumer-impact context while they write code, before the pull request is opened.
Earlier guidance will not replace pull-request analysis. The PR assessment will still verify the concrete diff and catch changes that were not recognized during coding. Coverage, freshness, ambiguity, unsupported platforms, and truncation must travel through both checks in machine-readable form. An agent should not turn “no observed usages in the available index” into “safe to remove.”
Today, agents can query Quasar through MCP when prompted. We are working toward making that context part of the coding workflow, then using identified call sites to prepare migration changes. Quasar supplies semantic evidence, an agent reduces migration toil, and the library producer remains responsible for API and release decisions.
What We Learned
Building this workflow led us to four practical lessons.

Separate compatibility from reach. A removed method can break the API contract even when Quasar finds no callers. A list of affected repositories and their library versions shows the migration work ahead. Producers need both signals to choose a release path.
Make the evidence inspectable. A repository count is more useful with sample call sites and a version breakdown. The result also needs to show which commits were indexed, how fresh the consumer indexes are, and whether evidence was truncated. Otherwise, “no usage found” can be mistaken for proof that nobody is affected.
Keep usage and compatibility separate across languages. SCIP lets Quasar find symbol references in several ecosystems. Deciding whether an API change is breaking requires compatibility rules or a trusted producer-side signal for that ecosystem.
Bring evidence to the producer while choices are open. Pull-request findings can prompt a producer to retain an API, publish a migration path, or coordinate consumers before merge. Moving the same evidence into the coding workflow could shape the edit earlier. After release, it still helps locate consumers that need to migrate.

Today, Quasar indexes JVM, Go, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Rust code for cross-repository usage analysis. It compares JVM APIs and traces Protobuf changes through generated Java. Producers can review change findings through Quasar’s REST and GraphQL APIs or its MCP server, then investigate affected repositories and call sites. We are extending this foundation toward more ecosystem-specific compatibility checks, deeper code-review integration, and agent-assisted consumer migrations that keep release approval with the producer.
Quasar is internal to Netflix, but the pattern is portable: index code semantically, retain API definitions, compare them at the point of change, query affected consumers, and report the quality of the evidence. Library producers need more than a compatibility verdict. They need to know who may be affected and have enough time to act before release.
A huge thank you to the Java Platform team at Netflix. Their expertise, collaboration, and support made this work possible
Related Talks

From Lag to Lightning: Transforming Dependency Update Timelines explores how Netflix shortened dependency-update timelines.
Netflix’s Journey to Confident Automated Code Changes discusses building confidence in automated changes at scale.

posts.title: From GDScript to GDExtensions: One IDE for Your Godot Code
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
JetBrains has been a Platinum sponsor of the Godot Foundation since August 2025, and we’ve renewed our sponsorship into 2027. Over the past year, Rider has expanded its Godot support to cover GDScript, C#, and C++ GDExtensions in one place. It’s free for non-commercial use, including hobby projects, learning, open source, and content creation.
At GodotCon in Amsterdam, the Netherlands, this April, many developers we talked to didn’t know Rider handles GDScript, and many assumed Rider required a paid subscription. If you know Rider mainly as a C# IDE, there’s more in Rider for your Godot project than you might expect.
Along the way, we’ve bundled GDScript support, expanded debugging and testing, introduced an official Godot editor addon, and added project templates for addon developers. The Rider 2026.3 Early Access Program brings another set of improvements you can try today.
Here’s what all that support looks like when you sit down to build your game.




Work with your scripts and scenes together
A growing Godot project gives you more to keep track of: scripts, signals, resources, and the scene nodes that connect them. Rider helps you follow those connections while you work.
Rider 2025.2 bundled GDScript support, built on what was previously a community-driven plugin. It brought GDScript-specific code completion, Find Usages, Rename refactoring, documentation, and inspections into the IDE, alongside the Scene Preview tool window, which shows the nodes in your current scene.
That gives you practical ways to explore and change a project: Find where a function is used before editing it, navigate to a declaration, or catch a missing return type while you’re still writing the script.
Rider 2026.2 made working across scenes and code more direct. You can drag nodes from Scene Preview into your script to insert their paths, or generate @onready and @export variables. You can select several nodes at once, with paths resolved relative to the script you’re editing. The release also introduced a configurable GDScript formatter and improved resolution of Autoloads and uid:// resource references. See the 2026.2 updates for more details.
You can keep building your scenes in Godot while using Rider to navigate, edit, debug, and understand the code behind them.
Connect Rider to the Godot editor
The official JetBrains Rider Integration addon makes setting up that workflow easier.
It detects your Rider installations, lets you choose the version you want to use, and adds a Use Rider toggle to Godot’s toolbar. It also applies recommended editor settings, reducing the manual configuration needed to get started.
The addon is available from the Godot Asset Store. Install it in your project, select Rider, and continue working with both editors.
Debug and test your gameplay
You can debug GDScript in Rider: Set breakpoints in your scripts and launch the game from Rider, and then execution will stop at your breakpoint. As of Rider 2025.3, you can also debug specific scenes and tool scripts and pass arguments to a debugging session.
For C# projects, Rider combines .NET editing and refactoring tools with Godot-specific navigation and debugging. 
When a gameplay bug only appears under particular conditions, conditional breakpoints help you stop at the relevant moment. Logging breakpoints let you inspect values without interrupting the game, so you don’t have to scatter print() calls through your scripts. If your project mixes GDScript and C#, you can attach the .NET debugger to a GDScript debugging session and debug GDScript and C# at the same time.
Rider 2025.3 added integration with the Chickensoft GoDotTest runner, so you can run and debug C# tests from the IDE. It also introduced automatic rebuilding when Rider loses focus, helping changes to exported properties appear in the Godot Inspector without a separate manual build.
Mega Crit moved Slay the Spire 2 from Unity to Godot, and the team uses C# and Rider to develop it.
“It always feels easy and intuitive to navigate Slay the Spire 2’s codebase using Rider. Setting up multiplayer configurations, running unit tests locally, and getting the rest of the team up to speed has been a breeze as well!”

            
Casey Yano
                                                                CEO & Co-Founder, Mega Crit
                                    







Build native extensions and reusable addons
Rider’s C++ support covers the native side of a Godot project. Whether you’re writing a GDExtension, contributing to the engine, or maintaining your own engine fork, that code lives in the same IDE as your scripts.
At GodotCon, one developer opened a 5,000-line C++ file that had been slow to work with in their usual editor and found it to be fast in Rider.
CMake support came out of Beta in Rider 2026.2. The same release added Natvis support to the C++ debugger on Linux and macOS, including support for Godot’s godot-cpp.natvis visualizers. Those visualizers make Godot’s native types easier to inspect while debugging. 
Explore the native development updates
                                                    
For addon authors, Rider 2026.2 introduced templates for Godot games, assets, and editor plugins, with an optional C++ GDExtension managed through CMake. The templates provide project structure, build settings, and run configurations, giving you a starting point for developing and debugging your addon.
When the new Asset Store launched in May, the Godot Foundation highlighted Rider’s support for addon developers. Whether you’re sharing a small editor tool or maintaining a native extension, Rider now provides a dedicated workflow for addon development. 
Try the next improvements in the 2026.3 EAP
The Rider 2026.3 Early Access Program includes more Godot improvements. These are available in preview builds; they aren’t part of the current stable 2026.2 release. The stable Rider 2026.3 release is due later this year.
For GDScript, the changes make it easier to trace how your scenes and scripts connect:
Get completion for unique node names. Rider suggests %UniqueName references using the nodes marked as unique in your scene.
Navigate from code to nodes. $Node and %UniqueNode references link to the corresponding scene node.
Find signal connections. Find Usages now includes connections made through Callable, helping you trace how a callback is connected.
Explore expressions while debugging. Code completion is available in the debugger’s Immediate window.
Navigate longer scripts. Code regions appear in the Structure view, making it easier to move between sections.
These changes are documented in the EAP 2 notes, EAP 4 notes, and Structure view issue.
A new capability is available for C# debugging. EAP 3 introduced the ability to use the Remote Scene tree and node inspector while debugging C# to see the running game’s live node tree and inspect node properties.
Rider is more reliable when working with several Godot projects at once, too. When Rider launches Godot editors, it can allocate separate language-server and debugger ports, reducing conflicts between instances. 
We’re still improving GDScript support, and the conversations at GodotCon helped us understand where it needs more work. Trying the EAP with your own project and telling us what gets in your way helps us make useful improvements.
Supporting the engine and the people building with it
Beyond the sponsorship, some of our work happens in Godot itself. In October 2025, an upstream contribution from Rider developer Ivan Šachov extended Godot’s Debug Adapter Protocol support with scene selection and command-line arguments. That’s what lets Rider debug specific scenes and pass arguments to a session. Because the change lives in Godot, other external development tools can build on it too.
Conversations with developers and issue reports also help us identify specific problems to fix.
Feedback from Photon Engine helped us identify an issue with how Rider handled GDExtension singletons in GDScript. The resulting highlighting fix is available in the 2026.3 EAP – a concrete example of a report from a Godot tool developer improving the experience for others. If you build tools or middleware for Godot and something in Rider gets in your way, we want to hear about it.
For a walkthrough of Rider across scripting and native development, watch Matt Ellis’s GodotCon session, From Game to Engine: JetBrains Rider as Your One-Stop Godot IDE.
If you already work with an AI agent, Rider can fit into that workflow. Air, our plugin for agentic development, is now in Early Access. It lets you start coding agents from Rider, follow what they’re doing, attach your own skills, and review their changes, while you keep using the debugger and refactorings on the code they produce. Compatible agents you run outside Rider, such as Junie, Claude Code, or Codex, can connect to Rider’s MCP server and use its tools, from the Rename refactoring to run configurations.
At JetBrains GameDev Day in September, Sharmishtha Sen showed one version of this in a Godot project. In Prompt to Playable World: Live-Building AI-Driven PCG with Godot, C#, and Gemini, she built a procedural generation pipeline in C# driven by language models, tuned in the Godot Inspector, and debugged in Rider.
Try it with your project
Download Rider and install the Rider Integration addon to get started. Rider is free for non-commercial use. To explore the preview features described above, download a 2026.3 EAP build.
Open a scene, follow a signal connection, or debug the part of your game you’re working on. We’d like to hear what helps, and what still needs work. Share your feedback on YouTrack.
A few of us from the Rider team will be at GodotFest in Munich, Germany, on November 3–4. If you spot us, say hi and tell us what you’d like Rider to do better.
You can also support the engine directly through the Godot Development Fund.

posts.title: SEGGER Tools Gain Deeper Integration in CLion with AI-assisted Debugging
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Amsterdam, Netherlands — October 29, 2026
SEGGER’s embedded development tools are now more deeply integrated into JetBrains CLion. CLion provides dedicated configuration for J-Link debug probes as well as direct access to SEGGER’s Ozone debugger and SystemView real-time software analysis tool, connecting coding and ultra-fast flash programming with advanced debugging and real-time system analysis.
CLion’s newest release introduces AI-powered debugging tools. Its new AI skill for hard-fault debugging uses dedicated tooling to automatically decode fault registers and trace issues back to their source on Cortex-M devices, including targets connected via J-Link.
The combination of CLion’s AI capabilities and J-Link’s fast, reliable access to embedded targets enables agentic development to go beyond code generation. Developers can use information obtained from the actual hardware to analyze faults, identify their underlying causes, and accelerate the process of finding and fixing bugs.
“Embedded development is where AI agent has to understand more than code – it needs real evidence from the target,” says Artemy Pestretsov, Head of C/C++ Ecosystem at JetBrains. “CLion brings SEGGER’s J-Link, Ozone, and SystemView workflows closer to the development environment while giving agents access to real debugger context. This moves agentic AI usage beyond code generation toward hardware-aware engineering: investigating faults, reasoning from the state of the device, and helping developers reach a verified fix faster.”
“J-Link is about giving developers fast, reliable access to their hardware, whichever IDE they use,” says Dirk Akemann, Head of Technical Marketing at SEGGER. “With CLion’s support for J-Link and direct access to Ozone and SystemView, developers can move easily from development and debugging to in-depth system analysis. CLion’s new agentic capabilities also show how AI can go beyond code generation and help developers investigate problems directly on real hardware.”
Join a free webinar hosted by JetBrains and SEGGER
on November 10, 2026, at 2:00 pm (CET) / 1:00 pm (UTC)
to see the integration in action.
Register for the Webinar
J-Link supports more than 15,000 microcontrollers and SoCs across a broad range of architectures from over 120 silicon vendors and integrates with more than 35 leading IDEs and development environments. Its ultra-fast flash programming speeds and broad device support give developers fast, reliable access to their target hardware. Together, J-Link, Ozone, and SystemView give CLion users access to SEGGER’s debugging and system analysis ecosystem directly from their development environment.
For more information about J-Link, please visit: https://www.segger.com/products/debug-probes/j-link/
For more information about Ozone, please visit: https://www.segger.com/products/development-tools/ozone-j-link-debugger/
For more information about SystemView, please visit: https://www.segger.com/products/development-tools/systemview/
About SEGGER
Founded in 1992, SEGGER Microcontroller GmbH has over three decades of experience in embedded systems, producing cutting-edge RTOS and software libraries, J-Link and J-Trace debug and trace probes, a line of Flasher ISPs, and software development tools. 
SEGGER’s all-in-one solution emPower OS provides an RTOS and a complete spectrum of software libraries for, among other things, communication, security, data compression and storage, user-interface software, and more. emPower OS gives developers a head start, allowing them to benefit from decades of experience in the embedded industry.
SEGGER’s professional embedded-development software and tools are simple in design, optimized for embedded systems, and support the entire embedded-system development process with their affordability, high quality, flexibility, and ease of use.
SEGGER, with headquarters in Monheim am Rhein, Germany, also has an office in Boston, Massachusetts, United States, and branch operations in Silicon Valley, California, United States; Shanghai, China; and the United Kingdom. With distributors on most continents, SEGGER’s full product range is available worldwide.
For more information on SEGGER, visit www.segger.com.
About JetBrains
JetBrains creates intelligent software development tools that help developers and organizations build, understand and maintain software with confidence. Trusted by more than 15 million users and 88 Fortune Global Top 100 companies, JetBrains combines deep code intelligence with AI to help teams stay in control as software development evolves. Its portfolio of more than 30 products includes award-winning IDEs such as IntelliJ IDEA and PyCharm, as well as the JetBrains AI-powered coding assistant, coding agent Junie, and Mellum, JetBrains’ focal LLM purpose-built for code-related tasks. It also includes JetBrains Central, which gives organisations visibility and governance over AI across their development environments. The portfolio is complemented by productivity tools such as YouTrack, Qodana and TeamCity. JetBrains is also the creator of Kotlin, a cross-platform language used by more than 2.5 million developers a year, worldwide. The company is headquartered in Amsterdam, the Netherlands, and has offices around the world.

posts.title: Prompts That Can Write Themselves: A Kotlin Experiment
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
TL;DR
Koog Agents Optimization Library is a research library developed by JetBrains Research for optimizing the prompts of Koog agents. With it, you write a first version of each instruction, mark the steps worth tuning, provide the library with a training set, and specify a way to score the agent’s output. The library then runs your agent, learns from what happens, and hands back better instructions as a separate JSON file you can read, review, and commit. No rewrite of the agent is needed.
The examples in this post use GEPA, a prompt optimizer that learns from your agent’s failures and successes. In this post, we walk you through examples running on the privacy benchmark PUPA. GEPA improved our agent’s score from 81.19 to 94.22.
👉 Koog Agent Optimization Library (GitHub) 
👉Docs
👉 Examples
An agent to optimize
Koog is JetBrains’ Kotlin framework for building agents. It treats an agent as a program: you declare control flow as a typed graph of nodes and edges, and each step can carry its own prompt, tools, and model.
We have a whole agent written in it: our port of PAPILLON, a privacy pipeline that GEPA uses as one of its benchmarks. It runs on PUPA, a dataset of user queries that carry personal details. The agent has to answer such a query with help from a big external model without handing that model any of those details, so it rewrites the question without the details, sends that version out, and writes the reply from what comes back.
fun pupaStrategy(untrustedModel: LLModel) = strategy("pupa-papillon") {
    val craftRedactedRequest by subgraphWithTask<PupaAgentInput, PupaRedactedRequest>(
        name = "craft_redacted_request",
    ) { input -> REDACT_INSTRUCTION + "\n\nuser_query:\n${input.userQuery}" }

    val callUntrustedModel by subgraph<String, String>(
        name = "untrusted_model",
        llmModel = untrustedModel,
    ) { /* one call to the big model */ }

    val respondToQuery by subgraphWithTask<PupaResponseInput, PupaFinalResponse>(
        name = "respond_to_query",
    ) { input -> RESPOND_INSTRUCTION + "\n\n" + input.rendered() }

    // …plus three small nodes carrying state
}




Only three steps are needed to do the work here: the first rewrites the question, the second calls the big model, and the third writes the reply. Everything else is plumbing. Two of those three steps hold an instruction that a human wrote, and they are the ones you would want an optimizer to take over.
Marking a step as optimizable
The library adds one builder. Swap subgraphWithTask for optimizableSubgraphWithTask on the steps you want tuned, and lift the instruction out of the string it was buried in:
fun pupaStrategy(untrustedModel: LLModel) = strategy("pupa-papillon") {
    val craftRedactedRequest by optimizableSubgraphWithTask<PupaAgentInput, PupaRedactedRequest>(
        name = "craft_redacted_request",
        optimizableInstruction = REDACT_INSTRUCTION,
    ) { _, input -> "user_query:\n${input.userQuery}" }
    
    val callUntrustedModel by subgraph<String, String>(
        name = "untrusted_model",
        llmModel = untrustedModel,
    ) { /* one call to the model */ }

    val respondToQuery by optimizableSubgraphWithTask<PupaResponseInput, PupaFinalResponse>(
        name = "respond_to_query",
        optimizableInstruction = RESPOND_INSTRUCTION,
    ) { _, input -> input.rendered() }

    // …and the same plumbing and wiring as before.
}




With the step marked as “optimizable”, the graph itself remains unchanged. The instruction just moved into a parameter of its own, where an optimizer can find it and replace it. When there is no artifact to load, the step runs on the text you wrote.
Running the optimizer
GEPA runs your agent over the training set, shows a second model what went wrong, and asks it for a better instruction. Then it tries that instruction and repeats it, round after round, within the budget you set. Across those rounds it keeps several candidate instructions alive at once, so it does not drop one that only wins on your hardest items.
The optimizer needs one thing from the agent’s author: a function that, given a finished run, returns a score and a short summary of how it went. The score decides which candidates survive, and the text is what the second model reads. Here, that text is one line of numbers:
PUPA overall score: 0.50. Quality score: 1.00. Privacy score: 0.00. PII leakage ratio: 1.00.
That line, plus what the step itself received and produced, is everything GEPA had to work from when it wrote the instruction in the next section.
The rest is just two calls:
val optimizer = GEPAOptimizer(
    gepaFeedback = pupaFeedback,
    reflectionModel = OpenAIModels.Chat.GPT4_1Mini,
    numRollouts = 2426, // a practical start is 6 to 20x your training set
    storagePath = ResilientPath("build/artifacts/pupa-gepa.json"),
)

optimizer.train(session) // the session wraps your agent, dataset, and metric
val optimized = optimizer.loadOptimizedAgent(agent)




train writes the artifact, and loadOptimizedAgent reads it back and hands you a copy of your agent running the new instructions. Every optimizer in the library has those same two methods, so switching between them leaves the surrounding code alone.
What GEPA wrote
The step that strips the personal details started with this instruction:
Given a private user query, create a privacy-preserving request for a powerful external LLM.
The LLM may assist without learning private information about the user.
Two lines, deliberately vague. It says nothing about how much redaction would be enough.
By the end of the run, that same step was running a 4,456-character instruction. Here are three pieces of it:
2. Redaction and Generalization
   - Replace all such information with broad, generic placeholders or neutral terms
     (e.g., "the minor," "the course," "the company," "a noted musician," "two large
     urban communities," "the agency," "the program," or "a fellowship honoring an
     individual").
[...]
Additional Domain-Specific Considerations:
- For academic or educational content, avoid exposing real professor names, specific
  course titles or codes, individual student names, or direct internal feedback. Use
  neutral terms like "the minor," "the course," "professors," "students," and "mentors."
[...]
Overall Strategy:
Create a balanced abstraction that ensures zero leakage of private or identifiable data
while preserving the user's original task in sufficient detail for accurate execution
by a LLM.




Every detail in the instruction above came out of the runs, not from us. You would probably not sit down and write the placeholder vocabulary, the rule about professor names and course codes, or the overall strategy at the end. That strategy states a trade-off we never mentioned: keep the leakage at zero, but leave enough detail to do the job.
Results
We wanted to know whether our GEPA in Koog does what it is supposed to, so we ran it on the benchmarks the project itself uses and checked whether the agents performed better.
Take PUPA, for example, the benchmark that the above agent runs on. Its baseline was already 81.19, with little room left above it, but optimization still improved it by 13 points to 94.22. Both numbers are the mean of five runs, and the gain is statistically significant.
The rest of the benchmarks, including how our numbers line up with the original implementation, can be found in the docs.
Three more optimizers
Besides GEPA, the library implements three more optimizers behind the same interface:
BootstrapFewShot mines demonstrations out of your successful runs. It makes no LLM calls beyond running your own agent, making it the cheapest option to try first.
MIPROv2 searches across instructions and demonstrations.
ACE grows a playbook of insights that rides along with the system prompt, for when you want the agent to accumulate knowledge rather than a better-worded instruction.
Swapping between them is one constructor; the train and loadOptimizedAgent calls around it stay as they are. Writing your own means implementing those same two methods, and all four of ours fit behind them without an escape hatch.
Where to find it
The library, its documentation, and the full benchmark results are in the open-source repository. The optimizable-subgraph support it relies on currently lives in a fork of Koog; we expect it to land upstream.
