posts.title: Junie Local became 70% faster on Mac M5
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Junie Local now delivers ~70 tokens/s on M5 Max for coding tasks, up from ~40 tokens/s, with bursts up to 107 tokens/s. Two changes made this possible: the Splash inference engine and a new DFlash2 draft model.




Back in August, when we first released Junie Local for Mac M5, we spent a lot of time optimizing Junie and the MLX-VLM inference engine to achieve the maximum possible (at that time) performance. But two months is apparently a very long period at the current pace of LLM development. During this time, new, exciting ways to speed up inference were released by the community. We looked at and tested all of them, then picked the most promising parts to include in Junie Local.
In September, Inco AI released its Splash engine, built around the Qwen models. Focusing on just a couple of models lets Splash do what a general-purpose engine can’t: every decode step verifies eight drafted tokens at once, and attention over the context costs an order of magnitude less per position, so decode speed barely drops as context grows. The prefill, though, was on par with our optimized MLX-VLM engine. Since we had already taught MLX-VLM to use int8 operations on M5 chips, we ported the same optimization to Splash. In this release, Splash replaces MLX-VLM as Junie Local’s inference engine.
But a good engine is only part of the equation. We also needed a model-drafter that would enable more efficient speculative decoding. When using a speculator, acceptance rate defines the decode speed. A low acceptance rate could make decoding even slower.
Out of the box, Splash uses the DFlash2 drafter model for Qwen 3.8-27B. But Qwen 3.8 has a slight issue – it tends to overthink a lot. So the whole win of the generation speed is killed by the enormous amount of thinking tokens that need to be generated. 
To address this problem, we previously released the Qwen3.8-3.6-27B-blend, which is more capable than Qwen 3.6 yet uses only 30% more tokens. And in this release, we are also including the DFlash2 draft model for Qwen3.8-3.6-27B-blend.
DFlash-based models are fast but very sensitive to in-domain distribution: acceptance rate on familiar tasks is higher, so the agent will work faster on familiar tasks and slower on unfamiliar ones.
To train this DFlash2 model, we generated a diverse set of agentic coding trajectories by running the Junie Local harness inside our internal coding environment with Qwen3.8-3.6-27B-blend. We then took the Qwen 3.8 DFlash2 draft model as a starting checkpoint and fine-tuned it with SpecForge on those coding trajectories. This way, our DFlash2 drafter delivers the highest speed and acceptance rate when you use it to code with Junie Local.
What surprised us was that you don’t need many trajectories to fine-tune a drafter. It took us just ~1 million generated tokens (with ~71M tokens read) to match Inco’s acceptance rate! As a side bonus, we also created a DFlash2 drafter for Qwen 3.6, trained in a similar fashion




And this acceptance rate, together with the Splash engine, pays off: compared to the previous MTP + MLX-VLM approach, we have ~ 2x improvement.
Combining all these improvements together, in this release we:
improved the generation speed from ~40 t/s to ~70 t/s
got 850 t/s → 1200 t/s prefill improvement
reduced memory consumption: on 100k context, we need ~ 24 GB of RAM
And starting with this release, you can use it on M4 Macs and newer with 64GB of RAM.
Please note that on M4, prefill is approximately 4 times slower than on M5. It means that loading the system prompt and other context will be slow.
How to upgrade
Run junie update to upgrade Junie to the latest version, then launch the CLI. Once you’re inside Junie, run /local and press ctrl + r to update the inference engine.
If you don’t have Junie yet, you can install Junie and the local model by running:
curl -fsSL https://junie.jetbrains.com/install.sh | bash -s -- --local-model
You can find both DFlash2 drafters on HuggingFace:
Qwen3.8-3.6-27B-blend-DFlash2
Qwen3.6-27B-DFlash2

posts.title: Junie Eco Mode
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Not every step of a coding task needs the smartest model in the world.
Junie Eco Mode uses your selected model to investigate a coding task and create a plan, then hands implementation and testing to a lower-cost model. In two internal benchmarks, this approach reduced average model cost per task by 48% and 57%, while average resolve rates changed by less than one percentage point.
Watch any AI coding agent work on a task and you’ll see it moves in small steps. It opens a file, searches the project, makes an edit, runs the tests, reads an error message, fixes a missing line, runs the tests again. That’s simply what writing software looks like, and experienced engineers work the same way. Only a handful of those steps call for hard judgment, understanding the request, finding the right place in the code, deciding on an approach. The rest is execution, carrying out a decision that has already been made.
Yet, coding agents usually run one AI model for the whole task. If that’s the smartest, most expensive model available, you pay its premium price for every single step, including the twentieth “run the tests again”.
Think about how a building gets built. You hire an architect to design it, not to lay every brick. The architect makes the hard decisions, writes them down, and a construction crew does the building.
Eco mode brings that idea to Junie. The model you chose (Opus, Fable, Grok, GPT) acts as the architect, it studies the code and writes a plan. A much cheaper model acts as the builder, it takes the plan and does the actual work. In our latest internal benchmarks, Eco mode cut average model cost per task by about half: 57% on benchmark B and 48% on benchmark A. Average resolve rates across the tested configurations changed by less than one percentage point.
Eco mode is currently available to JetBrains Air EAP users in IDEs: in IntelliJ IDEA 2026.3 Beta, with other IDEs’ Betas to follow, and in 2026.2 versions of JetBrains IDEs. It is generally available in the Junie CLI starting with version 26.10.20. Eco mode is on by default for supported model-and-effort configurations.
How Junie Eco mode works
Eco mode splits a coding task into two parts and gives each part to the model that suits it best.
Step 1: the architect makes a plan. When you ask Junie to change your code, it first hands the task to the model you chose, at the effort level you chose. In this phase the model is only allowed to look: it reads and searches the code but doesn’t change anything. (The one exception: if you reported a bug, it may write a small test that shows the bug happening.) It already knows everything you’ve discussed with Junie so far, so you never have to repeat yourself. It’s built to be quick, usually about 15 steps, and it stops as soon as it knows what to change and how.
The result is a short plan with a fixed structure:
Goal: what the change should achieve
Scope: what is in and what is out
Where to change: the specific files and parts of the code
Approach: how to make the change
Tests: how to check that it works
Risks and corner cases: what could go wrong




Step 2: the builder follows the plan. Junie then hands the same conversation, plan included, to a much cheaper model (currently GPT-6 Luna). The builder does the long, hands-on part: it edits files, runs the build and the tests, fixes what breaks, and finishes the task. 




Junie investigates with your selected model, then hands the conversation and structured plan to a lower-cost model for implementation.
This works because of how the cost of a task adds up. Planning takes only a few steps, but it needs good judgment. Building takes many steps, and most of them just follow the plan. With Eco mode, you pay premium prices only for the part that needs premium judgment.
Why not just pick a model for each task?
The obvious alternative is to look at each request and guess up front whether it’s hard (use the expensive model) or easy (use the cheap one). We don’t think that works well:
You can’t tell how hard a task is from the request alone. “Fix the test that sometimes fails” might be a one-line fix or a week-long investigation. Guessing up front means deciding before anyone has looked at the code. Eco mode has the smart model look first.
Every task still gets top-quality thinking. The cheap model never decides what to build. It only carries out decisions the smart model has already made.
The handoff is a written plan, not a guess. Because the plan always has the same structure, the builder starts out knowing which files to touch, how to test the change, and what to watch out for.
One handoff per task
Some tools let a cheap model “call a smarter friend” for advice whenever it gets stuck. Each of those calls means re-sending a big chunk of the conversation to the expensive model, and that adds up quickly. Eco mode hands off once, from architect to builder, and never switches back and forth. That keeps things simple and cheap.
When Eco mode stays out of the way
Eco mode only steps in where it’s likely to help:
Only for tasks that require code changes. The planning step runs only when your task calls for a code change you intend to keep. Questions, explanations, setting up a project, “run this and tell me what happens”, all of these stay with your chosen model from start to finish.
Off where it doesn’t save money. Eco mode is unavailable in /remote sessions and with certain model-and-effort combinations, including Opus 5.5 at low effort and Sonnet 5.5.
Benchmark results
For each tested model-and-effort configuration, we ran the same tasks with Eco off and on. Our latest evaluation covered two internal benchmarks: benchmark B (29 paired configurations) and benchmark A (21 paired configurations). These are configuration counts, not task counts. Each pair compares Eco with the same model-and-effort baseline.
Both benchmarks consist entirely of real-world tasks of varying complexity drawn from private repositories. Benchmark B covers a broad range of private repositories of different sizes and project contexts. Benchmark A includes tasks from very large repositories, whose scale makes many tasks significantly more challenging.
Resolve rate is the share of benchmark tasks marked as successfully resolved by the evaluation. We report model cost per task and resolve rate averaged across the tested configurations.
Model cost and resolve rate




Latest internal evaluation. Averages across 29 model-and-effort pairs on benchmark B and 21 on benchmark A. Results vary by model and workload.
On benchmark B, average model cost per task fell from \$2.61 to \$1.11 (57.3%), while the average resolve rate moved from 49.1% to 48.5%, a decrease of 0.6 percentage points.
On benchmark A, average model cost per task fell from \$2.51 to \$1.30 (48.1%). Average resolve rates round to 32.1% both with and without Eco.
Individual configurations can show larger changes in resolve rate. The percentages for cost reduction are calculated from the more precise values shown in the chart; dollar amounts in the text are rounded to cents.
Examples from evaluation
The following examples come from an evaluation on 100 real coding tasks from benchmark B. In that evaluation, Eco reduced the model cost per task by approximately 63% for Opus 5.5 at max effort.

Opus 5.5 (max) + Eco56%$1.81

Fable 5.1 (high) + Eco52%$1.38
Grok 4.7 (high)46%$3.37

Try it
Eco mode is available in:
JetBrains Air in IDEs: In 2026.2 versions of JetBrains IDEs and in IntelliJ IDEA 2026.3 EAP starting with the Beta build, with other IDEs’ 2026.3 EAP builds to follow.
Junie CLI: Generally available in version 26.10.20 and later.
In these environments, Eco mode is on by default for Opus 5, Opus 5.5 (medium effort and above), Fable 5.1, Grok 4.5 / 4.6 / 4.7, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Sol, GPT-5.6 Terra, and GPT-6 Astra. You can turn Eco off whenever you want one model to handle the entire task.
Use the model picker to turn Eco on or off. Pick the model you trust to do the thinking, and Eco mode will take care of the rest.
One model per task is becoming a thing of the past
The smartest AI models keep getting better, but still come at a higher cost. Meanwhile, cheap models have quietly become good enough to do most of the hands-on work, as long as someone tells them exactly what to do. We don’t think the future of AI coding assistants is a single model, or a system that guesses one model up front. It’s a team where each part of the job goes to the model best suited for it.
Eco mode is our first step in that direction. Try it on your real work and tell us where it works well and where it falls short.

posts.title: Getting Started with Air in JetBrains IDEs – Part 1
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Setting coding agents up to handle several tasks while you continue working is easy. The harder part is knowing where each task stands, what each agent has changed, and what still needs your attention.
Recently, we introduced Air in JetBrains IDEs. It brings coding agents into the environment where you already write, review, run, and test your code. From one workspace, you can manage different agent sessions, track their progress, and review their changes with familiar JetBrains tools.
In the first video of our Air in IDEs series, Developer Advocate Kristel Cocoli puts this workflow into practice. Starting with an existing project, she asks agents to extend it, reviews the changes, and tests the result.
You can watch the full video below to see the workflow in action.






Get started with Air in your IDE
Air is available as a plugin from JetBrains Marketplace, and it’s also built into the JetBrains IDEs in the 2026.3 EAP. 
If you install Air from the notification in AI Assistant, AI Assistant will be turned off so the two don’t run side by side.  To switch back, press Shift twice, select Actions, and search for Open AI Assistant. You can also open Options in the Agent Sessions tool window and select Open AI Assistant. There’s no need to disable Air.
Choose an AI Agent for each task
Air can detect compatible agents already installed on your machine. Open Manage Agents to install them from the registry or connect custom ones, then choose the one you want to use for each task.
Codex, Gemini, GitHub Copilot, Claude Agent, and Junie are supported, alongside other agents connected through the Agent Client Protocol (ACP). A JetBrains AI subscription supports all these agents. Only Claude Agent requires a JetBrains AI subscription in Chat view, while its terminal interface lets you use your Claude subscription.
This gives you room to use agents you already know while trying others when a task calls for a different approach.
Installing Air does not install or activate any agents, or cause your project code to be sent to an AI provider. You decide which ones to connect and use. If you connect a third-party agent, your data goes directly to that provider under your existing agreement.
If you are using JetBrains AI, the JetBrains AI Terms of Service apply.
Start your first agent session
Once you’ve chosen an agent, press Cmd+2 (macOS) or Alt+2 (Windows/Linux) to start a new agent session.
From there, describe what you want the agent to do. You can give it more context by attaching a file or selecting relevant code. A focused request gives the agent a clearer starting point, whether you want it to explore part of the project, investigate a bug, or implement a feature.
For a step-by-step introduction, Developer Advocate Mike Hartington walks through the setup in our latest onboarding video below.






Manage agent sessions while you work
Running several sessions is useful only if you can still see what the agents are doing. Air brings their sessions together so you can follow progress, check updates, and identify work that needs your input.
Ask one agent to explore an unfamiliar part of the project and another to implement a change, or run several sessions with the same agent. While the agents work, you can focus on your own code and return later to review their changes. 
Agent sessions open in the editor as tabs, so you can easily switch between them and your code. Changed files and diffs remain accessible from the session, keeping the agent’s work close to the code it affects. Compatible agents can be used through chat or terminal interfaces, and you can use your Claude subscription in Air’s terminal, which opens as a full-screen tab. Where available, you can also use voice input to provide instructions or feedback. 
You can also view session-level cost estimates, helping you understand how agent and model choices affect usage.
Review your code with JetBrains IDE tools
The most important part of delegated work is deciding whether the result is ready for you to accept. Air lets you move from the agent session into the surrounding project, where you can inspect the diff, navigate related code, run tests, and use the other tools available in your JetBrains IDE. If something needs changing, you can send feedback on the diff back to the agent.
Try Air for yourself
Once you’re set up, give Air a focused task in one of your own projects. 
You can currently try Junie in Lite mode without a paid subscription. Just sign in with your JetBrains Account and get started.
In the next part of this series, we’ll explore more advanced Air workflows, including how to use worktrees, add code notes, and generate commit messages.

posts.title: The Terminal in JetBrains IDEs Now Runs on libghostty
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
More and more of your terminal work now runs through tools that push the terminal harder than a shell prompt ever did: AI coding agents like Claude Code and Codex, full-screen apps like Neovim and tmux, system monitors and dashboards. These tools lean on modern terminal protocols, the kind today’s best standalone terminals are built on.
Starting with 2026.3, the built-in terminal in JetBrains IDEs speaks that same language. It now runs on libghostty, the terminal emulation library that powers Ghostty itself.
Many projects already embed libghostty, and it’s widely regarded as a reliable, performant library, so we preferred it over the other options we considered.
In our IDEs, libghostty replaces JediTerm, the terminal emulator we relied on for many years. TUI apps increasingly depend on modern protocols that JediTerm never supported. That gap felt more like a minor inconvenience, since the experience didn’t quite match other terminals, but it wasn’t disruptive enough to warrant a bug report. Now libghostty takes over parsing and terminal state in our IDEs, while the IDE still handles rendering, and higher-level features and integrations.
Here is what those changes mean in practice.
Multi-line prompts and keybindings work the way the docs say
With support for the Kitty keyboard protocol, terminal apps can now distinguish among Enter, Shift+Enter, and Ctrl+Enter, and can request  key-release and repeat events. CLI AI agents like Claude Code, Codex, and Pi, as well as the fish shell, and applications like Neovim, all use this protocol. The terminal also supports xterm’s modifyOtherKeys, an older keyboard protocol that Vim uses.
For you, this means Shift+Enter starts a new line in your prompt instead of sending a half-written message, and shortcuts that combine Ctrl, Shift, or Alt with other keys reach the app intact. Terminal-based editors and tools respond the way they should, with no IDE settings to adjust. The old setting that sent Esc+CR on Shift+Enter is no longer needed and is ignored.
Your tools follow your IDE theme
Switching the IDE to Dark mode used to leave terminal apps guessing, and you ended up with dark text on a dark background or a bright color scheme inside a dark IDE, unless you configured each tool by hand.
Now the terminal answers the dark/light query (CSI ? 996 n) from the current IDE theme and sends a notification through mode 2031 when you switch. Claude Code, OpenCode, Pi, Neovim, and tmux subscribe to these theme-change notifications, so most of them switch automatically with the IDE. 
The terminal also answers OSC 4 palette queries and the Kitty OSC 21 color query, in addition to the OSC 10/11 queries that JediTerm already handled. OpenCode and Pi read the palette, and Junie CLI asks whether the terminal is dark or light. Programs can now set the extended palette colors 16 to 255 with OSC 4, while colors 0 to 15 stay under the control of the IDE theme.
Terminal applications with rich output now draw better
AI agents, system monitors, file managers, and dashboards are only as good as the terminal that renders them. The new engine handles almost 50 control sequences that JediTerm either ignored or misread. A few you may have hit:
REP (CSI Ps b): ncurses uses it for runs of 7 or more identical characters, so some lines previously rendered with missing characters.
Colon-separated SGR colors (38:2::r:g:b): JediTerm printed the colons and merged the digits into the wrong attribute.
Unknown APC, SOS, and PM strings: JediTerm printed them as text. They are now silently dropped.
Also supported are left/right margins (DECSLRM), protected areas, tab-stop control, insert mode, XTSAVE/XTRESTORE, the Kitty CSI 22 J scroll-and-clear, and X10 mouse reporting. Cursor blink mode (?12) is respected now; before, the cursor always blinked. There’s much more – to see the full list of supported escape-sequences, please refer to this table.
In summation: lines, borders, and separators no longer come out broken, colored output no longer shows stray colons or the wrong colors, and leftover invisible codes no longer show up as garbage text. 
And this is just the start
The libghostty library already parses many sequences that the IDE doesn’t act on yet: OSC 52 clipboard, desktop notifications (OSC 9/777), ConEmu progress bars, Kitty graphics, and styled and colored underlines. Parsing is no longer the bottleneck. Only the IDE side is left, so expect these to arrive faster than they did with JediTerm.
In practice, that groundwork covers features you may know from standalone terminals: copying to your clipboard from a program running on a remote server, getting notified when the app in the terminal finishes a task (for example, Claude finishes processing a prompt and is waiting on you), seeing a progress bar for long tasks, and showing images directly in the terminal.
Try it now, enabled by default in 2026.3
The libghostty-based engine is already on by default in the reworked terminal in the 2026.3 EAP builds of your IDEs, and it will stay that way through the Beta and Release Candidate builds and in the stable release.
If something goes wrong, you can switch back to JediTerm: go to Help | Find Action, open Registry…, and turn off terminal.use.ghostty.emulator. We’d appreciate it if you also let us know what happened by leaving a comment on IJPL-218849 or by filing a bug report. 
Thank you, Ghostty
The Ghostty team has been engaged and supportive throughout the transition. Many thanks to Mitchell Hashimoto, Tim Culverhouse, and all the Ghostty contributors. You built libghostty as a reusable library and kept improving it while we integrated it. Over the past months, libghostty also gained features that JediTerm users relied on, which made the switch possible. We’re glad to build on your work, and we look forward to contributing back.

posts.title: AI on Your Terms: How We See AI in YouTrack
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
AI on your terms
When we published our YouTrack roadmap at the beginning of the year, we only briefly touched on our plans for AI. Now it’s time to share more details about how we see its role within YouTrack. 
Most project management tools now ship with AI built in and switched on by default. We’ve taken a different path. You decide whether AI belongs in your workflow, and if it does, which tools you want to use. Some teams run coding agents against their backlog all day. Others have strict policies and keep AI out completely. YouTrack is built to work well for both approaches.
With YouTrack, you choose whether and how to use AI, while we also make it easier to work with the tools you already trust. In this post, we explore the three options YouTrack gives you: connect your existing tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), use the built-in YouTrack AI Assistant, or keep AI switched off. We’ll also preview Ask YouTrack, an agentic AI chat we’re releasing later this year.
With any of these approaches, you get the same projects, Knowledge Base, and Helpdesk on Server or Cloud. This makes YouTrack an affordable alternative to the Atlassian stack and other AI-first solutions.
AI is becoming the default. With YouTrack, it remains your choice
Atlassian, monday.com, ClickUp, and other project management vendors are steadily expanding the role of AI in their products. Many of the teams we talk to aren’t completely ready for this shift, and their reasons vary. For some, it’s the effect on pricing; for others, it’s features they don’t need or unanswered questions about how their data is used in AI services. 
When we discuss migration from Atlassian with customers, their main concerns are the announced end of Data Center support and Atlassian’s updated data contribution practices. Effective August 17, 2026, de-identified and aggregated customer data may be used to improve Atlassian’s AI experiences, with opt-out options varying by plan.
YouTrack puts AI on your terms. If you switch it on, there are three ways to use it:
Connect your preferred AI chats, coding agents, automation platforms, IDEs, and workplace apps through YouTrack’s remote MCP server.
Enable our built-in AI Assistant to turn selected text into tasks, summarize content, get reply suggestions, improve your writing, and more.
Coming soon: Ask YouTrack, an agentic AI chat that understands your work. Search in YouTrack with prompts, get answers, create tasks, and propose updates – all within the chat and based on your project context. We also plan to let you bring your own key and use the LLM of your choice.
If you keep AI switched off, you still get YouTrack’s complete project management functionality, with nothing hidden behind AI features.
Option 1. Connect your AI stack to YouTrack through MCP
You can work with YouTrack from the AI applications and services your teams already use. The remote MCP server gives compatible tools access to the current YouTrack context while respecting each user’s existing permissions.
Choose from a variety of tools
AI chats – ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, and others
Search and summarize tasks, support tickets, and Knowledge Base articles, or create and update work directly from an AI conversation. 
For example, you can easily connect YouTrack to Claude and search your project context using whatever details you have. If you’re a QA engineer managing multiplatform testing tasks, you can ask Claude to find unresolved tasks for testing on desktop, review them, and create a related task for similar testing on mobile devices in the same chat.




Coding agents and IDEs – PyCharm, IntelliJ IDEA, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and others
Give agents the YouTrack context they need, so they can find related documentation and reflect development progress in tasks, all without leaving your coding environment. For example, when implementing a new product feature, developers can ask Claude Code directly in IntelliJ IDEA to create the subtasks they need to tackle next.




Delegating task management to coding agents is becoming a common practice, and for such teams, YouTrack evolves from automating individual processes to serving as a shared “agentic database” for agent and human-led tasks.
The Fullworks case study shows how a software company supporting 12 products, including Broadcaster, a messaging platform for UK trade businesses, has integrated agents throughout its software development lifecycle. The team connects Claude Code to YouTrack through MCP to manage development work directly from its coding tools. Its agents create and update tasks, verify release requirements, and help coordinate development across its products.



    
Read the Fullworks case study
                                    
Automation platforms – n8n, Zapier, Make, OpenAI AgentKit, and others
If you rely on process automation on a platform of your choice, as a part of it, you can build agentic workflows that route requests, create and update tasks, log time, and trigger actions in YouTrack. Marketing teams, for example, can use the n8n integration to automatically turn budget requests submitted through a form into YouTrack tasks.




Beyond this example, you can integrate YouTrack into every step of your automation to update work items in response to actions from AI agents, share YouTrack content with other systems, and support a wide range of cross-tool workflows.
Workplace tools – service desks, internal portals, custom applications, and others
Your teams can work with project information through organization-level apps or internal AI assistants. You can add custom MCP actions with YouTrack apps or build automation using workflows and API-based scripts – in-house or with help from one of the YouTrack consulting partners.
This approach can scale to meet the needs of large enterprise customers. For example, Gurtam develops telematics and IoT platforms for B2B customers and operates in more than 160 countries. The team connected its internal AI platform, Nova, to YouTrack MCP. Managers and employees now use AI agents to create structured tasks, review feature requests, monitor backlogs, prepare changelogs, and turn meeting notes into actionable work.



    
Read the Gurtam case study
                                    
Choose the right connection method
How you connect depends on what the tool supports. YouTrack supports OAuth authorization for compatible MCP clients, so users do not need to create or store permanent tokens. OAuth works with browser-based, desktop, and mobile AI applications, as well as shared organization-level services. You can also add YouTrack directly from the ChatGPT or Claude connector directory and set it up company-wide. The connection is available for ChatGPT Business, Enterprise, and Edu workspaces.
Simplify setup with CIMD
If an MCP client supports CIMD, a YouTrack administrator can allow it to register automatically. This removes most of the manual configuration and makes approved tools easier to connect.
Register an OAuth client manually
Manual registration is required when an application supports OAuth but not CIMD. This may apply to custom internal applications or AI clients that cannot register automatically.
Use a permanent token as a fallback
For local agents, custom scripts, and other tools without OAuth support, permanent-token authorization remains available. Tokens should be stored securely and are best suited to controlled local or custom integrations.
Learn how to connect AI tools
                                    
Option 2. Enhance efficiency with built-in AI assistance
The second option is our built-in AI Assistant that can handle routine work across YouTrack. Administrators have the option to manage access or disable AI entirely. Your data remains yours and is never used to train AI models, whether you choose YouTrack Cloud or Server.
Currently, AI Assistant includes a limited number of free credits, replenished weekly. It is available to YouTrack Cloud customers, including teams on the free plan, and to YouTrack Server customers using the free plan or an active paid subscription.
When Ask YouTrack and BYOK are introduced in Q4 2026, AI access will change:
Free AI Assistant credits will be included only with paid YouTrack Cloud plans.
Paid credits will be available through a connected JetBrains AI subscription to YouTrack Cloud and Server customers on free plans or with active paid subscriptions.
BYOK will also be available to YouTrack Cloud and Server customers on free plans or with active paid subscriptions.




Text-to-issue transformation
Scan selected text for action items, choose which ones to turn into tasks, and create them together.
Writing assistance
Check grammar, spelling, and punctuation in tasks, articles, support tickets, and comments. Get phrase suggestions while writing in English or German. 
The built-in YouTrack writing assistant is powered by JetBrains AI and will continue to run exclusively on JetBrains infrastructure.
Effortless summaries with AI
Generate concise summaries of project tasks, articles, and support tickets, regardless of the discussion length or language.
Reply suggestions
Generate context-aware replies, including general responses, apologies, or requests for more time. Use the suggested text as written or edit it before posting.
Text recognition from images
Extract editable and searchable text from screenshots, document photos, and other image attachments. YouTrack can also include images containing matching text in search results.
The text recognition feature doesn’t require a connection to external services. For YouTrack Cloud, processing takes place on JetBrains infrastructure, while for YouTrack Server, it runs within your local environment.
Discover YouTrack AI Assistance
                                    
Coming soon: Ask YouTrack and BYOK
Ask YouTrack, a built-in agentic AI chat, is planned for Q4 2026. It works with your current YouTrack context: Search through prompts, ask it about your projects, get answers in chat, understand the state of work, create tasks, and propose updates for your review.
We plan to add BYOK (Bring Your Own Key) support, so you can connect your own AI providers and use the LLM of your choice – in line with your company’s policies and budget.




Coming soon: Task creation from Slack threads
For teams that use Slack for everyday collaboration, we also plan to add a new AI-powered feature available in the YouTrack Slack app in Q4 2026 that lets you create a task from a thread. You’ll be able to automatically turn a conversation in your team channel into a task, or add instructions along the way to specify what it should include.




Option 3. Experience high-quality project management without AI
YouTrack’s core functionality does not depend on AI. Administrators can disable AI features entirely. Teams with strict AI policies can plan projects, track tasks on Agile boards and Gantt charts, maintain documentation in the Knowledge Base, and manage customer or internal requests in Helpdesk – all without AI anywhere in their workflow.
Server or Cloud – your choice!
For greater control over your infrastructure and data, you can choose YouTrack Server. It scales to hundreds of thousands of users, supports GDPR and SOC 2 compliance, integrates with existing identity systems, and provides real-time monitoring. 
YouTrack Cloud is hosted and maintained by JetBrains, with a choice of AWS regions in Northern California, Frankfurt, Ireland, and Singapore. Both versions offer the same functionality, with AI on your terms, whichever you choose.
Save up to 70% compared with Jira and Confluence
Whether or not you enable AI, YouTrack’s total cost of ownership can be up to 70% lower than Jira and Confluence combined, and that’s before Atlassian’s service management and plugin costs are added.
YouTrack is free for a team of up to 10 users. YouTrack Server subscriptions start at \$900 per year for 15 users, while YouTrack Cloud starts at \$4.50 per user per month for teams of 11 or more users.
YouTrack Helpdesk includes three support agents and unlimited reporters for free. Additional agents cost \$6 per agent per month.
If you have any other questions about AI in YouTrack or migration, please share them in the comments below or get in touch with our technical support. We’re always here to help.
Your YouTrack team
AI or no AI, Server or Cloud – you choose!

posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Your quarterly dose of plugin dev news, tools, and tips from JetBrains
⚡JetBrains Plugin Developer Conf 2026 Is Coming!
November 10, 2026 | Online | Free
Join our annual free virtual event on developing plugins for JetBrains products. You’ll hear talks from SAP, Broadcom, JetBrains experts, and independent plugin authors.
Register Now
                                    
🤖 AI meets plugins: ACP and MCP integrations, plus where AI-assisted development helps – and where it doesn’t.
⚙️IntelliJ Platform updates: The latest Gradle Plugin, Plugin DevKit, Plugin Verifier, and API updates.
💻 Real-world techniques: LSP, WSL, Dev Containers, web-based UIs, and plugin architectures that scale. 




🧩 Marketplace Updates
New Way to Edit Plugin Description 
Keeping your plugin page up to date just got easier! You can now edit your plugin description directly on the plugin’s page. The description is stored separately from the plugin archive, so you can update it without uploading a new plugin version. Learn more  →
UI Freeze Reports Are Now Available in the Freezes Tab
Users say the IDE froze, but you can’t reproduce it? JetBrains Marketplace now collects UI freeze reports for your plugin, with full thread dumps and CPU snapshots. In his guide, Jakub Chrzanowski explains how to read the reports, enable reporting, and use an AI agent to find the cause. You can also watch his video or see the Marketplace documentation →.




🔧 Plugin Development Tooling Updates
IntelliJ Plugin Verifier 1.411
Tool that checks binary compatibility between IntelliJ-based IDE builds and plugins. 
Content modules are now supported in dependency resolution, dependency trees, and module visibility checks, and dependencies.txt lists each plugin’s content modules.
New public APIs for plugin name validation, rebuilding dependencies, and keeping only direct dependencies in verification results.
Lower memory usage for check-trunk-api and report generation, which now streams dependencies.txt and HTML reports.
Reports are now written in UTF-8.
Updated Gradle, Bouncy Castle, and Byte Buddy.
View Changelog →
IntelliJ Platform Gradle Plugin 2.19.0
Plugin that helps configure your environment for building, testing, verifying, and publishing plugins for IntelliJ-based IDEs. 
New buildPluginVariants tasks build Linux, macOS, and Windows plugin distributions for x86_64 and arm64 (2026.1+).
New testFrameworks() helper, more test framework options, and per-plugin bundled-library exclusions.
Full --offline support, and Kotlin stdlib and Coroutines are no longer bundled into the sandbox by default.
verifyPlugin now runs against each IDE’s own bundled JBR and fails based on report files.
Removed the deprecated setupDependencies task (breaking change), and tasks are now organized into separate groups.
Plus fixes for download URL resolution, signature verification, and cache writes.
View Changelog →
💡 Tip of the Quarter
Use Release Channels for Pre-releases
Deploy plugins to non-default release channels (alpha, beta, canary, eap) to share work-in-progress with limited user groups and gather feedback before public release. This lets you test with real users without affecting your main release.
📚 Resources & Learning
📖 Blog
IDE Plugin Generator – The New Beginning
Creating an IntelliJ Platform plugin no longer means choosing between the IDE wizard and the GitHub template. The new web-based generator combines both, with dependency selection, GitHub workflows, and Split Mode support, all from the IDE or your browser. Find out why we made the change and what’s coming next. Read →
The Evolution of WSL Support in JetBrains IDEs
After trying three other approaches, JetBrains IDEs now open WSL projects in Native mode, up to 38% faster. Learn how the IJent agent and EelApi make this work, and how your plugin can run the same way in WSL, Docker, and Dev Containers. Read →
Why We Still Need an IDE
Agents write the code, but someone still has to steer, verify, and own it. Read why the IDE is becoming the cockpit for agentic development, and why its tools matter as much to agents as they do to developers. Read →




⭐ Community Spotlight
Native Calls in IntelliJ Platform Plugins: JNA vs FFM
The IntelliJ Platform is moving native integrations from JNA to Java’s Foreign Function and Memory API. In this video, Patrick Scheibe shows how to configure the IDE-bundled JNA, when your existing code can stay, and how to start with FFM if your plugin calls native code.






Save State in IntelliJ Plugins in 3 Lines!
Need your plugin to remember a setting after an IDE restart? In this short video, Róbert Novotný shows how to save booleans, numbers, strings, and string lists with PropertiesComponent in just three lines of Kotlin.






💌 Until next time — happy plugin development!

posts.title: JetBrains GameDev Day 2026: Watch the Recordings
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Missed JetBrains GameDev Day 2026, or want to revisit your favorite sessions? All the recordings are now available on YouTube!
On September 28, we brought together game developers, engineers, and industry experts for a full day of technical talks, live demos, and discussions about the tools and challenges shaping modern game development.
From Epic’s open-source Lore VCS and ECS in a live game to Unreal Engine profiling, Unity UI automation, AI-driven PCG in Godot, and debugging across C# and C++, this year’s sessions stayed close to real production problems.
Whether you joined us online, attended one of our watch parties in Belgrade or Limassol, or couldn’t make it this time, you can now catch up on everything at your own pace.
Watch the full JetBrains GameDev Day 2026 playlist on YouTube
Watch the sessions
Not sure where to start? Pick your engine or role:
Unreal Engine: Death by a Thousand Ticks and Agentic Development in Unreal Engine with JetBrains Rider
Unity: Fix Your CI Without Leaving the IDE and How We Automated Figma-to-Unity UI Integration With AI Agents
Godot: Prompt to Playable World
Engine and backend programmers: Evolving a Live Game Engine and Debugging Across Two Runtimes and Two Different Languages
Build, pipelines, and infrastructure: Splitting the Difference and Code Quality Never Changes
Everyone, especially leads and juniors: Pass the Controller?
Pass the Controller? Communities, Data, and AI in Game Development
Anthony Tešija (Discord), Jason Weimann (Boddle Learning), Gennadii Potapov (General Arcade), and Anton Licht (Sudden Forest)
Moderated by Denis Savosin (JetBrains)
Our opening panel explored the role of communities, data, and AI in game development. When should developers listen to community feedback, and when is it better to trust their own vision? How can AI support developers without replacing critical thinking, especially for those just entering the industry?
Fix Your CI Without Leaving the IDE: TeamCity MCP and CLI (with Unity)
Artem Rokhin (JetBrains)
Discover how TeamCity’s MCP support and CLI bring continuous integration workflows directly into your development environment. Using a Unity project as an example, Artem demonstrated how to investigate build failures and interact with CI pipelines without constantly switching between tools.
Learn more: TeamCity MCP and CLI for AI agents
Evolving a Live Game Engine: Introducing ECS Without a Full Rewrite
Alex Zhorau (Meta)
How do you bring an Entity Component System into a mass-market game that’s already live without rewriting the engine? Drawing on proprietary engines and Unreal Engine, Alex walked through a staged migration, the compromises around memory layout and scripting, and why a hybrid of ECS and legacy code is often where a live game should end up, not just a stop along the way.
Code Quality Never Changes: How Static Analysis Can Help in the Age of AI
Kai Schmithusen (JetBrains)
AI-generated code brings new productivity opportunities, but also new challenges for code quality. Learn how static analysis can help teams identify issues, manage technical debt, and maintain reliable development workflows, with practical examples using Qodana.
Learn more: Qodana
Prompt to Playable World: Live-Building AI-Driven PCG with Godot, C#, and Gemini
Sharmishtha Sen (Jet Heart Labs)
Watch a procedural world generation pipeline come together using Godot, C#, and AI. Sharmishtha demonstrated how to turn natural-language prompts into playable environments while combining AI-generated configurations with traditional procedural generation techniques and Rider’s development tools.
Learn more: Godot support in JetBrains Rider
Death by a Thousand Ticks: Why Gameplay Systems Become Slow
Konrad Słoń (Fool’s Theory)
Performance problems rarely appear overnight. Through Unreal Engine examples and live profiling, Konrad explored how small engineering decisions accumulate into gameplay bottlenecks and demonstrated practical optimization workflows using Unreal Insights and Rider.
How We Automated Figma-to-Unity UI Integration With AI Agents
Alina Chupakhina (Playkot) and Olia Chupakhina (Cubic Games)
Alina and Olia shared a Figma-to-Unity pipeline that grew over years of production and now runs through an AI agent over MCP. They covered the design foundation that makes automation possible, the lessons learned from building it, and a benchmark of which UI integration tasks the agent can handle today and which still need a human.
Agentic Development in Unreal Engine with JetBrains Rider
Alexander Dzerakh (JetBrains)
Go beyond AI-assisted code generation with agentic workflows tailored to Unreal Engine. Through live demos, Alexander showed how Rider, ACP, and Unreal Engine-specific skills can help AI agents navigate engine architecture, generate C++ code, investigate crashes, and automate development tasks.
Learn more: AI agent skills for Unreal Engine in Rider
Splitting the Difference: How Epic’s Lore VCS Handles Massive Binary Files
Ben Cooke and Ryn Slack (AWS)
Most version control systems were built for code, not multi-gigabyte assets that change every day. Ben and Ryn explained how Epic Games’ open-source Lore VCS splits files into content-addressable fragments so only the changed part of an asset moves, why its edge caches can fill on demand instead of being pre-seeded, and how to deploy it yourself with the Lore module in the AWS Cloud Game Development Toolkit.
Learn more: Lore on GitHub · Lore documentation · AWS Cloud Game Development Toolkit
Debugging Across Two Runtimes and Two Different Languages
Alex Drum (Hytale)
Your client is C#, your server is C++, and the bug lives somewhere in between. Alex showed how to debug both runtimes at once with Rider and CLion, read the data crossing the protocol, and figure out which runtime is lying, and discussed why the boundary between them is the last place to look, not the first.
Keep learning and building
A huge thank you to all our speakers, hosts, and everyone who joined us online or at our watch parties in Belgrade and Limassol! Special thanks to DevGAMM x FTW! for co-hosting our Belgrade watch party. We hope these sessions give you new ideas, useful techniques, and inspiration for your own projects.
Watch all JetBrains GameDev Day 2026 recordings on YouTube
If you’d like to explore the tools featured throughout the event, check out JetBrains tools for game development.
Many of the demos ran in JetBrains Rider, which is free for non-commercial use, including learning, pet projects, and open-source contributions.
To hear about the next GameDev Day first, subscribe to the JetBrains GameDev newsletter.
See you at the next GameDev Day!

posts.title: Preparing for Your Next Certification Could Start with Your Visual Studio Subscription
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Are you thinking about earning a Microsoft certification to help advance your career, build on your existing skills, or meet new requirements at work? 
If so, you may already be wondering where to start. Which courses, labs, and hands-on exercises will help you prepare? How much time will it take to find the right resources, and how much will that training cost? 
Here’s something you may not be aware of: Eligible Visual Studio Subscriptions already include many of the learning resources you need to prepare for your next certification. 
Visual Studio subscribers can access training from Cloud Academy and Pluralsight, including certification-focused courses, structured learning paths, and hands-on labs that can help you build your skills and prepare for certification exams. 
Let’s look at a few ways you can put those benefits to work. 
Interested in AI-powered applications?  
If Microsoft Certified: Azure AI Apps and Agents Developer is a certification you’re considering, your subscriber benefits can provide a useful starting point preparing for the required AI-103 exam. 
For developers looking to build AI skills, preparing for AI-103 offers an opportunity to learn how to develop generative AI applications, integrate AI services, and create intelligent agents and workflows. 
Pluralsight offers AI-103-aligned learning resources that can help you work through relevant concepts and build your knowledge of AI applications and agents. 

Preparing for Azure administration? 
If you want to be a Microsoft Certified: Azure Administrator Associate, your Visual Studio Subscription learning benefits can help you get ready for the necessary AZ-104 exam. 
Whether you’re new to Azure administration or looking to strengthen your existing skills, preparing for AZ-104 can help you develop practical knowledge of virtual networks, storage, compute resources, and identity management. 
Cloud Academy and Pluralsight offer AZ-104 training, helping you focus on relevant administration skills through in-depth coursework and learning experiences. 

Hoping to develop a higher level of cloud architecture expertise? 
If you’re Interested in becoming a Microsoft Certified: Azure Solutions Architect Expert, preparing for the required AZ-305 exam can help you strengthen your skills in designing Azure solutions for infrastructure, security, data storage, and business continuity.  
Pluralsight and Cloud Academy offer training aligned with the AZ-305 exam requirements, providing additional resources to study Azure architecture concepts as you work toward your certification goals. 
Note: To become a Microsoft Certified: Azure Solutions Architect Expert, you must earn the Microsoft Certified: Azure Administrator Associate certification. 
Put what you’re learning into practice 
Courses are a useful starting point, but applying what you’ve learned can help reinforce new skills. 
Your Visual Studio Subscription provides opportunities to do both. Pluralsight and Cloud Academy offer guided labs, technical courses, and practical learning experiences that can help you work with Azure technologies as you study. Beyond just providing content to study, they provide hands-on, practical application labs that allow you to grow your skills actively, with added support from AI powered learning assistants. 
And if your Subscription includes Azure monthly credits, you can use eligible Azure services to explore configurations, test ideas, and practice skills in a development environment. These opportunities can help you move beyond just reading about a technology and help you actually start working with it. 
Start preparing for your next certification with your Subscription benefits 
These are just several examples of the opportunities your Visual Studio Subscription provides. If you’re considering furthering your career, honing your technical skills, or meeting new professional requirements, you have a solid starting point through your Subscription benefits.  
Visit the Visual Studio Subscriptions portal to activate your eligible Cloud Academy and Pluralsight benefits and start preparing with learning resources aligned to your certification goals. Begin making progress toward your next certification today with the learning paths and hands-on resources you already have. 
 
Note: Learning benefit availability, eligibility, access duration, and course selection vary by Visual Studio Subscription. Specific training content may change or may not be included in every subscriber benefit offering. Certification exams and exam fees are separate from the learning benefits described here unless otherwise specified. Visit Professional and Technical Credentials and Certifications | Microsoft Learn for more information on certifications and requirements.

posts.title: Visual Studio October Update – Compare Commits to Your Code, Resolve Conflicts in Bulk, Keep Coding
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
The October Visual Studio update gives you a clearer view of how your code has changed and more control over resolving merge conflicts. Compare an earlier commit directly with your current working tree, including edits still in progress, and apply the same conflict resolution across multiple files at once.
There’s more to try beyond Git: a new Copilot chat experience, Hot Exit for unfinished work, keyboard shortcuts for organizing tabs, and a refreshed Fonts and Colors page. Update to the Visual Studio 2026 Stable Channel to get started.
Compare a Commit to Your Working Tree
Need to see how your current code differs from an earlier commit? You can now compare that commit directly with your working tree across your repository, including committed changes and edits still in progress. Use it to review a refactor across several commits or investigate what’s changed since a known-good version.
From commit history or the branch list in the Git Repository window, right-click a commit and select Compare with Working Tree. The compare view lets you browse changed files and inspect their diffs against the code you have today.


Bulk Resolve Merge Conflicts
When you already know which side to keep across several conflicted files, you shouldn’t have to repeat that choice for every file. You can now resolve conflicts across a group of files at once.
In Git Changes, right-click multiple selected files, a folder, or the repository root under Unmerged Changes and select Keep All Current or Take All Incoming. The selected resolution applies to all selected files, or all conflicted files within the selected folder or repository.

Try the New Copilot Chat Experience
The new GitHub Copilot Chat experience builds on the Copilot SDK foundation introduced with Agent (Preview). That foundation now extends to Ask mode, Agent mode, and the underlying chat infrastructure, sharing the SDK used by the Copilot CLI and GitHub Copilot app.
It brings more capable end-to-end agent workflows with less back-and-forth, longer-running sessions with more effective prompt caching, and consistent behavior across Copilot experiences. To try it, open Tools > Options > GitHub > Copilot > Copilot Chat, select Use new Copilot chat experience, then restart Visual Studio.

Enable it for your next coding session and let us know how it handles the work. If something is missing or isn’t working, use Help > Send Feedback > Report a Problem to tell us.
Keep Unsaved Work with Hot Exit
Closing Visual Studio doesn’t have to mean deciding where to save every unfinished file. Hot Exit preserves your unsaved work between sessions, including new files you haven’t saved and edits to existing files.
When you reopen Visual Studio, it restores those documents and changes, along with your tab and window layout. It also preserves undo functionality for saved files, including Ctrl+Z. Hot Exit is off by default; to enable it, open Tools > Options, expand All Settings > Projects and Solutions > General, and select Reopen unsaved documents on solution load or empty environment.
https://devblogs.microsoft.com/visualstudio/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2026/10/vs18.11_HotExit.mp4

Move Documents with the Keyboard
You can now reorder tabs without reaching for the mouse. Press Ctrl+Shift+PgUp to move the active tab left or Ctrl+Shift+PgDn to move it right. With vertical tabs, the same shortcuts move it up or down. They work for documents and tool windows hosted in the document well.
Pinned and unpinned tabs stay separate. Vertical tabs stay within their project group, and manual reordering isn’t available when alphabetical sorting is enabled. Preview tabs can’t be moved.
You can remap Window.MoveTabLeft and Window.MoveTabRight in Tools > Options > Environment > Keyboard. The defaults replace the previous Text Editor bindings for Edit.ViewTopExtend and Edit.ViewBottomExtend; those commands remain available if you want to assign them different shortcuts.
Personalize Fonts and Colors
Finding the right editor customization is easier with the refreshed Fonts and Colors experience, now built on Unified Settings. Category-based navigation and integrated search help you find the settings you want, while inline previews let you see colors and font styles alongside each item.

Foreground colors, background colors, font styles, and previews are all displayed in the settings grid, so you can review and update multiple items without repeatedly selecting each one. Changes also stay synchronized with settings.json, giving you a way to inspect, edit, share, or revert your customizations directly in the file.
From our entire team, thank you for choosing Visual Studio! For the latest updates, resources, and news, check out the Visual Studio Hub and stay in touch.
Happy coding!
The Visual Studio team

posts.title: Keep your investigation between sessions
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
A bug investigation often starts with a few notes: what you tried, which input reproduced the problem, and what you want to check next. You might not be ready to choose a filename or add those notes to a project. You still want them there when you return.
In Visual Studio 2026 version 18.11, you can create a standalone Markdown file from New File and use the opt-in Hot Exit preview feature to resume that unfinished note after closing and reopening Visual Studio. Start the note while the details are fresh, then return to it next session.
Start the note without adding a project item
Press Ctrl + N to open New File.
Select Markdown File.
Select Open and start writing.

This is separate from Add New Item, which creates a project item. The original feedback specifically asked for a Markdown template in New File, including when working without an open solution.
The Markdown editor itself isn’t new in this release. You can use it to turn your notes into headings, lists, and fenced code blocks, then check the rendered result. The Markdown preview guide explains its editing and preview controls.
Resume the same unfinished note
Hot Exit is off by default. To enable it, go to Tools > Options, expanding All Settings > Projects and Solutions > General, and selecting Reopen unsaved documents on solution load or empty environment.
With Hot Exit enabled, closing Visual Studio preserves session state. When you reopen Visual Studio, it restores open documents and unsaved edits, including new files you haven’t saved yet. Your note can remain unfinished without forcing you to choose a permanent home for it before you close the IDE.

Hot Exit also preserves changes to previously saved files, your tab and window layout, and undo functionality for saved files. For those saved files, you can continue using Ctrl + Z after restoring the session.
This is session preservation, not the same thing as deliberately saving a document to disk or committing it to source control. Save the note when you want to share it or keep it as part of the repository. The useful choice here is that a temporary note doesn’t have to become a project artifact merely to survive a normal close and reopen.
The Hot Exit request calls out exploratory work and temporary files as reasons to preserve unsaved documents. Keep the preview option off if you prefer your current close-and-save workflow.
Try the combination with a disposable investigation note: write down the next thing to check, close Visual Studio with Hot Exit enabled, and reopen it to continue the note.
The post Keep your investigation between sessions appeared first on Visual Studio Blog.

posts.title: Fedora 44에 CachyOS kernel 설치
posts.author: sunyzero
posts.content:
Fedora 44에 CachyOS의 최적화된 커널을 설치하는 방법을 다룬다. 방법은 Fedora Copr(Community Project)에 개인이 빌드해둔 CachyOS kernel rpm을 설치하는 방법이다. 그리고 Fedora 44 기본 커널과 CachyOS 최적화된 커널의 성능 차이가 얼마나 있는지도 살펴보도록 한다. 모든 작업은 root 권한을 필요로 하므로 root로 변경하거나 sudo 명령을 사용해야만 한다.

주의할 점은 copr 저장소는 인증받지 않은 저장소이므로 안정성이 떨어지거나 혹은 해커가 위장하여 뭔가를 숨겨둔 프로그램일 가능성도 있다. 따라서 서비스를 하거나 개발을 위한 작업이라면 되도록이면 copr을 쓰지 않는 것을 권장한다. (굉장히 잘 알려진 copr이나 많이 사용된 경우는 안전할 수도 있지만 그래도 위험성은 있는 편이다)

 

1. CachyOS kernel 관련 Copr repository 활성화

먼저 아래 명령으로 bieszczaders kernel-cachyos copr 저장소를 활성화 한다[1].

sudo dnf copr enable bieszczaders/kernel-cachyos

 

2. kernel-cachyos 패키지 설치

저장소가 활성화 되었다면 아래의 명령으로 최적화된 캐시오에스 커널을 설치한다.

sudo dnf -y install kernel-cachyos

설치가 완료되면 커널 모듈 빌드나 램디스크 등의 후처리 작업이 있으므로 top으로 백그라운드 작업을 확인하던지 아니면 4~5분 정도 지난 뒤에 재부팅하면 된다.

재부팅하면 새로 설치된 CachyOS 커널로 부팅하면 끝인데, 만일 GRUB에서 shim 관련 에러가 발생한다면 십중팔구 secure boot를 enabled 해놓아서 서명 문제가 생긴 경우이므로, BIOS에 들어가서 secure boot를 disabled로 변경해주면 된다.

 

3. 벤치마크(geekbench7)

성능이 얼마나 차이나는지 긱벤치7으로 확인해보았다. 3가지를 측정했으면 여러번 측정해서 중간 값을 가진 값을 채택했다. 첫번째는 Fedora 44 순정 커널, 두번째는 같은 하드웨어에 CachyOS 데스크탑 2026년 8월 9일 버전, 세번째는 Fedora 44에 kernel-cachyOS copr 패키지를 설치한 것이다. 먼저 3가지 커널의 점수부터 정리하고 이야기 하자.

리눅스 배포판, 커널 버전 Geekbench Single-core Geekbench Multi-core
Fedora 44 original, kernel 7.2.11 1868 13143
CachyOS 260809, kernel 7.1.6 1954 13452
Fedora 44 copr, kernel-cachyos 7.3.0 1948 13364

하드웨어는 GMKtec K12로서 AMD H 255를 장착하고 있으며, RAM은 32GB (삼성 5600MHz 16GB 모듈 * 2)이다. BIOS에서 balanced mode로 설정했고, power limit은 ECO 모드(35W)로 설정했다.

 

3.1. Fedora 44 vs CachyOS

먼저 Fedora 44 순정 커널 상태로 kernel 7.2.11의 geekbench7의 결과를 보도록 하자[2]. 여러번 실행해봤자 어차리 1~2%는 오차범위 안에서 수치가 차이나므로 1~2% 정도 차이는 무시해도 된다. 각각의 긱벤치 결과는 URL이 있으니 직접 링크를 따라가서 확인해봐도 된다.

 

아래는 CachyOS 26년 8월 9일자 데스크탑의 geekbench7 값의 이미지이다. 역시 약간의 성능 향상이 있기는 하다. 특히 싱글 코어 부분이 두드러지는데 2가지 항목에서 큰 차이가 나기 때문에 점수차이가 벌어졌다[3].

Fedora 순정 커널과  CachyOS의 커널의 대부분은 값이 비슷했으나 약간씩은 CachyOS가 높았다. 그러나 1% 정도는 거의 오차범위이므로 넘어간다고 쳐도 Navigation, Structure from motion은 매우 크게 차이가 났다.

  Fedora 44 CachyOS CachyOS의 성능 우위
Navigation 1960 2308 17.7%
Structure from Motion 1907 2615 37.1%
HDR 1860 1927 3.6%
Photo Editor 2167 2339 7.9%

Navigation이나 Structure from motion이 Shortest path를 찾는 기능과 3D modeling을 위한 성능 측정이라고 하는데, 이부분이 크게 차이가 났고, 그 외에는 HDR, 사진 에디터 정도가 약간 차이가 있었다.

clang 컴파일러나 HTML5 브라우저, 게임, 비디오, 오디오는 거의 오차범위 안에서 1~2%의 근소한 차이였다. 1~2%도 차이가 아예 없는 정도는 아니지만 체감이 가능한 영역은 아닐 것이다.

 

3.2. Fedora 44에 kernel-cachyos로 부팅한 경우

Fedora 44에 kernel-cachyos로 부팅해서 긱벤치7으로 다시 측정해보았다. 결과는 다음과 같다[4].

 

오리지널 CachyOS와 비교하면 다음과 같다. 이제 거의 차이가 없다고 봐도 무방할 정도이다. 앞서 37.1%나 차이가 났던 Structure from motion은 0.1%로 거의 같다고 보면 되고, 나머지도 1%대이므로 거의 비슷하다고 볼 수 있다.

Navigation 2278 2308 1.3%
Structure from Motion 2611 2615 0.1%
HDR 1908 1927 1.0%
Photo Editor 2307 2339 1.4%

 

4. 결론

CachyOS는 커널 이외에도 애플리케이션이나 중요 유틸리티를 최적화했다고 한다. LTO나 profile guided optimization을 했다고 한다. 그런데 LTO는 아마도 대부분의 배포판이 다 하고 있을거다. PGO는 특정 배치 데이터 처리 애플리케이션 같은 경우가 아니면 큰 효과를 보기 어려우니까 큰 차이는 아닐 것이다. 다만 실제로 CachyOS를 사용해보면 조금은 빠릿한 느낌이 드는데, 기분탓일 수도 있다. 물론 Fedora 44에 CachyOS의 최적화된 커널을 올리면 거의 느낌도 비슷해진다. 뭔가 스케줄링쪽의 차이가 아닌가 생각되기도 한다.

하지만 Fedora 44 순정 커널을 쓴다고 해도 느린 것은 아니며, 일반적인 작업에 영향을 주는 clang 컴파일러, HTML5, Video, Audio는 거의 비슷하다. 그래서 긱벤치 점수로는 확실히 cachyOS가 우위지만 실사용에서도 우위라고 말하기는 어렵다고 생각된다. 실제로 대규모 빌드 같은 것을 해보면 거의 비슷하게 끝나고 컨테이너 서비스 성능도 비슷하다. 긱벤치 점수는 재미일뿐 절대적인 기준도 아니고 세부적인 항목을 봐야 한다.

물론 3D 모델링 같은 것을 한다면 CachyOS의 커널을 올려서 사용하거나 아니면 CachyOS를 사용하는 것도 괜찮다고 생각한다.

posts.title: Splunk의 sourcetype 변경 - 2nd
posts.author: 강명훈
posts.content:
collect 명령 사용 시 소스타입 옵션은 필드 추출 작업에 관여하지 않는다. 하는 일이 뭐야?


원본 인덱스와 동일한 테이블 구조를 유지하려면 output_format=hec 옵션을 사용해야 함.


참고로 'output_format=hec' 옵션이나 소스타입 별도 지정 시 추가되는 용량은 라이센스 사용량에 포함된다. 라이센스 사용량이 부담된다면 collect 명령을 기본 옵션(output_format=raw)으로 실행 후, 별도 필드 추출 작업을 진행해야 함.

posts.title: 윈도우11 26H2 업데이트 총정리: 새 기능, 지금 설치하는 법, 설치 전 체크리스트 (AI 점검 프롬프트 포함)
posts.author: 어떤오후의 프리웨어 이야기
posts.content:
2026년 9월 29일부터 윈도우11 26H2 배포가 시작됐습니다. 이번 버전은 연 1회 나오는 기능 업데이트지만, 24H2·25H2를 쓰는 PC라면 운영체제를 통째로 다시 까는 방식이 아니라 작은 활성화 패키지(enablement package)로 올라갑니다. 이 글에서는 Microsoft 공식 문서에서 확인한 내용만 골라 새 기능, 설치 방법, 설치 전 체크리스트를 정리하고, 업데이트 전에 AI로 내 PC 상태를 점검하는 프롬프트도 함께 드립니다.

이 글의 핵심 요약
1. 26H2는 24H2·25H2 PC에서 활성화 패키지로 설치되며, 대부분 재시작 1번이면 끝납니다.
2. 설치하면 지원 기간이 새로 시작됩니다. Home·Pro 24개월, Enterprise·Education 36개월입니다.
3. 시작 메뉴·작업 표시줄·검색·파일 탐색기 개선이 묶여 들어오고, WMIC는 제거됐습니다.
4. '기본 활성' 3가지(설정 백업, 작업 표시줄 앱 액션, 파일 탐색기 개선)는 공식 문서상 상업용(기업) 장치 기준입니다.

1. 윈도우11 26H2는 어떤 업데이트인가요?

Microsoft에 따르면 26H2, 25H2, 24H2는 같은 서비스 분기(코드 기반)를 공유합니다. 그래서 새 기능 상당수는 이미 매월 누적 업데이트로 PC에 내려와 있고, 26H2 활성화 패키지는 그 기능을 켜 주는 역할을 합니다. 공식 문서가 설명하는 특징은 다음과 같습니다.

  • 작은 다운로드: 월간 품질 업데이트처럼 설치됩니다.
  • 빠른 설치: 대부분의 경우 재시작 1번으로 끝납니다.
  • 지원 기간 초기화: 26H2를 설치한 시점부터 새 지원 기간이 적용됩니다.
  • 단계적 배포: 호환성 문제가 예상되지 않는 PC부터 순차적으로 제공됩니다.
에디션 26H2 지원 기간
Home 24개월
Pro 24개월
Enterprise 36개월
Education 36개월

 

2. 26H2 주요 새 기능 (일반 사용자 체감 기능)

시작 메뉴와 작업 표시줄

  • 새 시작 메뉴: 스크롤되는 '모두' 영역과 범주 보기·그리드 보기가 생겼고, 고정됨·최근·모두 섹션을 각각 보이거나 숨길 수 있습니다.
  • 작업 표시줄 위치: 화면 아래뿐 아니라 위, 왼쪽, 오른쪽에 둘 수 있고, 아이콘과 높이를 줄이는 작은 작업 표시줄 옵션도 추가됐습니다.
  • AI 에이전트 진행 상황 표시: 작업 표시줄에서 지원되는 AI 에이전트의 진행 상황을 볼 수 있으며, 첫 지원 대상은 Microsoft Copilot의 Researcher입니다.

파일 탐색기

  • AI 작업: 지원되는 이미지 편집, 문서 요약 기능이 들어왔습니다. 다만 OneDrive·SharePoint 파일 요약은 Microsoft 365 구독과 Copilot 라이선스가 필요합니다.
  • 압축 형식 추가: uu, cpio, xar, nupkg 형식을 지원합니다.
  • 보기·정렬 유지: 다운로드, 문서 폴더의 보기·정렬 설정이 유지됩니다.
  • 이름 바꾸기 음성 입력, 홈 화면 실행 속도 개선도 포함됩니다.

검색, 보안, 기타

  • Windows 검색: 열지 않고 결과 미리 보기, 오타·부분 이름으로 앱 찾기, 결과 종류(앱·설정·파일·웹) 표시가 개선됐습니다.
  • 스마트 앱 컨트롤: 윈도우를 새로 설치하지 않아도 켜고 끌 수 있습니다.
  • 패스키: 지원되는 외부 비밀번호 관리자에 저장된 패스키를 쓸 수 있습니다.
  • 윈도우 업데이트 재시작 감소: 해당되는 업데이트를 월간 보안 업데이트와 함께 설치해 재시작 횟수를 줄입니다.
  • 음성 액세스 한국어 지원: 지원되는 Copilot+ PC에서 자연어 명령과 함께 한국어 등이 추가됐습니다.
  • 작업 관리자 NPU 표시: NPU가 있는 PC에서 NPU 사용률 열을 켤 수 있습니다.

3. 가정용과 기업용, 이 부분은 구분해서 보세요

일부 블로그에서 "26H2부터 설정 백업이 기본으로 켜진다"고 소개하는데, 공식 문서 표현은 조금 다릅니다. Microsoft Learn 문서는 아래 3가지를 상업용(조직) 장치에서 임시 상업용 제어로 막혀 있던 기능을 기본 활성화한 것이라고 설명합니다.

항목 공식 문서 내용 가정용 PC에서
Windows 설정 백업 대상 상업용 장치에서 기본 활성, 관리자 정책은 그대로 존중 직접 설정에서 확인하세요
작업 표시줄 앱별 작업(앱 액션) 상업용 장치에서 기본 활성 이미 월간 업데이트로 들어왔을 수 있음
파일 탐색기 개선 임시 상업용 제어 해제, 기본 활성 이미 월간 업데이트로 들어왔을 수 있음
관리자 보호(Administrator protection) 기본 꺼짐, Intune 또는 그룹 정책으로 켬 일반 사용자가 신경 쓸 일은 거의 없음
내장 Sysmon 기본 꺼짐, 켜야 사용 보안 담당자용 기능

 

정리하면, 가정용 PC에서는 26H2를 설치해도 "갑자기 크게 바뀌는" 느낌이 적을 수 있습니다. 많은 기능이 이미 매월 업데이트로 들어와 있기 때문입니다.

4. 제거된 기능: WMIC

WMIC(Windows Management Instrumentation 명령줄)는 24H2 이상에서 제거됐고, 이제 선택적 기능(FoD)으로도 설치할 수 없습니다. 오래된 배치 파일이나 사내 스크립트에서 wmic 명령을 쓰고 있다면 PowerShell 명령으로 바꿔야 합니다. 대체 명령은 별도 글에서 자세히 정리했습니다.

5. 지금 26H2 설치하는 법

24H2 또는 25H2를 쓰고 있다면 Windows 업데이트에서 직접 받을 수 있습니다. 단계적 배포라 PC마다 표시 시점이 다를 수 있습니다.

  • 1단계: 설정 > 시스템 > 정보에서 현재 버전(24H2/25H2)을 확인합니다. 23H2 이하라면 먼저 최신 버전으로 올려야 합니다.
  • 2단계: 설정 > Windows 업데이트에서 업데이트 확인을 누릅니다.
  • 3단계: "Windows 11, 버전 26H2로 기능 업데이트" 항목이 보이면 다운로드 및 설치를 누릅니다. 항목 이름은 화면에서 확인하세요.
  • 4단계: 설치가 끝나면 재시작하고, 설정 > 시스템 > 정보에서 26H2로 바뀌었는지 확인합니다.

항목이 보이지 않는다면 아직 내 PC 차례가 아닌 것입니다. 무리해서 다른 방법으로 설치하기보다 기다리는 편이 안전합니다. 10월 누적 업데이트(KB5127648) 관련 오류는 따로 정리한 글을 참고하세요.

6. 설치 전 체크리스트

점검 항목 확인 방법 이유
중요 파일 백업 외장 드라이브나 클라우드에 복사 문제 발생 시 복구용
저장 공간 설정 > 시스템 > 저장소 설치 중 공간 부족 방지
알려진 문제 Windows release health 페이지 내 환경에 해당하는 이슈 확인
wmic 사용 스크립트 배치 파일에서 wmic 검색 WMIC 제거로 동작 안 함
VPN·원격 데스크톱 회사 업무용이면 IT 담당자에게 문의 10월 업데이트 관련 이슈가 공지됨
전원 노트북은 전원 연결 설치 중 종료 방지

 

Microsoft release health 페이지에는 10월 기준으로 비관리자 사용자의 원격 데스크톱 연결 오류(0xC000000D) 같은 알려진 문제가 올라와 있습니다. 업무용 PC라면 설치 전에 꼭 확인하세요.

7. 업데이트 전 AI로 PC 점검하는 프롬프트

아래 명령 결과를 복사해 챗GPT, 제미나이, 클로드 같은 AI에 붙여 넣으면 업데이트 전에 확인할 점을 정리해 줍니다. 결과에는 개인 정보가 거의 없지만, 컴퓨터 이름이나 사용자 이름은 지우고 붙여 넣는 것을 권장합니다.

프롬프트 1. 업데이트 준비 상태 점검

너는 윈도우 PC 점검 도우미야. 나는 윈도우11 26H2 기능 업데이트를 설치하려고 해.
아래는 PowerShell에서 실행한 결과야.
[Get-ComputerInfo -Property OsName,OsVersion,OsBuildNumber,WindowsVersion 결과 붙여넣기]
[Get-PSDrive C 결과 붙여넣기]
1. 현재 버전이 활성화 패키지로 26H2를 받을 수 있는 버전(24H2 또는 25H2)인지 알려줘.
2. C 드라이브 여유 공간이 충분한지 판단하고, 부족하면 정리 방법을 알려줘.
3. 설치 전에 내가 해야 할 일을 체크리스트로 5개 이내로 정리해줘.
확실하지 않은 내용은 추측하지 말고 "확인 필요"라고 표시해줘.

프롬프트 2. 오래된 스크립트 WMIC 사용 여부 점검

아래는 내가 쓰는 배치 파일(.bat) 내용이야.
[배치 파일 내용 붙여넣기]
윈도우11 24H2 이상에서는 WMIC가 제거됐어.
1. wmic 명령이 들어간 줄을 모두 찾아줘.
2. 각 줄을 같은 결과를 내는 PowerShell 명령(Get-CimInstance 등)으로 바꿔줘.
3. 바꾼 뒤 테스트하는 방법도 알려줘.

프롬프트 3. 업데이트 후 달라진 점 확인

윈도우11 26H2로 업데이트했어. 가정용 Home 에디션이야.
시작 메뉴, 작업 표시줄, 파일 탐색기, 검색에서 새로 써 볼 만한 기능을 설정 경로와 함께 5개만 알려줘.
메뉴 이름이 정확하지 않을 수 있으면 "화면에서 확인"이라고 덧붙여줘.

8. 자주 묻는 질문 (FAQ)

Q1. 26H2를 꼭 바로 설치해야 하나요?

급할 필요는 없습니다. Home·Pro는 버전마다 지원 기간이 24개월이므로, 쓰고 있는 버전의 지원 종료 전에만 올리면 됩니다. 다만 26H2를 설치하면 지원 기간이 새로 시작된다는 장점이 있습니다.

Q2. 업데이트 항목이 안 보이는데 고장인가요?

아닙니다. Microsoft는 26H2를 단계적으로 배포하고 있어서 PC마다 제공 시점이 다릅니다. 업데이트 확인을 눌러도 보이지 않으면 며칠 뒤 다시 확인하세요.

Q3. 설치 후 문제가 생기면 되돌릴 수 있나요?

기능 업데이트는 일반적으로 설정 > 시스템 > 복구에서 일정 기간 이전 버전으로 되돌릴 수 있습니다. 되돌리기 가능 기간과 메뉴 이름은 PC 화면에서 확인하세요.

Q4. 파일 탐색기 AI 요약은 무료인가요?

공식 문서 기준으로 OneDrive·SharePoint 파일의 Copilot 요약은 Microsoft 365 구독과 Copilot 라이선스가 필요합니다. 모든 PC에서 무료로 쓸 수 있는 기능은 아닙니다.

마무리: 크게 바뀌진 않아도, 지원 기간은 새로 시작됩니다

윈도우11 26H2는 큰 변화보다는 1년 동안 들어온 기능을 정리하고 지원 기간을 새로 여는 업데이트입니다. 백업과 저장 공간만 확인하고, Windows 업데이트에 항목이 보일 때 차분히 설치하시면 됩니다. 설치 전에 위 프롬프트로 한 번 점검해 보세요.

작업 표시줄 앱별 작업(앱 액션)
상업용 장치에서 기본 활성
이미 월간 업데이트로 들어왔을 수 있음


파일 탐색기 개선
임시 상업용 제어 해제, 기본 활성
이미 월간 업데이트로 들어왔을 수 있음


관리자 보호(Administrator protection)
기본 꺼짐, Intune 또는 그룹 정책으로 켬
일반 사용자가 신경 쓸 일은 거의 없음


내장 Sysmon
기본 꺼짐, 켜야 사용
보안 담당자용 기능



 
정리하면, 가정용 PC에서는 26H2를 설치해도 "갑자기 크게 바뀌는" 느낌이 적을 수 있습니다. 많은 기능이 이미 매월 업데이트로 들어와 있기 때문입니다.
4. 제거된 기능: WMIC
WMIC(Windows Management Instrumentation 명령줄)는 24H2 이상에서 제거됐고, 이제 선택적 기능(FoD)으로도 설치할 수 없습니다. 오래된 배치 파일이나 사내 스크립트에서 wmic 명령을 쓰고 있다면 PowerShell 명령으로 바꿔야 합니다. 대체 명령은 별도 글에서 자세히 정리했습니다.
5. 지금 26H2 설치하는 법
24H2 또는 25H2를 쓰고 있다면 Windows 업데이트에서 직접 받을 수 있습니다. 단계적 배포라 PC마다 표시 시점이 다를 수 있습니다.
1단계: 설정 > 시스템 > 정보에서 현재 버전(24H2/25H2)을 확인합니다. 23H2 이하라면 먼저 최신 버전으로 올려야 합니다.
2단계: 설정 > Windows 업데이트에서 업데이트 확인을 누릅니다.
3단계: "Windows 11, 버전 26H2로 기능 업데이트" 항목이 보이면 다운로드 및 설치를 누릅니다. 항목 이름은 화면에서 확인하세요.
4단계: 설치가 끝나면 재시작하고, 설정 > 시스템 > 정보에서 26H2로 바뀌었는지 확인합니다.
항목이 보이지 않는다면 아직 내 PC 차례가 아닌 것입니다. 무리해서 다른 방법으로 설치하기보다 기다리는 편이 안전합니다. 10월 누적 업데이트(KB5127648) 관련 오류는 따로 정리한 글을 참고하세요.


6. 설치 전 체크리스트
점검 항목
확인 방법
이유


중요 파일 백업
외장 드라이브나 클라우드에 복사
문제 발생 시 복구용


저장 공간
설정 > 시스템 > 저장소
설치 중 공간 부족 방지


알려진 문제
Windows release health 페이지
내 환경에 해당하는 이슈 확인


wmic 사용 스크립트
배치 파일에서 wmic 검색
WMIC 제거로 동작 안 함


VPN·원격 데스크톱
회사 업무용이면 IT 담당자에게 문의
10월 업데이트 관련 이슈가 공지됨


전원
노트북은 전원 연결
설치 중 종료 방지



 
Microsoft release health 페이지에는 10월 기준으로 비관리자 사용자의 원격 데스크톱 연결 오류(0xC000000D) 같은 알려진 문제가 올라와 있습니다. 업무용 PC라면 설치 전에 꼭 확인하세요.
7. 업데이트 전 AI로 PC 점검하는 프롬프트
아래 명령 결과를 복사해 챗GPT, 제미나이, 클로드 같은 AI에 붙여 넣으면 업데이트 전에 확인할 점을 정리해 줍니다. 결과에는 개인 정보가 거의 없지만, 컴퓨터 이름이나 사용자 이름은 지우고 붙여 넣는 것을 권장합니다.
프롬프트 1. 업데이트 준비 상태 점검
너는 윈도우 PC 점검 도우미야. 나는 윈도우11 26H2 기능 업데이트를 설치하려고 해.
아래는 PowerShell에서 실행한 결과야.
[Get-ComputerInfo -Property OsName,OsVersion,OsBuildNumber,WindowsVersion 결과 붙여넣기]
[Get-PSDrive C 결과 붙여넣기]
1. 현재 버전이 활성화 패키지로 26H2를 받을 수 있는 버전(24H2 또는 25H2)인지 알려줘.
2. C 드라이브 여유 공간이 충분한지 판단하고, 부족하면 정리 방법을 알려줘.
3. 설치 전에 내가 해야 할 일을 체크리스트로 5개 이내로 정리해줘.
확실하지 않은 내용은 추측하지 말고 "확인 필요"라고 표시해줘.
프롬프트 2. 오래된 스크립트 WMIC 사용 여부 점검
아래는 내가 쓰는 배치 파일(.bat) 내용이야.
[배치 파일 내용 붙여넣기]
윈도우11 24H2 이상에서는 WMIC가 제거됐어.
1. wmic 명령이 들어간 줄을 모두 찾아줘.
2. 각 줄을 같은 결과를 내는 PowerShell 명령(Get-CimInstance 등)으로 바꿔줘.
3. 바꾼 뒤 테스트하는 방법도 알려줘.
프롬프트 3. 업데이트 후 달라진 점 확인
윈도우11 26H2로 업데이트했어. 가정용 Home 에디션이야.
시작 메뉴, 작업 표시줄, 파일 탐색기, 검색에서 새로 써 볼 만한 기능을 설정 경로와 함께 5개만 알려줘.
메뉴 이름이 정확하지 않을 수 있으면 "화면에서 확인"이라고 덧붙여줘.


8. 자주 묻는 질문 (FAQ)
Q1. 26H2를 꼭 바로 설치해야 하나요?
급할 필요는 없습니다. Home·Pro는 버전마다 지원 기간이 24개월이므로, 쓰고 있는 버전의 지원 종료 전에만 올리면 됩니다. 다만 26H2를 설치하면 지원 기간이 새로 시작된다는 장점이 있습니다.
Q2. 업데이트 항목이 안 보이는데 고장인가요?
아닙니다. Microsoft는 26H2를 단계적으로 배포하고 있어서 PC마다 제공 시점이 다릅니다. 업데이트 확인을 눌러도 보이지 않으면 며칠 뒤 다시 확인하세요.
Q3. 설치 후 문제가 생기면 되돌릴 수 있나요?
기능 업데이트는 일반적으로 설정 > 시스템 > 복구에서 일정 기간 이전 버전으로 되돌릴 수 있습니다. 되돌리기 가능 기간과 메뉴 이름은 PC 화면에서 확인하세요.
Q4. 파일 탐색기 AI 요약은 무료인가요?
공식 문서 기준으로 OneDrive·SharePoint 파일의 Copilot 요약은 Microsoft 365 구독과 Copilot 라이선스가 필요합니다. 모든 PC에서 무료로 쓸 수 있는 기능은 아닙니다.
마무리: 크게 바뀌진 않아도, 지원 기간은 새로 시작됩니다
윈도우11 26H2는 큰 변화보다는 1년 동안 들어온 기능을 정리하고 지원 기간을 새로 여는 업데이트입니다. 백업과 저장 공간만 확인하고, Windows 업데이트에 항목이 보일 때 차분히 설치하시면 됩니다. 설치 전에 위 프롬프트로 한 번 점검해 보세요.

posts.title: RTX 스파크 노트북 비교: 델 XPS 16 vs 레노버 요가 프로 9n vs ASUS 프로아트 P16·P14 (가격·무게·화면 정리)
posts.author: 어떤오후의 프리웨어 이야기
posts.content:
엔비디아가 처음 내놓은 노트북용 슈퍼칩 RTX 스파크를 넣은 노트북이 10월 중순부터 국내에서 판매되기 시작했습니다. 같은 칩을 쓰는데도 제조사마다 화면, 무게, 가격이 꽤 다릅니다. 이 글에서는 국내 출시가 확인된 델 XPS 16 크리에이터 에디션, 레노버 요가 프로 9n, ASUS 프로아트 P16·P14를 공식 보도자료와 제조사 페이지 기준으로 비교하고, 구매 전에 AI에게 물어보면 좋은 프롬프트도 함께 정리했습니다.

이 글의 핵심 요약
1. 세 제품 모두 같은 RTX 스파크 칩(최대 20코어 CPU, 최대 6,144코어 블랙웰 GPU, 최대 128GB 통합 메모리)을 씁니다.
2. 가장 가벼운 쪽은 ASUS 프로아트 P14(약 1.48kg), 화면이 가장 밝은 쪽은 프로아트 P16(최대 1,600니트)입니다.
3. 국내 가격은 레노버 요가 프로 9n만 공식 공개(64GB 모델 674만 9,000원부터)됐고, 델은 출시 당시 국내 가격을 공개하지 않았습니다.
4. 메모리 용량이 로컬 AI 활용 범위를 좌우하므로, 쓰려는 AI 모델 크기부터 정하고 고르는 것이 좋습니다.

1. RTX 스파크가 뭐길래 다들 이 칩을 넣었을까

RTX 스파크는 엔비디아의 Arm 기반 그레이스 CPU와 블랙웰 RTX GPU, 통합 메모리를 하나의 칩에 묶은 윈도우 PC용 플랫폼입니다. 보도에 따르면 GPU는 쿠다 코어 6,144개를 갖췄고, AI 연산 성능은 FP4 기준 1페타플롭스, 전체 소비전력은 80W 수준입니다.

가장 큰 차이는 CPU와 GPU가 최대 128GB 메모리를 함께 쓴다는 점입니다. 일반 게이밍 노트북은 그래픽 메모리 용량이 작아 큰 AI 모델을 통째로 올리기 어려운데, 통합 메모리 구조에서는 더 큰 모델을 노트북에서 직접 돌릴 수 있습니다. 엔비디아 관계자는 국내 출시 행사에서 RTX 스파크 노트북 가격이 약 470만 원부터 시작해 사양에 따라 최대 1,000만 원까지 올라간다고 밝혔고, 그 이유로 메모리 가격 상승을 꼽았습니다.

이미지 출처: 델 테크놀로지스 (베타뉴스 보도 사진)

2. 세 제품 스펙 한눈에 비교

아래 표는 각 제조사 보도자료와 공식 페이지에 나온 수치만 옮겼습니다. 같은 모델이라도 메모리·저장공간·화면 구성에 따라 무게와 가격이 달라지니, 구매 직전에 판매 페이지의 세부 사양을 꼭 확인하세요.

항목 델 XPS 16 크리에이터 에디션 레노버 요가 프로 9n ASUS 프로아트 P16 / P14
국내 출시 10월 16일 10월 19일 10월 16일
화면 16형 3.2K 탠덤 OLED, 최대 1,000니트, DCI-P3 100% 15형 OLED, 최대 1,100니트, 165Hz P16: 최대 4K OLED, 최대 1,600니트 / P14: 최대 3K OLED, 최대 1,100니트 (HDR 피크)
무게 최소 2.02kg (델 코리아 페이지 기준) 약 1.65kg P16 약 1.77kg / P14 약 1.48kg
두께 17.8mm 16.7mm P16 12.9mm / P14 13.9mm
배터리 공식 수치 확인 필요 92.5Wh P16 최대 99.9Wh / P14 90Wh
국내 가격 출시 당시 미공개 (미국 3,799.99달러부터) 64GB 모델 674만 9,000원부터 국내 공식가 확인 필요 (미국 2,599.99달러부터)

 

표에서 보듯 휴대성은 ASUS 프로아트 P14, 화면 밝기는 프로아트 P16, 국내 가격 정보가 명확한 쪽은 요가 프로 9n입니다. 델 XPS 16 크리에이터 에디션은 출고 전 색 보정을 거친 탠덤 OLED와 XPS 특유의 CNC 알루미늄 디자인이 강점이지만, 무게는 세 제품 중 가장 무겁습니다.

3. 제품별로 보면: 누구에게 맞을까

델 XPS 16 크리에이터 에디션

XPS 제품군 중 처음으로 RTX 스파크를 넣은 모델입니다. 델은 4K·8K 영상 편집, 3D 렌더링, 로컬 AI 모델 개발과 추론을 주요 용도로 소개했고, 깃허브 코파일럿, 클로드 코드, 컴피UI, 커서 같은 개발 도구를 기기에서 쓸 수 있다고 밝혔습니다. 색 정확도가 중요한 영상·사진 작업자, 책상 위에서 주로 쓰는 개발자에게 어울립니다.

레노버 요가 프로 9n

이미지 출처: 한국레노버 (뉴스와이어 보도자료)

레노버의 첫 RTX 스파크 노트북으로, 최대 80W TDP를 지원하는 냉각 시스템 '레노버 X 파워'와 15형 165Hz OLED를 갖췄습니다. 햅틱 포스패드를 드로잉 패드로 쓸 수 있고 와콤 AES 3.0 기반 요가 펜 2세대를 지원해 펜 입력이 필요한 크리에이터에게 장점이 있습니다. USB-A, USB4, HDMI 2.1, SD 카드 리더까지 갖춰 동글 없이 쓰기 좋습니다. 레노버는 출시 기념으로 우발적 손상 보장(ADP)과 프리미엄 케어 서비스를 각 2년 지원한다고 밝혔습니다.

ASUS 프로아트 P16·P14

이미지 출처: 에이수스 (IT 인벤 보도 사진)

두 모델 모두 ASUS 루미나 프로 OLED 터치 화면(120Hz, Delta E 1 미만)을 쓰고, 미 국방성 밀스펙(MIL-STD) 테스트를 완료했다고 에이수스는 밝혔습니다. 생성형 이미지 앱 뮤즈트리, 미디어 정리 앱 스토리큐브, 컴피UI 연동 등 로컬 생성형 AI 앱을 기본으로 묶어 준다는 점이 특징입니다. 자주 들고 다니면 P14, 큰 화면과 밝기가 중요하면 P16이 맞습니다.

4. 구매 전에 꼭 확인할 3가지

  • 메모리 용량: RTX 스파크 노트북은 메모리를 나중에 늘리기 어렵습니다. 돌리고 싶은 AI 모델 크기를 먼저 정하고 그에 맞춰 고르세요. 보도에 따르면 128GB 구성에서는 70B급 개방형 모델 구동이 가능하다고 소개됐습니다.
  • Arm 윈도우 호환성: RTX 스파크의 CPU는 Arm 기반입니다. x86용 프로그램은 윈도우의 프리즘 에뮬레이션으로 실행되므로, 꼭 써야 하는 업무용 프로그램·게임 안티치트·주변기기 드라이버가 Arm 윈도우를 지원하는지 확인하세요.
  • 실제 판매가: 같은 모델명이라도 메모리·SSD·화면 구성별로 가격 차이가 큽니다. 공식 판매처와 가격비교 사이트의 세부 모델명을 맞춰 보고 결정하세요.

6. 자주 묻는 질문 (FAQ)

Q1. RTX 스파크 노트북으로 게임도 할 수 있나요?

엔비디아는 최신 AAA급 게임을 2560×1440 해상도에서 초당 100프레임 이상으로 구동할 수 있다고 설명했습니다. 다만 Arm 윈도우 환경이라 게임별 안티치트 지원 여부는 따로 확인해야 합니다.

Q2. 메모리는 얼마짜리를 사야 하나요?

문서 작업과 클라우드 AI 위주라면 낮은 구성으로도 충분하지만, 큰 로컬 AI 모델을 돌리려면 64GB 이상이 유리합니다. 위의 프롬프트 1로 내 작업 기준 필요 용량을 먼저 계산해 보세요.

Q4. 기존 인텔·AMD 노트북 대신 꼭 RTX 스파크여야 하나요?

로컬에서 큰 AI 모델을 돌리거나 GPU 가속 창작 작업을 많이 한다면 장점이 크지만, 사무 작업 위주라면 가격 대비 이점이 작습니다. Arm 호환성까지 고려해 용도부터 정하는 것이 좋습니다.

마무리: 같은 칩, 다른 노트북. 용도와 메모리부터 정하세요

엔비디아가 처음 내놓은 노트북용 슈퍼칩 RTX 스파크를 넣은 노트북이 10월 중순부터 국내에서 판매되기 시작했습니다. 같은 칩을 쓰는데도 제조사마다 화면, 무게, 가격이 꽤 다릅니다. 이 글에서는 국내 출시가 확인된 델 XPS 16 크리에이터 에디션, 레노버 요가 프로 9n, ASUS 프로아트 P16·P14를 공식 보도자료와 제조사 페이지 기준으로 비교하고, 구매 전에 AI에게 물어보면 좋은 프롬프트도 함께 정리했습니다.

1. 세 제품 모두 같은 RTX 스파크 칩(최대 20코어 CPU, 최대 6,144코어 블랙웰 GPU, 최대 128GB 통합 메모리)을 씁니다.

3. 국내 가격은 레노버 요가 프로 9n만 공식 공개(64GB 모델 674만 9,000원부터)됐고, 델은 출시 당시 국내 가격을 공개하지 않았습니다.

1. RTX 스파크가 뭐길래 다들 이 칩을 넣었을까
RTX 스파크는 엔비디아의 Arm 기반 그레이스 CPU와 블랙웰 RTX GPU, 통합 메모리를 하나의 칩에 묶은 윈도우 PC용 플랫폼입니다. 보도에 따르면 GPU는 쿠다 코어 6,144개를 갖췄고, AI 연산 성능은 FP4 기준 1페타플롭스, 전체 소비전력은 80W 수준입니다.
가장 큰 차이는 CPU와 GPU가 최대 128GB 메모리를 함께 쓴다는 점입니다. 일반 게이밍 노트북은 그래픽 메모리 용량이 작아 큰 AI 모델을 통째로 올리기 어려운데, 통합 메모리 구조에서는 더 큰 모델을 노트북에서 직접 돌릴 수 있습니다. 엔비디아 관계자는 국내 출시 행사에서 RTX 스파크 노트북 가격이 약 470만 원부터 시작해 사양에 따라 최대 1,000만 원까지 올라간다고 밝혔고, 그 이유로 메모리 가격 상승을 꼽았습니다.

각 제품의 장단점을 내 조건 기준으로 점수화해서 표로 비교하고, 최종 추천 1개와 그 이유를 3줄로 정리해 줘.
6. 자주 묻는 질문 (FAQ)
Q1. RTX 스파크 노트북으로 게임도 할 수 있나요?
엔비디아는 최신 AAA급 게임을 2560×1440 해상도에서 초당 100프레임 이상으로 구동할 수 있다고 설명했습니다. 다만 Arm 윈도우 환경이라 게임별 안티치트 지원 여부는 따로 확인해야 합니다.
Q2. 메모리는 얼마짜리를 사야 하나요?
문서 작업과 클라우드 AI 위주라면 낮은 구성으로도 충분하지만, 큰 로컬 AI 모델을 돌리려면 64GB 이상이 유리합니다. 위의 프롬프트 1로 내 작업 기준 필요 용량을 먼저 계산해 보세요.
Q3. 델 XPS 16 크리에이터 에디션 국내 가격은 얼마인가요?
출시 보도 당시 델은 국내 가격을 공개하지 않았고, 미국 가격은 3,799.99달러부터였습니다. 국내 판매가는 델 코리아 공식 판매 페이지에서 확인하세요.
Q4. 기존 인텔·AMD 노트북 대신 꼭 RTX 스파크여야 하나요?
로컬에서 큰 AI 모델을 돌리거나 GPU 가속 창작 작업을 많이 한다면 장점이 크지만, 사무 작업 위주라면 가격 대비 이점이 작습니다. Arm 호환성까지 고려해 용도부터 정하는 것이 좋습니다.
마무리: 같은 칩, 다른 노트북. 용도와 메모리부터 정하세요
RTX 스파크 노트북 3종은 같은 칩을 쓰지만 화면, 무게, 펜 지원, 기본 앱 구성이 다릅니다. 가볍게 들고 다니려면 프로아트 P14, 밝고 큰 화면은 프로아트 P16, 펜과 포트 구성은 요가 프로 9n, 색 보정된 탠덤 OLED와 XPS 디자인은 델 XPS 16 크리에이터 에디션이 강점입니다. 위 프롬프트로 내 작업에 필요한 메모리와 호환성부터 점검한 뒤 결정하시길 바랍니다.
